title: Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback
section: The three rules: step, covered or uncovered, climb
text:
The three rules: step, covered or uncovered, climb
Every zone play, inside or outside, runs on the same three rules. Learn these and you can draw a zone play against any front.
Rule 1: everyone steps play-side. At the snap, all five linemen (and the tight ends) take their first step toward the side the play is going. On a broadcast this is the single clearest tell of a zone run: the whole line moves the same direction together. On a gap run, by contrast, linemen block in different directions and at least one usually pulls.
Rule 2: covered or uncovered decides your job. You met these words in 03-01; here is how zone teams count them. A lineman is covered if a defensive lineman is head-up on him or shaded to his play-side, that is, sitting in the gap he is stepping into. He blocks that man. A defender shaded to a lineman’s backside belongs to the neighbor on that side, not to him. A lineman with nobody head-up or play-side of him is uncovered. He does not stand around: his first step is still play-side, but his hands go to the defender in the gap on his backside, the man his covered neighbor is blocking, while his eyes find the linebacker behind that defender. Coaches count this in slightly different ways (some staffs call a lineman covered whenever anyone is shaded on him), but the pairs and the jobs come out the same.1
Rule 3: double-team to the second level. That help is the heart of zone blocking. When a covered and an uncovered lineman both have hands on the same defensive lineman, they form a combo block (a double team). Two men move one defensive lineman, and while they do it both keep their eyes on the linebacker behind him. When the linebacker commits to a gap, one of the two linemen comes off the double team and “climbs” to block him, leaving the other to finish the defensive lineman alone. The double team gets you movement; the climb gets you the second level (the linebackers).
Which of the two climbs? Usually the uncovered man, the one who started with his eyes on the linebacker; the covered man’s job is the defensive lineman, and he finishes him. When the climber leaves varies by coach: in one survey of line coaches, the largest group taught linemen to come off as soon as they saw the linebacker run over the top of the double team or underneath it.2 Come off too early and the defensive lineman splits the double team; too late and the linebacker is already in the hole.
Edge cases. Three situations the rules seem not to cover come up in this chapter’s pictures and drills:

Two uncovered linemen side by side. An uncovered lineman helps the covered man on his backside. If his backside neighbor is uncovered too, there is nobody to help, so he skips the double team and climbs straight to the nearest linebacker.
The last man on the play side, with a defender outside him (a tight end with an end lined up on his outside shoulder). He is covered, and there is no play-side neighbor to help him, so he has to block that man alone. That is the hardest block in zone, and it changes where the play hits.
The last man on the backside, with a defender outside him. Nobody needs to reach a backside defender; the job on the backside is to stop chasers. So the last backside blocker steps inside and protects the gap inside him (coaches call it hinging, swinging shut like a door), and the man outside him is left to the quarterback’s fake or read. That outside man is the “unblocked backside end” you will meet again and again.

The front in the next few pictures is a common four-man even front: four defensive linemen, none of them head-up on the center. Its name and its variations belong to the defense’s side of the book, in 05-02; here it is just a front to practise on.


Show the Python
off = [q for q in named_line(offense("singleback")) if q.key in OL_NAMES or q.key == "Y"]
p = Play(off, front7(+1), los=35, to_go=None, title="Zone rules: who is covered? (play going right)")
cov = {"LT": "covered", "LG": "uncovered", "C": "covered", "RG": "uncovered", "RT": "covered",
       "Y": "uncovered"}
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-8, 8.5), window=(-4.6, 8.8))
play_arrow(fld, p, 6.4, -4.5, 4.5, "first step: everyone goes right")
for k, v in cov.items():
    d = -1.9 if k in ("LT", "C", "RT") else -2.9
    say(fld, p, d, p.players[k].w, v, fontsize=7.5,
        color=style.DEFENSE_DARK if v == "covered" else ZONE_GREEN)
for (dw, tgt, txt) in [((2.6, -5.6), "BT", "in LT's\nplay-side gap"), ((2.6, -0.9), "PT", "in C's\nplay-side gap"),
                       ((2.6, 7.0), "PE", "in RT's\nplay-side gap")]:
    t = p.players[tgt]
    point_to(fld, p, dw, (t.d, t.w), txt, fontsize=6.6)
plt.show()








Figure 4.1: The zone rules against an even front, play going right. A lineman is covered if a defender is head-up on him or in the gap he is stepping into. The 3-technique lines up on the LG’s outside shoulder, but that is the LG’s backside, so the 3 belongs to the LT. Each uncovered lineman will help the covered man on his backside and look for a linebacker.





Work through Figure 4.1 from left to right, play going right. The left tackle’s play-side gap is the B gap between him and the left guard, and the 3-technique sits in it: the LT is covered. The left guard has nobody head-up on him and nobody in his play-side gap (the A gap to his right): he is uncovered, so he helps the LT on the 3-technique and looks for the Will linebacker. The center has the 1-technique in his play-side gap: covered. The right guard is uncovered, so he helps the center and looks for the Mike. The right tackle has the 5-technique in his play-side gap: covered. The tight end is uncovered, so he helps the right tackle on the 5-technique and looks for the Sam.
Two things are worth noticing. First, the rules found three natural double teams (LT and LG on the 3, C and RG on the 1, RT and Y on the 5) without the coach drawing them; a different front would produce different pairs from the same rules, which is exactly the point. Line coaches give these pairs short code names so two linemen can tell each other “we’re together on this one” before the snap; the names vary by staff. Second, the defender who lines up farthest from the play on the backside, the left 5-technique, is not on anyone’s list. Zone plays almost always leave someone unblocked on the backside. Much of this chapter is about how the offense deals with him.
Who decides all this? Before every snap the center usually identifies the front out loud and makes a “Mike” call: he points out one linebacker and names him the Mike for this play, so all five linemen count defenders from the same starting point and nobody disagrees about which linebacker is whose (how lines use that call in pass protection is in 04-02). The linemen then confirm their pairs with one-word calls. When a pair gets it wrong, two linemen block the same man, or nobody blocks one, and you see a defender in the backfield untouched at the snap.






CautionCommon misconception



“Zone linemen just block whoever is in front of them.” Not quite. A lineman whose man is directly in front of him but shaded to the backside is uncovered under zone rules, because what matters is the gap he is stepping into. That is why two linemen facing the same front can get different jobs depending on which way the play goes, and why zone teams spend hours of practice on “who’s covered?” against every front they might see.



The payoff: movement gets picked up
Now the claim this chapter opened with, in one picture. In Figure 4.2 the defense runs a simple pressure at the snap: the 1-technique slants from the center’s right shoulder into the gap on his left, and the Mike linebacker blitzes into the gap the 1-technique just left. On the left, the run is blocked by name: the center was told “block the 1,” the right guard “block the Mike.” On the right, the same run is blocked by zone rules.


Show the Python
def movement_play(zone):
    off = [q for q in named_line(offense("singleback")) if q.key in OL_NAMES or q.key in ("Y", "QB", "RB")]
    p = Play(off, front7(+1), los=35, to_go=None)
    go_to(p, "PT", (0.9, -0.8), "path", speed=2.2)                   # the 1 slants into the left A gap
    for k in ("LT", "RT", "Y"):
        go_to(p, k, (-0.3, p.players[k].w + 0.5), speed=1.5)         # everyone else: a step right
    if zone:
        go_to(p, "MIKE", (0.95, 0.8), "path", speed=5.0)             # the Mike blitzes the right A gap ...
        go_to(p, "LG", (0.05, -0.8), speed=2.0, via=[(-0.5, -1.2)])  # LG: the 1 came into his gap
        go_to(p, "C", (0.05, 0.75), speed=2.0, via=[(-0.5, 0.35)])   # C: the Mike came into his gap
        go_to(p, "RG", (2.6, 2.4), speed=3.0, via=[(-0.4, 2.0)])     # RG: nobody came, so he climbs
    else:
        go_to(p, "MIKE", (-2.0, 0.9), "path", speed=6.0)             # ... and runs through untouched
        go_to(p, "C", (0.1, -0.55), speed=2.0, via=[(-0.4, -0.1)])   # C chases "his" man left, late
        go_to(p, "RG", (3.2, 1.9), speed=3.6, via=[(-0.2, 1.8)])     # RG climbs to the Mike's old spot
        go_to(p, "LG", (2.6, -2.4), speed=3.0, via=[(-0.3, -1.6)])   # LG goes to the Will as drawn
    return p


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.6))
for ax, zone, ttl in [(axes[0], False, "Blocked by name"), (axes[1], True, "Blocked by zone rules")]:
    p = movement_play(zone)
    f = panel(ax, p, tracking(p), 1.05, lateral=(-6.0, 6.0), window=(-4.5, 6.5),
              rings=(("PT", style.DEFENSE), ("MIKE", style.DEFENSE)))
    if zone:
        point_to(f, p, (-3.2, -3.6), (0.05, -0.8), "LG: the 1 came\ninto my gap", color=ZONE_GREEN, fontsize=6.8)
        point_to(f, p, (-3.2, 3.4), (0.05, 0.75), "C: the Mike came\ninto my gap", color=ZONE_GREEN, fontsize=6.8)
        point_to(f, p, (4.6, 4.4), (2.6, 2.4), "RG: nobody came,\nso he climbs", fontsize=6.8)
    else:
        point_to(f, p, (-3.4, 3.6), (-2.0, 0.9), "Mike: unblocked", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
        point_to(f, p, (-3.2, -3.6), (0.1, -0.55), "C chases\n\"his\" man", fontsize=6.8)
        point_to(f, p, (5.0, 4.0), (3.2, 1.9), "RG: to where the\nMike used to be", fontsize=6.8)
    ax.set_title(ttl + " (1 second after the snap)", fontsize=8.5, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 4.2: Why zone exists. The same defensive movement against two blocking plans, play going right, one second after the snap (faint lines are where each player came from; the two moving defenders are ringed). The 1-technique slants left and the Mike blitzes the gap he left. Left, blocking by name: the center chases his man across the formation, the right guard climbs to where the Mike used to be, and the Mike runs through untouched. Right, zone rules: every lineman steps right and blocks whoever enters his play-side gap, so the left guard picks up the slanting 1 and the center picks up the blitzing Mike.





The zone line did not guess the pressure; it did not have to. Each lineman’s question (“who enters my play-side gap?”) is answered after the snap, so whatever arrives gets blocked. One coaching manual describes exactly this case: when the defensive lineman slants into the uncovered lineman’s gap, the uncovered man simply takes him.3 That is the promise zone makes. It is not a promise to win every block, as you will see when the movement goes with the line instead of against it.

title: Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback
text:
Inside zone: the downhill version
Inside zone is the zone play that attacks the middle of the line. The linemen take short, firm steps play-side (more forward than sideways), the double teams try to drive the defensive linemen backward, and the running back aims between the guard and tackle.
That target has a name. The aiming point is the spot the running back’s first steps point at. On inside zone it is usually the play-side guard’s outside hip, the B gap (some teams teach the A gap; it varies with the team and with whether the quarterback is under center or in the shotgun). The aiming point is not necessarily where the back will end up. It is where he starts, so that the defense has to respect the play-side gaps and the back can read the blocks from there.


Show the Python
off = named_line(offense("singleback"))
p = Play(off, even_front(+1), los=35, to_go=10, title="Inside zone right vs an even front")
p.block("C", pts=[(0.9, 0.5)])                        # C on the 1 ...
p.block("RG", pts=[(0.8, -0.8), (4.3, -0.4)])         # ... RG helps, then climbs to the Mike
p.block("LT", pts=[(0.9, 0.7)])                       # LT on the 3 ...
p.block("LG", pts=[(0.8, -0.6), (4.3, -0.8)])         # ... LG helps, then climbs to the Will
p.block("RT", pts=[(0.9, 0.6)])                       # RT on the 5 ...
p.block("Y", pts=[(0.6, -0.6), (3.6, 1.5)])           # ... Y helps, then climbs to the Sam
p.path("QB", [(-0.6, 0.6), (-1.9, 0.9)], speed=3.0)   # open and hand off ...
p.path("QB", [(-2.6, -5.5)], speed=4.0, delay=0.2)    # ... then fake a bootleg the other way
p.run("RB", [(3.0, 1.8), (7.0, 2.4), (13.0, 2.6)])
p.handoff("RB", t=0.75)
p.highlight("RB"); p.highlight("BE", color=style.DEFENSE)
fld = draw(p, width_in=6.2, lateral=(-12, 12), window=(-8, 13))
for d, w, wd in [(0.15, -2.4, 3.7), (0.15, 0.8, 3.7), (0.15, 4.0, 3.5)]:
    pair_oval(fld, p, d, w, wd, 3.2)
spot(fld, p, -1.7, 2.25)
say(fld, p, -3.0, 6.4, "aiming point:\nplay-side B gap", color=ZONE_GREEN, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, 3.0, -8.4, "unblocked: the QB's\nfake tries to hold him", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, -4.2, -8.6, "QB: hand off,\nthen fake a boot", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, 8.0, -0.6, "double teams;\none man climbs to a LB", fontsize=7)
plt.show()








Figure 4.3: Inside zone right against the even front. The three green ovals are the double teams the rules produced (LT and LG on the 3, C and RG on the 1, RT and Y on the 5); in each, the uncovered man climbs to a linebacker (the T-bars at W, M and S). The back aims for the play-side B gap (green X). The left 5-technique (ringed) is unblocked. H is a slot receiver on the left, too wide to block that end; the wide receivers X and Z are outside the picture.





Why build a run this way? Because the double teams are where inside zone wins. Two 300-pound men on one defensive lineman can move him, and moving the defensive tackles off the line of scrimmage is what opens everything else. The linebackers then face an impossible choice. If a linebacker fills the play-side B gap early, the climbing lineman meets him there and walls him toward the sideline, and the back cuts just inside that block, into the gap the linebacker left. If he waits, the double team is still moving his teammate backward and the back gets downhill before anyone arrives.
What about the unblocked backside end? Count the box in Figure 4.3: six blockers (five linemen and the tight end) against seven defenders. One defender is always left over, and inside zone chooses the one with the longest way to go to the ball: the end farthest from the play. That does not make him harmless. If he simply chases down the line, he can tackle a back who cuts back toward him. After the handoff the quarterback fakes a bootleg (a rollout the other way, which you will meet properly near the end of the chapter) to make him hesitate; that is the only help plain inside zone gives against him. The H standing on that side in the picture is a slot receiver, too far out to block him. Later sections show the ways teams deal with him: a second tight end to block him (the U in the two-tight-end pictures), a crossing tight end to kick him out (split zone), or the quarterback reading him and keeping the ball, the zone read of 03-04.
What inside zone gives up: it is a grind-it-out play. It needs linemen strong enough to move a defensive tackle with help, and when the defense wins those double teams (a big, penetrating defensive tackle who splits the double team) the play dies in the backfield. Its average gain is modest; its virtue is that it is hard to make go badly, and it sets up everything else.

title: Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback
section: Outside zone: get the defense running sideways
text:
Outside zone: get the defense running sideways
Outside zone, also called wide zone, has the same rules and a different intent. Inside zone wants to move the defense backward; outside zone wants to move it sideways. The linemen take a lateral first step (some coaches teach a “bucket step,” opening the hips and stepping slightly back to gain width) and run, trying to get their heads across the play-side shoulder of the defender in front of them. “Head across” is literal, and it is the whole idea of outside zone: a blocker whose helmet and shoulders are on the play-side of a defender is standing between that defender and the ball, so the defender can only go inside, away from where the back is heading. A blocker whose head ends up on the inside has only got in the defender’s way; the defender can still run around him toward the ball. The running back’s aiming point moves out to the outside leg of the tight end (or of the tackle, if there is no tight end on that side).
That difference is the one you can see from the stands, and Figure 4.4 puts the two side by side.


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.1))
for ax, (ttl, step, track, aim, note) in zip(axes, [
        ("Inside zone: steps go up", (1.6, 0.7), [(-4.0, 1.8), (-1.0, 2.4)], (0.0, 2.4), "aims at the\nB gap"),
        ("Outside zone: steps go across", (0.5, 1.5), [(-4.3, 2.6), (-1.4, 5.1)], (-0.2, 5.5), "aims at the\nY's outside leg")]):
    off = [q for q in ace_condensed() if q.key not in ("X", "Z")]
    p = Play(off, None, los=35, to_go=None)
    go_to(p, "RB", track[-1], "run", via=track[:-1])
    p.highlight("RB")
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-7.5, 9.5), window=(-8, 3.8), title=False)
    for k in ("U", "LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT", "Y"):         # each lineman's first step, exaggerated
        q = p.players[k]
        (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = _P(f, p, 0.15, q.w), _P(f, p, 0.15 + step[0], q.w + step[1])
        ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((float(x0), float(y0)), (float(x1), float(y1)), arrowstyle="-|>",
                                     mutation_scale=9, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.6, zorder=6))
    spot(f, p, *aim)
    say(f, p, -3.2, 6.4 if aim[1] < 3 else 7.6, note, color=ZONE_GREEN, fontsize=7)
    say(f, p, 2.9, -5.0, "first step", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 4.4: How to tell them apart in the first half-second. Inside zone (left): short, forward steps, and the back’s first steps point at the guard-tackle gap. Outside zone (right): flat, sideways steps, the whole line drifting toward one sideline, and the back running at the tight end’s outside leg. On the broadcast camera, watch the linemen’s helmets: up, or across.





Now look at all eleven jobs on outside zone in Figure 4.5 before watching the play move.


Show the Python
def oz_play():
    """Outside zone right, simulated for the frame strip and video."""
    p = Play(ace_condensed(), even_front(+1, cb_w=10.0), los=35, to_go=10)
    # the defense reacts: the play-side end fights to stay outside, linebackers flow
    go_to(p, "PE", (1.4, 6.5), "path", speed=2.0)
    go_to(p, "PT", (1.45, 1.55), "path", speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "BT", (1.2, -1.6), "path", speed=1.4)
    go_to(p, "BE", (1.0, -3.0), "path", speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "SAM", (3.6, 8.1), "path", speed=2.0)
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (3.1, 2.6), "path", speed=2.0, delay=0.3)
    go_to(p, "WILL", (3.4, 0.9), "path", speed=2.6, delay=0.2)
    go_to(p, "FS", (9.0, -2.5), "path", speed=4.0, delay=0.4)
    go_to(p, "SS", (7.5, 7.0), "path", speed=4.0, delay=0.4)
    go_to(p, "LCB", (12.0, -10.0), "path", speed=5.0)
    go_to(p, "RCB", (5.4, 9.6), "path", speed=1.5)
    go_to(p, "Y", (0.3, 5.3), speed=2.0, via=[(-0.2, 5.0)])     # hands on the 5 ...
    go_to(p, "Y", (2.8, 7.7), speed=3.0, delay=0.1)             # ... then climb to the Sam
    go_to(p, "RT", (0.9, 5.9), speed=2.2, via=[(-0.5, 4.0)])    # overtake the 5 and ride him wide
    go_to(p, "RG", (0.4, 1.9), speed=2.0)                       # hands on the 1 ...
    go_to(p, "RG", (2.6, 3.2), speed=2.6, delay=0.1)            # ... then wall off the Mike
    go_to(p, "C", (0.55, 2.3), speed=2.2, via=[(-0.4, 0.9)])    # overtake the 1, ending play-side of him
    go_to(p, "LG", (2.5, 0.6), speed=2.6, via=[(-0.4, -0.9)])   # climb to the Will
    go_to(p, "LT", (0.4, -2.2), speed=2.2, via=[(-0.6, -2.6)])  # cut off the 3
    go_to(p, "U", (0.2, -3.6), speed=2.2, via=[(-0.6, -4.2)])   # cut off the end
    go_to(p, "Z", (4.4, 9.4), speed=4.0, via=[(2.8, 9.8)])      # stalk the corner
    p.route("X", [(0, 0), (12, -0.5)])                          # run the corner off
    go_to(p, "QB", (-3.7, 1.7), "path", speed=2.8)              # reverse pivot to a deep mesh
    go_to(p, "QB", (-6.0, -4.5), "path", speed=4.0, delay=0.15)
    go_to(p, "RB", (6.6, 4.4), "run", speed=5.2,
          via=[(-4.4, 2.4), (-1.4, 5.1), (0.4, 4.4)])           # press the Y's outside leg, cut up
    p.handoff("RB", t=0.75)
    return p


p = Play(ace_condensed(), even_front(+1, cb_w=10.0), los=35, to_go=10,
         title="Outside zone right vs an even front: all 11 jobs")
go_to(p, "Y", (2.9, 6.8), via=[(0.1, 4.6)])            # hands on the 5, climb to the Sam
go_to(p, "RG", (3.5, 2.0), via=[(0.3, 1.25)])          # hands on the 1, climb to the Mike
go_to(p, "LG", (3.6, -1.9), via=[(-0.4, -0.9)])        # climb to the Will
go_to(p, "LT", (0.6, -1.7), via=[(-0.4, -2.6)])        # cut off the 3
go_to(p, "U", (0.6, -3.3), via=[(-0.4, -4.1)])         # cut off the end
go_to(p, "Z", (5.4, 10.0), via=[(3.0, 10.4)])          # stalk the corner
p.route("X", [(0, 0), (11, 0)])                        # run the corner off
go_to(p, "QB", (-3.6, 1.8), "path", speed=3.2)
go_to(p, "QB", (-6.0, -5.0), "path", speed=4.0, delay=0.15)
go_to(p, "RB", (2.5, 5.3), "run", via=[(-4.3, 2.6), (-1.3, 4.9)])
p.handoff("RB", t=0.7)
p.highlight("RB")
fld = draw(p, width_in=6.4, lateral=(-11, 11), window=(-8, 13.5))
overtake(fld, p, "RT", [(-0.4, 3.9), (0.1, 5.0)], (0.9, 5.6), lw=2.6)    # RT overtakes the 5
overtake(fld, p, "C", [(-0.4, 0.5), (0.1, 1.3)], (0.9, 1.8), lw=2.6)     # C overtakes the 1
spot(fld, p, -1.1, 5.4)
say(fld, p, -4.6, 7.4, "aiming point:\noutside leg of Y", color=ZONE_GREEN, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, 8.6, 1.6, "dashed green = overtake: C takes\nover the 1, RT the 5, so RG and Y\ncan climb",
    color=ZONE_GREEN, fontsize=6.8)
point_to(fld, p, (-2.8, -7.4), (0.6, -3.3), "backside\ncut-offs", fontsize=6.8)
say(fld, p, -6.6, -6.2, "QB: fake the\nother way", fontsize=6.8, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
point_to(fld, p, (8.4, 7.4), (5.4, 10.0), "stalk", fontsize=6.6, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
point_to(fld, p, (6.4, -6.6), (6.4, -9.0), "run off", fontsize=6.6, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
plt.show()








Figure 4.5: Outside zone right vs an even front: all eleven jobs. Play-side, two reach-and-overtake pairs: the Y and the RG get their hands on the 5 and the 1 first, then climb to the Sam and Mike, while the RT and the C race flat and take those defenders over (dashed green, ending play-side of each defender). Backside, the LT and U cut off the 3 and the end, and the LG climbs to the Will. Z stalk-blocks his cornerback; X runs his cornerback off. The quarterback hands off and fakes the other way.





Two new ideas are hiding in that picture.
The receivers’ jobs. Z stalk-blocks his cornerback: he runs at him as if on a route, then breaks down, squares up and stays between the corner and the ball. X runs his cornerback off: he sprints straight downfield so the corner, who cannot know it is a run yet, has to turn and run with him, which takes him out of the play without a block.
Reach-and-overtake. On outside zone, a covered lineman wants to reach his defender: get his head and body to the play-side of the defender so the defender is sealed inside and the running back can get outside him. Physically, a reach is a long lateral first step to gain ground, then a second step aimed through the defender’s play-side leg, with the inside hand driving into his chest to stop him running.4 The trouble is that a defender sitting in your play-side gap is already a step closer to the play than you are, and he is moving the same way you are: he only has to take one step sideways to stay outside you. Reaching him alone is close to impossible. So zone teams do it in pairs: the reach-and-overtake. The pairs are the same ones the rules produced for inside zone; what changes is who touches the defender first. The uncovered man of the pair (here the Y beside the 5-technique, and the RG beside the 1-technique) is already outside the defender, so he gets his hands on him first, just enough to stop him running wide. The covered man (the RT, the C) races flat down the line and overtakes the block, getting in front of the defender from the inside. As soon as the overtake arrives, the first lineman lets go and climbs to the linebacker. The covered man still ends up with his own defender; his uncovered neighbor just got there first to hold him. It is the outside-zone cousin of the inside-zone double team: inside zone’s combo goes forward and splits; outside zone’s combo goes sideways and hands off.
The backside cut-off. Away from the play, the linemen are not trying to move anyone. Their job is the backside cut-off: step play-side and get in front of the defenders on their side, so those defenders cannot chase the play down from behind. A backside defender who is cut off is out of the play even if he is never knocked back an inch. Notice who cuts off the backside end here: the U. Against the even front in Figure 4.1, nobody had that man; a second tight end gives the backside a blocker for him, which is a big reason zone teams like two-tight-end sets. As you will see, the backside cut-off is also what makes the cutback possible.
Now watch it move. The animation (a numbered frame strip in the PDF) is simulated, not a real play, but every player’s path follows the rules above.


Show the Python
pa = oz_play()
zone_animation(pa, [0.0, 0.4, 0.9, 1.45, 1.95, 2.4],
               notes=["snap", "line steps play-side", "handoff; RT races flat",
                      "RT overtakes the end; Y climbs", "end widens: crease inside him",
                      "one cut, downhill"],
               rings=(("RB", style.THIRD), ("RT", PURPLE)),
               lateral=(-6.4, 10.0), window=(-7.7, 7.0))





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 4.6: Outside zone right, frame by frame (simulated play; positions in Big Data Bowl coordinates, generated by gridiron; faint lines are each player’s path so far). The whole line moves right together and the linebackers flow with it. The Y gets his hands on the end and climbs to the Sam; the right tackle (purple ring) overtakes the end and, because the end fights to stay outside, rides him wider. The back (green ring) presses the tight end’s outside leg, sees the crease open inside the right tackle’s block, and cuts up into it: bang.




Notice the timing. Under center, the quarterback turns and hands off several yards deep, and the back takes a second and a half or more to reach the line. That is by design: the line needs time to get the defense moving sideways, and the back needs time to see which way it moved. It is why a good outside-zone back can look slow for two steps and then very fast.

Why outside zone exists, and what it gives up
Outside zone was built to beat a defense that is bigger than you. You cannot drive a 320-pound defensive tackle backward, but you can make him run, and a running defensive lineman is a defensive lineman who is not holding his gap. Stretch the whole front laterally, and gaps open between defenders who are moving at different speeds. Linebackers, flowing fast to stay level with the back, over-run the play. The back only has to find one crease.
It gives up a few things in return:

It needs a particular kind of lineman. Outside zone favors lighter, quicker linemen who can run laterally and reach, over bigger, stronger linemen who can drive straight ahead. Teams built around outside zone have often gone smaller on the line; the scheme shapes the roster.
Fast movement with the line hurts it. Zone keeps every defender accounted for when the defense moves, but it cannot make movement harmless. A defensive lineman who slants hard toward the play at the snap is moving the same way as his blocker with a head start, and the blocker may never get his head in front of him. One who knifes straight upfield into the gap a lateral-stepping blocker just left is in the backfield before the block exists, and the back’s track is so wide that he is tackled for a loss. (Figure 4.13, later, draws it.)
It is patient by design, which means it can lose yards. The back runs sideways for a couple of yards before he turns upfield. When the crease never appears, the result is a loss.







NoteMadden vs. real life



In Madden you choose “HB Stretch,” a lane lights up, and you steer the back into it. On a real zone run, nobody knows where the lane is when the play is called. The play call tells the line which way to step and the back where to aim; the hole is created by the defense’s reaction, and the back has to see it at full speed. Two identical calls of outside zone can hit three different gaps. That is not the play failing; that is the play working. The same goes for inside zone, which is not Madden’s “HB Dive”: a dive goes to one numbered hole, while inside zone’s hole is wherever the double teams and the back’s read put it.

title: Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback
text:
Stretch: the widest track
The word stretch causes confusion because teams use it differently. In many playbooks “stretch” is simply another name for outside zone. When coaches distinguish them, stretch is the widest member of the family: the aiming point moves outside the tight end, toward the numbers, and the back’s first intent is to get the edge (the outside boundary of the defense, where the last defender on the line stands). The blocking is the same lateral, reach-first zone blocking; the difference is how hard the back works to get outside before he even considers cutting up.
Why have it? Because some fronts invite it. When the defensive end lines up inside the tight end (a 7-technique, on the tight end’s inside shoulder), the tight end is already outside him before the snap: half the reach is done. By the rules the end belongs to the right tackle (he sits in the tackle’s play-side gap), so the uncovered tight end gets his hands on him, the tackle overtakes, and the pair can pin him inside and win the race to the sideline. An end lined up outside the tight end, as in the odd front below, is the opposite case: nobody can get outside him easily, and stretch becomes a bad bet. The Indianapolis Colts of the Peyton Manning era made “the stretch” a signature under line coach Howard Mudd, running it with Edgerrin James and later Joseph Addai.5 The cost is the same as outside zone’s, only more so: the wider the track, the more yards the back can lose if the edge is not there.
In this book, when a distinction matters we say inside zone (aimed inside), outside zone (aimed at the tight end, ready to cut up), and stretch (aimed outside the tight end, edge first). On a broadcast you will usually hear “outside zone” and “stretch” used interchangeably. That is fine. Watch the aiming point and you will know which one you are seeing.

title: Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback
section: Same play, different front: the rules re-pair
text:
Same play, different front: the rules re-pair
The most important thing about zone blocking is that the same call works against different fronts, because the rules re-pair the blockers after the defense shows its hand. Here is the same outside zone against an odd front, one with a nose tackle head-up on the center (a 0-technique), two 4i-techniques (on the inside shoulder of each tackle) and two outside linebackers on the line, each in a 9-technique (on the tight end’s outside shoulder). You will learn its name and logic in 05-03; for now it is “a different front.”
Apply the rules again (Figure 4.7). The Y is now covered (a 9-technique sits in his play-side gap), so he has to reach that man by himself, a hard block. The right tackle is uncovered: the 4i lines up on his inside shoulder, which is his backside, so that defender belongs to the right guard, whose play-side gap he sits in. So the RT and RG form the new reach-and-overtake pair: the RT gets his hands on the 4i first, the RG overtakes, and the RT climbs to the Mike. The center is covered by the nose head-up on him. The left guard is uncovered and right next to him, so he helps: the center works to the nose’s play-side half while the left guard hits the nose’s backside hip, and once the center has him, the guard climbs to the Will. The left tackle cuts off the backside 4i. The U is the last man on the backside with a defender outside him, the third edge case from the rules: he hinges, stepping inside to wall off anything that crashes down inside him, and the 9-technique outside him is left alone, as the backside end was on inside zone.


Show the Python
def odd_front(cb_w=10.0):
    return [
        D("POLB", "OLB", 1.0, 6.0, "9"),
        D("P4i", "DE", 1.0, technique("4i", 1), "4i"),
        D("NT", "NT", 1.0, 0.0, "0"),
        D("B4i", "DE", 1.0, technique("4i", -1), "4i"),
        D("BOLB", "OLB", 1.0, -6.0, "9"),
        D("MIKE", "ILB", 4.5, 2.4, "M"),
        D("WILL", "ILB", 4.5, -2.4, "W"),
    ] + secondary(cb_w)


p = Play([q for q in ace_condensed() if q.key not in ("X", "Z")], odd_front(), los=35, to_go=10,
         title="Same outside zone vs an odd front: the rules re-pair")
go_to(p, "Y", (0.4, 6.7), via=[(-0.4, 5.7)])            # reach the 9-tech alone
go_to(p, "RT", (3.4, 3.0), via=[(0.5, 2.4)])            # hands on the 4i, climb to the Mike
go_to(p, "LG", (3.6, -1.7), via=[(-0.3, -0.9), (0.4, -0.5)])  # hit the nose's backside hip, climb
go_to(p, "LT", (0.6, -1.9), via=[(-0.4, -2.4)])         # cut off the 4i
go_to(p, "U", (-1.1, -4.2), via=[(-0.9, -4.5)])         # hinge: wall off a crash inside
go_to(p, "QB", (-3.6, 1.8), "path", speed=3.2)
go_to(p, "QB", (-6.0, -5.0), "path", speed=4.0, delay=0.15)
go_to(p, "RB", (2.5, 5.0), "run", via=[(-4.3, 2.6), (-1.3, 4.9)])
p.handoff("RB", t=0.7)
p.highlight("RB")
p.highlight("NT", color=style.DEFENSE); p.highlight("POLB", color=style.DEFENSE)
fld = draw(p, width_in=5.6, lateral=(-11.5, 11.5), window=(-8, 9))
overtake(fld, p, "RG", [(-0.5, 2.0), (0.1, 2.8)], (0.9, 3.2))     # RG overtakes the 4i
overtake(fld, p, "C", [(-0.4, 0.3), (0.2, 0.8)], (0.9, 1.0))       # C works to the nose's play-side half
spot(fld, p, -0.2, 5.3)
say(fld, p, -3.0, 8.6, "Y must reach a\n9-tech alone", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
point_to(fld, p, (-3.6, -3.0), (0.0, -0.9), "C + LG on the nose:\nthe hardest block", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK,
         fontsize=6.8)
point_to(fld, p, (7.4, 5.4), (3.4, 3.0), "RT: hands on the 4i,\nthen climbs to the Mike", fontsize=6.6)
point_to(fld, p, (-4.2, -8.6), (-1.1, -4.2), "U hinges: steps\ninside, guards the\ngap inside him", fontsize=6.6)
point_to(fld, p, (3.4, -8.8), (1.0, -6.0), "left alone; the\nQB fakes away", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
plt.show()








Figure 4.7: The same outside zone right against an odd front (named in 05-03). Nothing in the call changed, but the rules re-pair: the RT gets his hands on the 4i and climbs while the RG overtakes (dashed green); the center works to the nose’s play-side half while the left guard hits his backside hip and then climbs; the Y must reach a 9-technique lined up outside him, alone. The two ringed defenders are where this play will be won or lost. On the backside the U hinges and the 9 outside him is left alone.





Compare the two pictures and you will see what coaches mean when they say “the front tells you where the play will hit.” Against the even front, the hardest block was the overtake on the 1-technique, and the edge was reachable. Against this odd front, the two hardest blocks are the center and left guard on a nose head-up on the center, and the tight end on a man lined up outside him. If the 9-technique cannot be reached, the back will not bounce. He will hit it up inside him, or cut back. The rules did not change. The likely hole did.






ImportantWhy it exists



A zone play is really a set of rules, not a drawing. Rules let one play call adapt to every front the defense can show, which is why zone teams can run a handful of plays all game without being predictable in the way that matters: the defense knows the call, but not where the ball will hit. Defenses fight back with fronts and movement that put the offense’s weakest blocker in the hardest job, a story you will pick up in Part 5.


Who picks inside or outside zone, and which way? The play-caller, from the sideline, as with every call (01-05). But the line of scrimmage still gets a vote. Many offenses let the quarterback flip a run to the other side (a kill call), or check out of it into a pass, when the defense’s alignment makes the called side a bad bet, for example when it shows more defenders in the box than the offense can block. How much freedom he has varies a great deal by team; the pre-snap chapter covers how checks work.

title: Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback
section: The runner’s half: bang, bend, bounce
text:
The runner’s half: bang, bend, bounce
Now the other half of the play. The zone back’s job is to take the handoff, press the aiming point (run at it hard enough that the defense believes the ball is going there), read the blocks, and choose. Coaches compress the choice into three words: bang-bend-bounce.

Bang: hit the designed gap and go straight upfield. The blocks went as drawn.
Bend: cut back against the flow, behind the double teams, usually into the backside A or B gap. The defense flowed too fast, and the space is behind them.
Bounce: take it outside. The edge defender got pinned inside, and the corner is open.



Show the Python
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(6.5, 4.2))
gs = fig.add_gridspec(1, 2, width_ratios=[1.0, 1.15], wspace=0.04)
ax1, ax2 = fig.add_subplot(gs[0]), fig.add_subplot(gs[1])
off = [q for q in named_line(offense("singleback")) if q.key in (*OL_NAMES, "Y", "RB")]
p = Play(off, front7(+1), los=35, to_go=None)
p.run("RB", [(3.0, 1.8), (5.8, 2.3)])
p.highlight("RB"); p.highlight("PT", color=style.THIRD)
fld = p.draw(ax=ax1, lateral=(-6.5, 9.5), window=(-8, 9.5), title=False)

                              mutation_scale=10, color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.8, zorder=9))

branch(fld, p, [(-1.2, 2.3), (-1.9, 0.2), (-0.7, -0.8), (1.2, -1.1), (6.4, -1.6)], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK,
       label="2 bend", label_at=(7.4, -1.8))
branch(fld, p, [(-1.2, 2.3), (-1.8, 5.0), (-0.4, 6.7), (1.4, 7.9), (4.6, 8.5)], color=PURPLE,
       label="3 bounce", label_at=(5.8, 7.6))

    style.OFFENSE_TINT, style.OFFENSE)
box(ax2, 0.71, 0.12, "Is he walled off, with daylight beside him?\nBANG: hit the play-side gap, get vertical",
    "#e5f5ee", ZONE_GREEN)

    "into the backside A or B gap", style.OFFENSE_TINT, style.OFFENSE_DARK)

    "outside (rare on inside zone)", "#e7e4f4", PURPLE)
arrow(ax2, 0.86, 0.775); arrow(ax2, 0.65, 0.54, "no"); arrow(ax2, 0.40, 0.30, "no")
ax2.text(0.02, 0.04, "Outside zone: first read the play-side end (reached? bounce),\nthen the next defensive "
         "lineman inside him (bang or bend?).", fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK_2, va="bottom")
plt.show()








Figure 4.8: The running back’s decision on inside zone. He presses the aiming point with his eyes on the first defensive lineman play-side of the center (the ringed 1-technique). If that man is walled off, bang through the B gap (green); if he flows over the top toward the play (the short orange arrow is his possible movement), bend back behind him between the center and left guard (blue); bounce (purple) only if everything inside is clogged and the edge is open. Outside zone uses the same three answers in a different order.





The order matters, and it is different for the two plays.
On inside zone the back thinks bang, bend, bounce. He reads the first defensive lineman play-side of the center, the man the first double team is working on. Why that man? Because he sits right next to the aiming point, and what happens to him answers both questions at once: if the double team is moving him, the play-side gap beside him is open; if he is sliding toward the play to get in front of it, he is taking the space behind him out of play for the defense, and the linebackers behind him usually flow the same way. One defender tells the back where the defense is going. If that defender is walled off and there is daylight beside him, bang. If he (and the linebackers behind him) flowed hard to the play-side, there is space behind them: bend. Bounce is the last resort on inside zone, because running outside on a play built to go inside usually means running away from your blockers. It is the right answer only when the play-side end has crashed inside and nobody has stayed outside to take his place.
On outside zone the order flips to bounce, bang, bend, and the back makes two reads in order. His first read is the play-side end, the first defensive lineman outside the tackle: is he reached? Remember who ends up with him: the reach-and-overtake pair, with the right tackle taking him over from the tight end. If the end is slow, or plays inside, and the tackle gets his head across him and pins him inside, the edge is open: bounce. That is uncommon against a good end lined up outside the tackle, which is why most outside-zone runs end up as bang or bend. If the end fights hard to stay outside, the tackle rides him wider and the back moves to his second read, the next defensive lineman inside, and asks where the hole is relative to him. If that man has been walled off, there is a crease between him and the end: bang, up inside the end. If he and the linebackers are racing to the sideline, the space is back the other way: bend, which on outside zone often becomes a full cutback (next section). The second read is the one to watch if you want to see a cutback coming.
Coaches teach this read in slightly different words and keys (some read a linebacker rather than a lineman), and you should expect that variety.6 The principle under all of them is the same: press, read, then make one cut.
For your own log, keep the boundary simple: bang if the back crosses the line in the play-side gaps, bounce if he goes outside the play-side end, bend if he comes back against the flow. Every bend is a cutback; the big ones that carry him outside the backside tackle are what broadcasters mean by “he found the cutback.”
That last phrase of the principle describes a style. A one-cut runner presses the aiming point with patience, plants one foot, and goes straight upfield; he does not dance, stutter or reverse field behind the line. Zone coaches prize this style above raw speed, because a zone run’s creases are open for a fraction of a second and close quickly. A back who hesitates or takes two cuts arrives after the hole has closed. It is why zone teams have often won with backs drafted in late rounds or signed off other teams’ rosters: the scheme rewards decisiveness and vision more than it rewards a top-10 pick’s raw talent. (The 1990s Broncos are the classic example; see below.)

title: Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback
text:
The cutback and the backside
Here is the play from the chapter’s opening: second-and-7, two tight ends, the line steps right in unison, the back runs at the right tight end, plants, and comes back through a hole near the center.
A cutback is a cut against the flow of the play, back toward the side the line stepped away from. On outside zone it is not a desperation move. It is one of the three answers the play was designed to produce. Here is why it works. When eleven defenders see five linemen and a running back all racing to their right, they race to their right too. Linebackers who are taught to stay level with the ball carrier take aggressive angles, and a fast defense can over-run the play: everyone ends up play-side of the ball. The space behind them is empty, as long as the backside defenders cannot get there first.
That condition is what the backside cut-off is for. The backside linemen do not need to move anyone; they need the defensive linemen on their side to be on the ground, turned around, or walled away from the cutback lane. When they succeed, the cutback is the most explosive play in the zone family, because the back runs into space that the defense vacated on purpose.


Show the Python
p = Play(ace_condensed(), even_front(+1, cb_w=10.0), los=35, to_go=7)
go_to(p, "PE", (1.8, 6.2), "path", speed=2.0)
go_to(p, "PT", (1.2, 2.8), "path", speed=2.6)               # slants hard play-side
go_to(p, "BT", (0.9, -2.5), "path", speed=1.2)              # cut down by the LT
go_to(p, "BE", (0.9, -4.3), "path", speed=1.4)              # cut down by the U
go_to(p, "SAM", (3.2, 8.2), "path", speed=2.4)
go_to(p, "MIKE", (2.4, 5.4), "path", speed=3.4, delay=0.1)  # over-runs
go_to(p, "WILL", (2.8, 3.4), "path", speed=3.6, delay=0.1)  # over-runs
go_to(p, "FS", (7.6, -3.9), "path", speed=4.5, delay=0.5)
go_to(p, "SS", (7.0, 7.5), "path", speed=4.5, delay=0.4)
go_to(p, "LCB", (11.0, -10.0), "path", speed=4.0)
go_to(p, "RCB", (5.4, 9.6), "path", speed=1.5)
go_to(p, "Y", (1.0, 6.9), speed=2.4, via=[(0.0, 5.6)])
go_to(p, "RT", (0.5, 5.0), speed=2.0, via=[(-0.4, 4.2)])
go_to(p, "RG", (1.6, 3.6), speed=2.2, via=[(-0.2, 2.2)])
go_to(p, "C", (0.4, 1.8), speed=2.0, via=[(-0.5, 0.9)])
go_to(p, "LG", (2.2, 2.4), speed=2.4, via=[(-0.4, -0.7)])
go_to(p, "LT", (0.5, -2.4), speed=2.2, via=[(-0.6, -2.7)])   # cut block: forward, at the thighs
go_to(p, "U", (0.5, -4.2), speed=2.2, via=[(-0.6, -4.5)])    # cut block
go_to(p, "Z", (4.4, 9.4), speed=4.0, via=[(2.8, 9.8)])
p.route("X", [(0, 0), (11, -0.5)])
go_to(p, "QB", (-3.7, 1.7), "path", speed=2.8)
go_to(p, "QB", (-6.0, -4.5), "path", speed=4.0, delay=0.15)
go_to(p, "RB", (8.4, -3.6), "run", speed=5.6,
      via=[(-4.4, 2.4), (-1.9, 5.6), (-1.6, 5.2), (-0.7, 0.6), (1.2, -1.6)])
p.handoff("RB", t=0.75)
zone_animation(p, [0.0, 0.75, 1.25, 1.9, 2.45, 2.95],
               notes=["snap", "handoff; everyone flows right", "back presses: no room",
                      "plant, cut back behind the C", "through the backside A gap",
                      "the safety must make the tackle"],
               down={"BT": 0.7, "BE": 0.7},
               lateral=(-9.0, 9.0), window=(-7.7, 9.5))





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 4.9: The opening play: the cutback (simulated play). The linebackers and the play-side defensive tackle (the 1) over-run the outside zone. On the backside, the LT and the U cut their defenders to the ground (faded, tagged ‘cut’ from frame 2), so nobody is left to close the backside. The back (ringed) presses the tight end’s outside leg, sees no room, plants, and cuts back through the backside A gap, beside the center; only the deep safety is left to make the tackle.










CautionCommon misconception



“The cutback is the running back freelancing.” It is the opposite. The back is following the play’s own logic: press the aiming point to pull the defense one way, then take the space the defense left. Zone coaches often say the back should expect to cut back on outside zone, and coach the backside linemen as if the ball will come their way. A back who never cuts back makes outside zone easy to defend, because the defense can then over-pursue for free.



New block: the cut block
To clear a cutback lane quickly, backside linemen often do not try to stand a defender up. They cut him. A cut block is a block aimed at a defender’s thighs or lower legs, from the front, to put him on the ground. A defender on the ground cannot chase, and for a lighter zone lineman facing a heavier defensive tackle who is trying to run down the line, a cut is often the most reliable way to take him out of the play. “From the front” matters, because the backside defender is running sideways, chasing the play: the blocker’s play-side step puts him in front of that path, so the defender runs into the block instead of being hit from behind or the side.
It is also the most controversial block in football, because a block at the knees can end a career. The NFL has narrowed it again and again: low blocks are now legal only near the ball, inside the “tight end box” around the line; never from behind or from the side while moving back toward your own goal line (since 2013); and never combined with a high block by a teammate, the chop block, banned in every situation since 2016.7 The details are in 09-03. Mike Shanahan’s Denver lines were criticized for years for backside cuts; in 2004, after a Broncos lineman’s cut block broke a Bengals defensive tackle’s ankle on Monday Night Football, opposing head coaches and the broadcast crew criticized the team publicly.8 Defenders call it dirty; zone coaches call it legal technique that lets small linemen block big ones. With the rules this much tighter, how often a modern line cuts on the backside depends on its line coach. When you do see a backside defensive tackle go down at the snap on a zone run, you have probably just seen one.

text:
Split zone: protecting the backside
Back to inside zone’s unblocked backside end, the man who can chase down a cutback. Split zone takes him away.


Show the Python
off = [q for q in named_line(offense("gun_2x2")) if q.key in (*OL_NAMES, "QB", "RB")] + [
    Player("Y", "TE", "off", -0.7, 4.8, label="Y"),
    Player("H", "TE", "off", -1.3, 6.4, label="H"),       # off-ball TE ("H-back") on the right
    Player("X", "WR", "off", -0.7, -11.0, label="X"),
    Player("Z", "WR", "off", -1.5, 11.0, label="Z"),
]
off = [q.moved(w=-1.6) if q.key == "RB" else q for q in off]
p = Play(off, even_front(+1, cb_w=11.5), los=35, to_go=10,
         title="Split zone: the H kicks out the backside end")
p.block("C", pts=[(0.9, 0.5)])
p.block("RG", pts=[(0.8, -0.8), (4.3, -0.4)])
p.block("LT", pts=[(0.9, 0.7)])
p.block("LG", pts=[(0.8, -0.6), (4.3, -0.8)])
p.block("RT", pts=[(0.9, 0.6)])
p.block("Y", pts=[(0.6, -0.6), (3.6, 1.5)])
go_to(p, "H", (0.3, -3.7), via=[(-1.8, 4.6), (-1.8, -2.6)])  # just behind the heels: kick out the end
go_to(p, "RB", (-1.4, 2.3), "run", via=[(-4.0, -0.2)])      # cross the QB's face to the B gap
go_to(p, "QB", (-5.5, -1.6), "path", speed=3.0)              # mesh, then fake a keep away
p.handoff("RB", t=0.7)
p.highlight("H"); p.highlight("BE", color=style.DEFENSE)
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-13, 13), window=(-8, 13))
spot(fld, p, 0.0, 2.4)
branch(fld, p, [(-1.4, 2.3), (-2.6, 0.6), (-1.9, -0.8), (0.6, -0.9), (2.6, -0.6), (6.6, 0.4)],
       color=ZONE_GREEN, label="bend", label_at=(7.6, 0.6))
say(fld, p, -3.6, -8.0, "H crosses just behind\nthe line, kicks out the end", fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, -6.8, 4.0, "back crosses\nthe QB's face", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
plt.show()








Figure 4.10: Split zone from the shotgun. The line blocks inside zone right exactly as before, and the back, offset to the quarterback’s left, crosses his face toward the right B gap. The H (an off-the-ball tight end) runs the other way, just behind the linemen’s heels and in front of the handoff, and kicks out the backside end. With that end blocked, the back’s bend lane (dashed green) runs between the double team on the 1 and the left guard’s block on the Will.





The line blocks exactly as it would on inside zone. The difference is one man: an H-back or tight end, lined up off the ball on the play-side, who at the snap runs across the formation, just behind the linemen’s heels and in front of the handoff, and kicks out the backside end. The name comes from the picture: the play “splits,” with the line and the back going one way and the H going the other.
Under center or in the shotgun. Every picture before this one put the quarterback under center, where he turns his back to the defense, hands off and fakes the other way; turning away hides the ball and puts him in position to carry out the fake. From the shotgun, where most NFL snaps happen, the back usually lines up beside the quarterback and on inside zone runs across the quarterback’s face at the handoff: a back offset to the left usually runs inside zone to the right. That gives him a running start toward the aiming point and keeps the exchange (the mesh, the moment the ball changes hands; not the pass concept of the same name in 04-04) moving downhill. Defenses know this tendency, so offenses break it on purpose with same-side zone (the back runs to the side he lined up on) and with the pistol, where the back stands directly behind the quarterback and his alignment says nothing about direction.
Why it exists. Split zone solves three problems at once. It blocks the one defender plain inside zone leaves free. It protects the cutback, so the back can bend without an end waiting for him. And the H’s path is misdirection: a linebacker who keys the H (follows his movement to find the play) takes a false step the wrong way. It also builds a family. The same H motion across the formation is the action for bootlegs and for passes to the H in the flat (the short area near the sideline, within a few yards of the line), so the defense cannot simply crash on the H’s path.
What it costs. The H is no longer available to block play-side, so the play-side is one blocker lighter than it could be. If the defense brings an extra defender to the play-side, split zone can be outnumbered there. Every zone variation is this kind of trade: put a blocker where the threat is, and accept that he is not somewhere else.

Zone teams rarely change the line’s rules. Instead they add a tag, a word added to the play call that changes one or two players’ jobs (you met tags in 01-04). Three zone tags are worth knowing, because you will see all three on Sundays.


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.7))

# insert
off = [q for q in named_line(offense("singleback")) if q.key in (*OL_NAMES, "Y", "QB", "RB")]
off.append(Player("H", "TE", "off", -4.4, -1.8, label="H"))            # offset fullback
p = Play(off, front7(), los=35, to_go=None)
p.block("C", pts=[(1.1, 0.6)]); p.block("RG", pts=[(1.0, -0.7)])      # the double stays on the 1
p.block("RT", pts=[(0.9, 0.6)]); p.block("Y", pts=[(0.6, -0.6), (3.6, 1.5)])
p.block("LT", pts=[(0.9, 0.7)]); p.block("LG", pts=[(0.8, -0.6), (4.3, -0.8)])
go_to(p, "H", (3.7, 1.8), via=[(-2.6, 0.6), (0.3, 2.3)])                 # insert on the Mike
p.run("RB", [(3.0, 1.0), (6.0, 2.7), (10.0, 3.0)], delay=0.25)
p.highlight("H")
f = draw(p, ax=axes[0], lateral=(-7.5, 8.5), window=(-8, 6.5), title=False)
point_to(f, p, (-6.2, -4.6), (-4.4, -1.8), "H: offset\nfullback", fontsize=6.8)
point_to(f, p, (-4.2, 5.4), (0.6, 1.0), "double team\nstays on the 1", fontsize=6.8, color=ZONE_GREEN)
axes[0].set_title("Insert: H leads up on the Mike", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")

# arc
off = [q for q in named_line(offense("gun_2x2")) if q.key in (*OL_NAMES, "QB")]
off += [Player("H", "TE", "off", -1.5, -6.6, label="H"), Player("RB", "RB", "off", -5.0, -1.6, label="R")]
dfn = [q for q in front7() if q.key != "SAM"] + [D("SS", "SS", 5.0, -9.6, "SS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
p.block("C", pts=[(0.9, 0.5)]); p.block("RG", pts=[(0.8, -0.8), (4.3, -0.4)])
p.block("RT", pts=[(0.9, 0.6)])
p.block("LT", pts=[(0.9, 0.7)]); p.block("LG", pts=[(0.8, -0.6), (4.3, -0.8)])
go_to(p, "H", (4.1, -9.3), via=[(0.4, -7.6), (2.6, -9.0)])               # arc past the end to the safety
go_to(p, "RB", (1.0, 2.6), "run", via=[(-4.0, -0.4), (-1.4, 2.3)])       # give: inside zone right
p.read("BE")
p.highlight("H"); p.highlight("BE", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[1], lateral=(-12, 4.0), window=(-8, 6.5), title=False)
branch(f, p, [(-5.0, 0.0), (-4.4, -2.0), (-2.6, -4.4), (-0.4, -5.4), (4.0, -6.2)], label="keep",
       label_at=(5.4, -6.0), fontsize=7, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
point_to(f, p, (-3.4, 2.8), (-1.4, 2.3), "give", fontsize=7, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
point_to(f, p, (-6.6, -9.0), (1.0, -4.0), "read end:\nnot blocked", fontsize=6.8, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
axes[1].set_title("Arc: H runs past the end", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 4.11: Two zone tags, both with inside-zone blocking to the right. Left, insert: the H (here an offset fullback) leads through the play-side B gap onto the Mike, a step ahead of the running back, so the double team on the 1 never has to climb. Right, arc: on the backside, the H (an H-back off the ball on the left) runs past the unblocked end without touching him and blocks the safety outside him. The quarterback reads that end (dashed line): if the end stays home, give; if he chases the back, keep and run behind the arc block.





Insert. On insert (or “zone insert”), a fullback, H-back or tight end leads up through a gap and blocks a linebacker, usually the play-side one (some staffs insert on the backside linebacker instead). That frees the play-side double team from having to climb: it can stay on the defensive lineman longer and move him farther. In effect, insert adds a blocker at the point of attack, which is how a zone team answers a defense that keeps one more defender in the box than the offense has blockers. The cost is the usual one: the inserting player is not available as a receiver, and his alignment (an offset fullback, or a tight end off the ball) can tip the play.
The other two tags borrow an idea from option football, which gets its own chapter: instead of blocking the unblocked backside end, the quarterback reads him (watches what he does after the snap) and decides whether to hand the ball off or keep it. For now, all you need is that idea; 03-04 builds it properly.
Arc. Arc happens on the backside, away from the line’s flow. The line zones right and the back runs inside zone to the right, while on the left a tight end or H-back makes an arc block: he releases outside the unblocked backside end, runs past him without touching him, and blocks the next defender out, the linebacker or safety responsible for the alley between the end and the sideline (the alley player of Part 5). The quarterback reads the end. If the end stays home, the quarterback gives and the back runs inside zone. If the end chases the running back down the line, the quarterback keeps, runs around the end the other way, and finds the arc block already waiting for the next man. Arc is why you sometimes see a tight end run right past a defensive end without touching him: he was never supposed to.
Bash needs one more step of background. On the standard zone read (03-04 draws it), the back runs the inside-zone track and the quarterback, reading the backside end, keeps the ball around that end if the end chases the back. Defenses learned an answer: the end crashes down hard at the back, inviting the keep, while a linebacker loops around behind him to meet the quarterback where he was about to run (a scrape exchange: the end and the linebacker swap jobs).9 The defense’s plan is a bet that the back will be inside and the quarterback outside.


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.5))
for ax, bash in [(axes[0], False), (axes[1], True)]:
    off = [q for q in named_line(offense("gun_2x2")) if q.key in (*OL_NAMES, "QB")]
    off += [Player("RB", "RB", "off", -5.0, 1.6 if bash else -1.6, label="R"),
            Player("Y", "TE", "off", -0.7, 4.8, label="Y")]
    p = Play(off, front7(), los=35, to_go=None)
    p.block("C", pts=[(0.9, 0.5)]); p.block("RG", pts=[(0.8, -0.8), (4.3, -0.4)])
    p.block("RT", pts=[(0.9, 0.6)]); p.block("Y", pts=[(0.6, -0.6), (3.6, 1.5)])
    p.block("LT", pts=[(0.9, 0.7)]); p.block("LG", pts=[(0.8, -0.6), (4.3, -0.8)])
    p.read("BE")
    p.highlight("BE", color=style.DEFENSE)
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-9.5, 7.0), window=(-8, 7), title=False)
    inside = [(-5.0, 0.0), (-3.6, 1.0), (-1.2, 2.3), (4.6, 2.7)]
    outside = [(-4.6, -1.0), (-3.6, -3.4), (-1.6, -6.2), (3.6, -7.6)]
    if bash:
        branch(f, p, [(-5.0, 1.6), (-4.8, 0.4)] + outside, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK,
               label="give (back)\nif the end squeezes", label_at=(-6.6, -5.6), fontsize=6.6)
        branch(f, p, inside, color=ZONE_GREEN, label="keep (QB) if the end\nwidens with the back",
               label_at=(6.2, 3.0), fontsize=6.6)
        ax.set_title("Bash: back outside, QB inside", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
    else:
        branch(f, p, [(-5.0, -1.6), (-3.8, 0.0)] + inside[2:], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK,
               label="give (back)", label_at=(6.0, 3.2), fontsize=6.6)
        branch(f, p, [(-5.0, 0.0)] + outside, color=ZONE_GREEN, label="keep (QB) if the\nend chases the back",
               label_at=(-6.6, -5.6), fontsize=6.6)
        ax.set_title("Zone read: back inside, QB outside", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK,
                     fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 4.12: The zone read and bash, both with the line zoning right and the quarterback reading the same backside end (dashed line). Left, the zone read: the back takes the inside-zone track, and the quarterback keeps around the end if the end chases the back. Right, bash: the back goes the other way, wide around the end, and the quarterback, if he keeps, runs the inside-zone track. The runners have swapped lanes, so a defense planning for ‘back inside, quarterback outside’ has it backwards.





Bash. Bash is short for “back away”: the running back runs away from the direction the line is zoning, on a wide path around the read end, while the quarterback, if he keeps, runs the inside-zone track behind the line (Figure 4.12). It flips the usual roles: the running back threatens the edge and the quarterback becomes the inside runner. The read is the same end, with the answers reversed: if he squeezes (closes down the line toward the zone flow), the quarterback hands the ball to the back going around him; if he stays wide to take the back, the quarterback keeps and runs inside him.10 Against a scrape exchange, that matters: the end who crashes down to take the inside runner has crashed onto the quarterback’s fake, and the ball is going outside him with the running back. Bash is the offense’s reply to the defense’s reply, and the full back-and-forth belongs to option football.
All three tags share one logic: keep the zone rules for the line, and change one or two players to fix the specific problem the defense is creating. Watch for the extra player (the inserting back, the arcing tight end, the back running the “wrong” way) and you will usually know which tag you are watching.

title: Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback
text:
How defenses fight zone
Zone’s rules guarantee that every defender is accounted for. They do not guarantee that every block is won, and defenses attack the places where zone is physically hardest. Figure 4.13 shows the two most common.


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.6))
# penetration: the 3-technique lines up on the play side this time (Sam still on the right)
dfn = [D("PE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", 1), "5"), D("PT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", 1), "3"),
       D("BT", "DT", 1.0, technique("1", -1), "1"), D("BE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", -1), "5"),
       D("SAM", "SAM", 4.0, 6.6, "S"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 0.6, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -3.0, "W")]
off = [q for q in ace_condensed() if q.key not in ("X", "Z")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
for k, st in [("LT", (0.1, 1.3)), ("LG", (0.1, 1.3)), ("C", (0.1, 1.2)), ("U", (0.1, 1.3)), ("Y", (0.2, 0.9))]:
    p.block(k, pts=[st])
p.block("RG", pts=[(-0.1, 1.1)]); p.block("RT", pts=[(0.0, 0.9)])
go_to(p, "PT", (-2.7, 3.0), "path")                       # the play-side 3-technique penetrates
go_to(p, "RB", (-2.8, 3.4), "run", via=[(-4.4, 2.4)])
go_to(p, "QB", (-3.6, 1.8), "path", speed=3.2)
p.highlight("PT", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[0], lateral=(-7.5, 8.5), window=(-8, 6.5), title=False)
x, y = _P(f, p, -2.9, 3.5)
axes[0].plot([x], [y], marker="X", ms=11, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, mec="white", mew=0.8, zorder=12)
say(f, p, -2.4, 6.4, "tackle\nfor loss", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
point_to(f, p, (-5.8, 6.0), (1.0, 2.35), "3-tech knifes upfield\nbefore the reach", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK,
         fontsize=6.8)
axes[0].set_title("Penetration", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")

# cutback player: the Will plays fast into the backside A gap before the LG can climb to him
# (the quarterback is left out of this panel so the bend lane behind the line stays visible)
p = Play([q for q in off if q.key != "QB"], front7(+1), los=35, to_go=None)
for k in ("LT", "C", "RG", "RT", "U", "Y"):
    p.block(k, pts=[(0.15, 1.3)])
go_to(p, "LG", (1.4, -0.3), via=[(-0.3, -0.9)])            # steps play-side to climb: late
go_to(p, "MIKE", (3.6, 4.6), "path"); go_to(p, "SAM", (3.4, 8.0), "path")
go_to(p, "WILL", (1.0, -1.1), "path", speed=4.0)           # downhill into the backside A gap
go_to(p, "RB", (-1.9, 4.8), "run", via=[(-4.4, 2.4)])
p.highlight("WILL", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[1], lateral=(-7.5, 8.5), window=(-8, 6.5), title=False)
branch(f, p, [(-1.9, 4.8), (-2.1, 2.4), (-1.8, 0.2), (-0.6, -0.6), (-0.1, -0.75)], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK,
       label="bend", label_at=(-3.2, 0.6), fontsize=7)
x, y = _P(f, p, 0.25, -0.85)
axes[1].plot([x], [y], marker="X", ms=11, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, mec="white", mew=0.8, zorder=12)
point_to(f, p, (-5.0, -4.6), (1.0, -1.1), "Will plays fast into\nthe backside A gap,\nbefore the LG can climb",
         color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
axes[1].set_title("The cutback player", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 4.13: Two ways defenses kill outside zone right. Left: penetration. This time the 3-technique lines up on the play side; at the snap he knifes upfield through the B gap, before the lateral-stepping guard and tackle can get in front of him, and meets the back on his track. Right: a cutback player. Instead of flowing, the Will comes downhill into the backside A gap at the snap, faster than the left guard can climb to him, so when the back bends, the lane he expected is filled.





Penetration and movement. A defensive lineman who gets upfield at the snap, or slants hard toward the play, can beat a lateral-stepping blocker to the spot. Defenses that want to stop zone often play their linemen this way, attacking a gap instead of reading the man in front of them; how defensive linemen are taught to do either is the subject of 05-01.
The cutback player. Because outside zone’s biggest gains come from the cutback, defenses assign someone to stay home for it: usually the backside linebacker, sometimes a safety rotating down. You saw the deep safety arrive late in Figure 4.9; a defense that gets a defender there early takes away the play’s third answer.
Spill or squeeze. When a blocker comes at a defender, the defense chooses whether that defender fights inside the block to force the ball to bounce wide toward pursuit (spill) or holds the edge and squeezes the play back inside (squeeze). Against zone, either plan can work if all eleven players agree on it, which is the subject of run fits in 05-05.11
And when the defense simply puts more defenders in the box than the offense has blockers, a zone team answers with the tools you have already seen: an extra blocker (insert), a read of the unblocked man (arc, bash, the zone read), or a pass that looks like the run.

title: Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback
section: Why wide zone and the bootleg are married
text:
Why wide zone and the bootleg are married
Outside zone’s greatest weapon is not a run at all. It is the pass that looks exactly like it.
Think about what outside zone teaches a defense. Every snap, the line steps hard to one side, the back runs at the tight end, and the linebackers learn that if they do not flow fast and hard, they lose. The backside end learns that if he does not chase, the cutback beats him. After a few of these, the defense is trained to run with the line’s first step.
The bootleg cashes that in. It is a play-action pass (a pass that begins with a fake handoff) in which the quarterback fakes outside zone one way and rolls out the other, away from where the line went, with receivers crossing the field to meet him. In the “naked” version nobody blocks for him at all; in the protected version a lineman or a back is assigned to the backside end. Both are built in 04-05; here, what matters is why they pair with zone.


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.3))
for i, ax in enumerate(axes):
    p = Play(ace_condensed(), even_front(+1, cb_w=10.0), los=35, to_go=10)
    for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
        p.block(k, pts=[(0.15, 1.4)])                      # identical first steps
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (4.3, 4.4), "path"); go_to(p, "WILL", (4.3, 1.2), "path")
    go_to(p, "SAM", (3.8, 8.2), "path")
    if i == 0:
        go_to(p, "U", (0.4, -3.4), via=[(-0.5, -4.2)])     # cut off the end
        go_to(p, "BE", (1.0, -3.0), "path")
        go_to(p, "Y", (0.3, 5.9))
        go_to(p, "QB", (-3.6, 1.8), "path", speed=3.2)
        go_to(p, "RB", (2.5, 5.0), "run", via=[(-4.3, 2.6), (-1.3, 4.9)])
        p.route("X", [(0, 0), (9, 0)]); go_to(p, "Z", (4.0, 9.8))
        p.highlight("RB")
        f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-13, 12), window=(-9, 17.5), title=False)
        ax.set_title("Outside zone right", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
    else:
        go_to(p, "BE", (-2.2, 2.6), "path", via=[(0.4, -3.6), (-1.75, -2.6), (-2.0, 0.0)])  # chases the fake
        go_to(p, "QB", (-3.4, 1.6), "path", speed=3.2)                  # the same fake ...
        go_to(p, "QB", (-6.0, -7.5), "path", speed=4.5, delay=0.1)      # ... then roll the other way
        go_to(p, "RB", (1.0, 5.6), "path", via=[(-4.3, 2.6), (-1.3, 4.9)])
        p.route("U", [(0, 0), (1.5, 1.0), (4.5, 7.5)], delay=0.6)       # flat, boot side
        p.route("Y", [(0, 0), (1.2, -1.0), (4.5, -4.0), (7.0, -8.0), (7.5, -12.5)])  # inside the 5, then across
        p.route("X", [(0, 0), (14, 0.5)])                               # clear out
        p.route("Z", [(0, 0), (10, -1.0), (15, -10), (16, -17)])         # deep over, all the way across
        p.highlight("QB")
        f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-13, 12), window=(-9, 17.5), title=False)
        say(f, p, 2.4, -10.6, "flat", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
        say(f, p, 8.6, -5.0, "cross", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
        say(f, p, 16.2, -3.0, "over", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
        point_to(f, p, (-7.6, 6.0), (-1.9, 0.6), "end chases\nthe fake", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        ax.set_title("Naked boot left, same first second", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK,
                     fontweight="bold")
    if i == 0:
        say(f, p, -6.8, -7.6, "first steps and linebacker\nflow: the same in both", color=style.MUTED, fontsize=6.6)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.5)
plt.show()








Figure 4.14: The same first second. Left: outside zone right; the U cuts off the backside end. Right: a naked bootleg left off the same look. The line’s first steps, the back’s track and the linebackers’ flow are identical (grey note). What differs: on the boot, nobody blocks the backside end; if he chases the fake down the line onto the back’s track, he ends up behind a quarterback rolling away from him, who has three receivers at three depths on the boot side: the U in the flat, the Y on a crossing route (releasing inside the play-side end) and the Z on a deep over route.





The two plays look identical for the first second, which is the second that decides how the defense moves. (The “over” route is a deep crossing route: the receiver runs across the field 15 or more yards downfield, over the linebackers.) On a bootleg the backside end’s job is to contain the quarterback: stay outside him and force him back toward the pursuit. An end who chased the run fake (as outside zone has taught him to) is now behind a quarterback rolling away from him, and nobody is there to make the quarterback hurry. The linebackers who flowed with the line are a step or two the wrong way, and the crossing routes (receivers running across the field) come open behind them. The boot gives the quarterback three receivers at three depths on the same side: a short one in the flat, one crossing at linebacker depth, and one deep. That simple read is what makes the play so reliable.
Why the pair works. Each play protects the other. If the defense sits back and refuses to flow, outside zone gets the edge or the crease. If it flows hard, the bootleg punishes the flow. And because the two share the same first step, the defense cannot wait to find out which one it is facing. This is the backbone of the Shanahan-family offenses you will meet in 12-03: a run game and a play-action game built to be indistinguishable for as long as possible.
How to tell them apart after the snap. Three plays send a tight end or H-back at the backside end, and before the snap they can look the same. Watch what he does when he gets there:

He hits the end and drives him out: split zone.
He runs past the end without touching him and blocks the next man out (a linebacker or safety), while the quarterback rides the ball with the back and watches the end: arc.
He runs past the end into the flat and turns to look for the ball, while the quarterback pulls the ball and rolls the other way: bootleg.

The cost. A naked bootleg leaves the quarterback with nobody blocking the backside end. If that end does not bite on the fake (if he stays home), he is waiting for a quarterback who has turned his back to him. That is why the bootleg works only once outside zone has earned the defense’s respect.
