title: Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback
text:
Where zone came from
Running backs reading blocks is as old as football. Vince Lombardi’s Green Bay Packers of the 1960s ran their famous power sweep with a simple instruction to the ball carrier: run to daylight, wherever the blocks open it, a phrase that became the title of a 1963 book Lombardi wrote with W. C. Heinz.12 That sweep was a gap play with pulling guards, not a zone play, but its runner’s freedom to choose the hole is the same idea zone backs live by.
Who invented zone blocking is disputed, and nobody serious claims a single inventor. The best-documented claims put it in the NFL of the 1980s. Jim McNally, the Cincinnati Bengals’ offensive line coach, was one of the era’s most copied line coaches, and Cincinnati’s run game finished in the league’s top five every year from 1986 to 1990. McNally himself said, “I didn’t invent zone blocking, but we and the Cleveland Browns did it back in the ’80s,” and he described it as an answer to the rise of the 3-4 defense and its penetrating linemen. Cleveland’s line coach in those years was Howard Mudd, the same coach who later made the stretch a Colts signature.13 Coaches who credit older roots point to blocking ideas in earlier college offenses; treat any one-name “inventor” story with suspicion.
What is not in dispute is who made outside zone the identity of an NFL offense. Alex Gibbs, an offensive line coach with a famously blunt teaching style and a reputation as one of the best line coaches of his era, built the Denver Broncos’ running game under head coach Mike Shanahan from 1995.14 Denver had a specific problem to solve. Pittsburgh defensive coordinator Dom Capers had popularized the zone blitz, in which a linebacker blitzes and a lineman drops into coverage in his place, so the defenders a man-blocking line had assigned itself kept changing. “When you’re in a man scheme, you’re getting picked off and you look bad,” Gary Kubiak, then Denver’s offensive coordinator, later remembered.15 (In blocking, “picked off” means a blocker’s path is cut off by a defender he was not assigned, so his own man runs free: exactly the left side of Figure 4.2.) Blocking by area meant that whoever came was blocked.
Gibbs’s system was close to a religion: a small number of runs, repeated until the linemen could execute them against any front; light, quick linemen who could reach and run; backside cut blocks; and backs taught to press the aiming point and make one cut. His clinic tapes on zone running circulated widely among coaches and are still sold as coaching videos, and many of the phrases in this chapter descend from his teaching.16
Denver’s results became the advertisement. The Broncos won back-to-back Super Bowls after the 1997 and 1998 seasons, and running back Terrell Davis, a sixth-round draft pick, ran for 2,008 yards in 1998 and was named the league’s MVP.17 When injuries ended Davis’s peak, Denver kept producing 1,000-yard rushers with a string of other backs, several of them mid- or late-round picks, which convinced the league that the scheme was doing much of the work.18
The system spread through a coaching tree. Gary Kubiak carried it to Houston as head coach and back to Denver, where he won Super Bowl 50 after the 2015 season. Kyle Shanahan, Mike’s son, coached under Kubiak in Houston and under his father in Washington, then became the 49ers’ head coach in 2017. From Kyle Shanahan’s staffs came Sean McVay (Rams), Matt LaFleur (Packers) and others, and Kubiak’s son Klint called plays for the 2025 Seattle Seahawks before becoming the Raiders’ head coach for 2026.19 By late in the 2019 season, ESPN’s charting found zone blocking in use by all 32 teams and on at least half of the runs of most of them; LaFleur’s Packers led the league at 70.3% of runs (same ESPN study). The tree and its offense get a full case study in 12-03.






NoteFilm room: Denver Broncos, Super Bowl XXXII (1997 season)



The game: Super Bowl XXXII, January 25, 1998: Denver 31, Green Bay 24. Terrell Davis carried 30 times for 157 yards and three touchdowns and was named MVP, despite a migraine that blurred his vision and kept him out of part of the second quarter.20 Coaches’ film from the 1990s is hard to find, but Super Bowl broadcasts are the easiest games of the era to track down, and this one is dominated by Gibbs’s zone running (Denver mixed in other runs and play-action too).
What to notice:

The line’s first step. Every lineman moves laterally together; you will seldom see a Denver guard pull.
Davis’s patience. He runs at the tight end’s outside leg for two or three steps and does not cut until the end commits. Then he cuts once, hard, and is going north.
The backside. Watch the defensive linemen away from the play. Many end up on the ground in the first second: that is the backside cut, and it is why Davis’s cutbacks so often had nobody in them.
The bootleg. John Elway faking the stretch and rolling away is the other half of the same system.









NoteFilm room: San Francisco 49ers 2019



The game: the NFC Championship Game after the 2019 season, 49ers vs. Green Bay Packers, January 19, 2020. San Francisco won 37–20 and threw the ball only eight times; running back Raheem Mostert, a former undrafted free agent, ran for 220 yards and four touchdowns.21
What to notice:

How often the 49ers ran the wide-zone family, and how little they disguised it. They were not a pure zone team (the same ESPN charting had them using zone on 55% of their runs that season), so gap runs and tosses came off the same formations. Make it a drill: classify each run with this chapter’s Watch-for-it checklist (does the whole line step together, or does a guard pull?).
The linebackers. As the game goes on, watch them flow harder and harder to the play-side, and watch the cutbacks and the inside creases that opens.
Mostert’s runs: many of his biggest gains come on one cut, at full speed, into a crease that appeared only after the defense flowed.









NoteFilm room: Seattle Seahawks, Super Bowl LX (2025 season)



The game: Super Bowl LX, February 8, 2026: Seattle 29, New England 13, the end of Klint Kubiak’s single season as Seattle’s offensive coordinator (he became the Raiders’ head coach for 2026, so this is one season’s offense, not Seattle’s current one). Running back Kenneth Walker III carried 27 times for 135 yards and was named MVP.22 Kubiak’s offense descends directly from the Gibbs-Shanahan-Kubiak tree, built on outside zone from tight, two-tight-end formations and the bootlegs that pair with it.23
What to do: watch Walker’s 27 carries with this chapter’s checklist. For each one, call it zone or gap (does the whole line step together?), inside or outside (up or across?), and bang, bend or bounce. Then count the bootlegs and play-action passes that started with the same first step. It is the 2019 49ers’ film, a quarter-century after Denver.


One more modern example worth finding: Christian McCaffrey’s 2023 season in San Francisco, when he led the NFL with 1,459 rushing yards and was named Offensive Player of the Year.24 He is not a pure one-cut back (he will press, hop sideways and cut again), which makes him a good contrast with Davis and Mostert: watch how he uses the same aiming points with a different running style.

title: Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback
section: Does it work? Reading the numbers
text:
Does it work? Reading the numbers
You might expect a data source to tell us how well zone runs work. It cannot, directly, and the reason is worth understanding before looking at any chart.
The NFL’s play-by-play data (which nflverse packages for free) records where a run went, not what play was called. Each run gets a run location (left, middle or right) and, unless it went up the middle, a run gap (guard, tackle or end). These are charted by the league’s scorers from where the ball carrier crossed the line, and they are coarser than the gap letters of 03-01: roughly, “middle” is between the guards (the A gaps), “guard” is over or just outside a guard (the B gap), “tackle” is over or just outside a tackle (the C gap), and “end” is outside the last man on the line. There is no “zone” flag. So a zone run that cuts back is logged where the back ended up, not where the play was aimed. (Commercial charting services such as PFF, Pro Football Focus, do label run concepts by watching film. In the sample of their labels released with the 2025 Big Data Bowl (2022 season), outside zone was the single most common run concept.25 That is the most recent public count we know of; no league-wide zone share for 2025 has been published that we could check.)
So to study zone we need a proxy: a team we know runs a lot of zone. We use Kyle Shanahan’s 49ers. LaFleur’s Packers ran an even higher share of zone in ESPN’s 2019 count, and would also do; the 49ers are the root of the coaching tree and the subject of the 12-03 case study, and Shanahan was their head coach for every season in the chart. (The Packers’ number appears below too.)
One more thing before the chart: expect negative numbers. Across the league, the average running-back carry loses a little expected value, because a typical run gains less than the down and distance needs to keep the offense’s scoring chances where they were. So “good” on this chart means “less negative than the league,” and a run game is judged by how far above the league line it sits, not by whether it clears zero.
With those caveats, here is the 49ers’ efficiency by run location against the league average from 2019 to 2025. The measures are EPA per rush (how much each run changed the offense’s expected points, on average; above zero is good for the offense) and success rate (the share of runs with positive EPA). Only running back and fullback carries count, so quarterback runs and receivers’ jet sweeps and end-arounds, which are not zone runs, stay out.


Show the Python
from gridiron.data import pbp, nfl

style.apply()
SEASONS = list(range(2019, 2026))
cols = ["season", "season_type", "posteam", "play_type", "run_location", "run_gap", "epa",
        "success", "qb_scramble", "qb_kneel", "down", "rusher_player_id"]
plays = pbp(SEASONS, columns=cols)
rosters = nfl().load_rosters(SEASONS).to_pandas()
back_ids = set(rosters.loc[rosters["position"].isin(["RB", "FB"]), "gsis_id"].dropna())

runs = plays[(plays["season_type"] == "REG") & (plays["play_type"] == "run")
             & (plays["qb_scramble"] == 0) & (plays["qb_kneel"] == 0)
             & plays["epa"].notna() & plays["down"].notna() & plays["run_location"].notna()
             & plays["rusher_player_id"].isin(back_ids)].copy()
runs["lane"] = np.where(runs["run_location"] == "middle", "Middle", runs["run_gap"].str.title())
runs = runs[runs["lane"].isin(["Middle", "Guard", "Tackle", "End"])]
LANES = ["Middle", "Guard", "Tackle", "End"]

def by_lane(df):
    return df.groupby("lane").agg(n=("epa", "size"), epa=("epa", "mean"),
                                  sr=("success", "mean")).reindex(LANES)

lg, sf = by_lane(runs), by_lane(runs[runs["posteam"] == "SF"])
gap = sf["epa"] - lg["epa"]
team = runs.groupby("posteam")["epa"].mean().sort_values(ascending=False)
sf_rank = list(team.index).index("SF") + 1
gb_rank, gb_all = list(team.index).index("GB") + 1, team["GB"]
n_pos = int((team > 0).sum())
lg_all, sf_all = runs["epa"].mean(), runs.loc[runs["posteam"] == "SF", "epa"].mean()
ordinal = lambda n: f"{n}{'th' if 10 <= n % 100 <= 20 else {1: 'st', 2: 'nd', 3: 'rd'}.get(n % 10, 'th')}"
pct = lambda v: f"{100 * v:.0f}%"

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.3))
x = np.arange(len(LANES))
for ax, col, ttl, fmt in [(axes[0], "epa", "EPA per rush", "{:+.2f}"),
                          (axes[1], "sr", "Success rate (axis from 30%)", "{:.0%}")]:
    for frame, name, color in [(sf, "49ers", style.SERIES[0]), (lg, "League", style.SERIES[1])]:
        ax.plot(x, frame[col], color=color, lw=2, marker="o", ms=7, mec=style.SURFACE, mew=1.5,
                label=name, zorder=3)
        ax.annotate(f"{name} {fmt.format(frame[col].iloc[-1])}", (x[-1], frame[col].iloc[-1]),
                    xytext=(7, 0), textcoords="offset points", va="center", fontsize=7.5, color=style.INK_2)
    if col == "epa":
        ax.axhline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1, zorder=1)
    else:
        ax.set_ylim(0.30, 0.48)
    ax.set_xticks(x, [f"{l}\n{lg.loc[l, 'n'] / 1000:.1f}k" for l in LANES], fontsize=7.5)
    ax.set_xlim(-0.3, 4.1)
    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=10)
    ax.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=7.5)
    ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
axes[1].yaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
axes[0].legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=7.5)
fig.supxlabel("Where the run went, from the middle out (league carries in each lane)", fontsize=8, color=style.INK_2)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 4.15: Rushing efficiency by run location, 49ers vs. the league, 2019-2025 regular seasons (running back and fullback carries only; runs pooled across left and right). Nearly every value is below zero: the average carry loses a little expected value. Runs to the end look best for everyone, partly by selection (explained below). The 49ers beat the league average in every lane, by small margins. Note the success-rate axis starts at 30%, so its gaps look bigger than they are. Data: nflverse play-by-play and rosters via nflreadpy.





Four things to read from Figure 4.15.
Runs that reach the end are the least bad, for everyone. League-wide, running back carries logged at the end averaged -0.022 EPA per rush, against -0.083 up the middle. That does not mean “always run outside.” It means that when a run gets outside, it is usually because the edge was open, and the runs that tried to get outside and failed were often logged somewhere else (or as losses at the tackle). This is a selection effect (backs only go outside when the edge is open, so the runs that get there are the lucky ones), and it is why no coordinator reads this chart as a play-calling instruction.
The 49ers were a little better everywhere, most of all at the two ends of the chart. Their EPA edge over the league was +0.031 per carry at the end and +0.025 up the middle, against +0.015 at guard and +0.011 at tackle. That fits outside zone’s two big answers, the bounce (logged at the end) and the cutback (often logged up the middle), but the gaps are small, a few hundredths of a point per carry, and the chart cannot prove the scheme caused them.
Success rate tells a slightly different story. San Francisco’s success rate beat the league’s by 2.6 points at guard and 2.5 up the middle, but only 0.2 at tackle. Success rate rewards steady, positive gains; EPA also rewards big ones. A team can be consistent inside and explosive outside, and the two panels let you see both.
Overall, good, not magic. Across all seven seasons the 49ers’ running back carries averaged -0.043 EPA per rush against a league average of -0.064, ranking 9th of 32 teams; only one team averaged above zero. LaFleur’s Packers, the other famous zone offense of the period, averaged -0.010 and ranked 2nd. So two of the period’s best-known zone offenses landed in quite different places, both above the league average. That spread is the lesson: zone is one input to a run game, alongside the backs, the linemen, the quarterback and what the passing game makes defenses fear. Part of the 49ers’ edge is surely talent rather than scheme (McCaffrey, the 2023 Offensive Player of the Year, carried for them), and run-location data cannot separate the two; that would take play-level scheme labels and a model of player quality. Teams still run, even though the average carry loses a little expected value, because a run game does things a single carry’s EPA does not capture: it keeps the defense honest, it shortens third downs, and above all it sets up the play-action passes that look like it. You will see that argument tested with data in 13-02.






CautionCommon misconception



“Run location tells you which runs a team called.” It tells you where the ball carrier went. On zone runs especially, those are different things: an outside zone that cuts back is logged up the middle. Treat run-location splits as a picture of outcomes, and be suspicious of anyone who ranks “best run plays” from them.








TipWatch for it



On Sunday: bang, bend, bounce. You cannot watch everything in two seconds, so watch in this order.
Before the snap (you have time here)

Count the tight ends and find the running back. Two tight ends and a back directly behind the quarterback (or in the pistol) is a natural zone look. In the shotgun, an inside-zone back usually runs away from the side he lines up on, crossing the quarterback’s face. (How deep the back stands varies too much by team to be a reliable tell on its own.)
Find the backside end, the defender farthest from where you think the play is going. Remember where he is; you will check on him after the play.

The first half-second: watch the line, nothing else

Do all five linemen step the same way? Zone. Does a guard pull? Gap scheme (03-03). Double teams but no zone steps, and the back aiming straight at a linebacker? Probably duo, also in 03-03.
Are the linemen’s helmets going up (inside zone) or across (outside zone)? The high end-zone replay angle shows this best (01-06); on the live sideline angle, look for the whole line drifting toward one sideline.

Then: watch the back’s feet

Where is he aiming: the guard, or the tight end? Wider than the tight end is stretch.
Watch him press, plant and cut. Call it as it happens: bang (play-side gaps), bend (back against the flow) or bounce (outside the end).

After the play (on the replay)

Did a tight end or H-back go at the backside end? Hit him: split zone. Ran past him to the next man: arc. Slipped into the flat looking for the ball: bootleg. Did someone lead up into the line? Insert.
Where was the backside end when the back made his cut? On the ground (cut), chasing (and how close), or blocked?
If the defense has been flowing hard all game, start watching for the bootleg off the same look.

For your prediction log (01-06): before each zone run write I (inside), O (outside) or S (split) from the alignment; afterwards write which of bang, bend or bounce the back chose.

title: Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback
text:
Predict the play






TipPredict the play



Drill 1. First-and-10 from your own 40. The offense is in the shotgun with one back and one tight end (11 personnel); the tight end is in-line on the right and the running back is offset to the quarterback’s left. The defense is in nickel with two deep safeties: six defenders in the box against six blockers. Its linemen are a 5 and a 1 on the left, and a 3 and a 7-technique (on the tight end’s inside shoulder) on the right. The offense calls inside zone. Which way is it most likely going, does the front change that, and why does the defense’s picture make a run attractive here?


Show the Python
off = named_line(offense("gun_2x2"))
off = [q.moved(d=-0.7, w=4.8) if q.key == "Y" else (q.moved(w=-2.0) if q.key == "RB" else
       (q.moved(d=-1.5) if q.key == "Z" else q)) for q in off]          # Z off the ball: 7 on the line
from gridiron import defense
DL_TECH = {"SDE": "7", "SDT": "3", "WDT": "1", "WDE": "5"}
dfn = []
for q in defense("nickel", "two_high", off):
    if q.key == "NB":
        q = q.moved(d=5.0, w=-8.5, label="NB")
    elif q.key in DL_TECH:
        q = q.moved(label=DL_TECH[q.key])
    elif q.pos == "CB":
        q = q.moved(label="CB")
    dfn.append(q)
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10, title="Drill 1: 1st and 10, gun, 11 personnel")
f = draw(p, lateral=(-17.5, 17.5), window=(-8, 13))
say(f, p, -6.9, -5.6, "RB offset to\nthe QB's left", fontsize=7)
plt.show()








Figure 4.16: Drill 1: gun, 11 personnel, back offset to the quarterback’s left, tight end in-line on the right; nickel defense (NB is the nickel back) with two deep safeties and six in the box. The 7 is a 7-technique, on the tight end’s inside shoulder.











NoteAnswer





Most likely to the right, toward the tight end. From the shotgun, inside zone usually has the back cross the quarterback’s face: he lines up on one side and runs to the other, which gives him a running start toward the aiming point and a downhill angle at the mesh. With the tight end on the right too, the right side is also where the offense has its extra blocker.
Does the front change it? Not the direction. Run the rules to the right: the RG is covered by the 3 and the RT by the 7, so the RG has no uncovered neighbor to help him and the 3-technique is the hardest block on the play side. That tells you where trouble is likely (a 3 who wins knocks the back off his track, and he bends), not which way the play is called. The back’s alignment is the stronger tell.
Why run here: two deep safeties and six in the box means six blockers for six defenders: “hat on a hat,” a fair fight up front, with both safeties starting 11–12 yards away. That is exactly the look zone teams want to run against, and it is a common look now: two-high shells rose from about a third of snaps in 2018 to 42% in 2025.26
The catch: good defenses know the “cross the face” tendency too, which is why offenses mix in same-side zone and the pistol. If you see a team do that a lot, that is why.











TipPredict the play



Drill 2. Outside zone to the right is called. The play-side end (on the offense’s right) is lined up wide, outside the tight end in a 9-technique, and the Sam linebacker lines up off the ball behind the right tackle. Before the snap, use the rules: who blocks the 9, who blocks the Sam, and where is the crease most likely to be? Which of bounce, bang or bend does that make the favorite?


Show the Python
dfn = even_front(+1, cb_w=10.0)
dfn = [q.moved(w=6.0, label="9") if q.key == "PE" else q for q in dfn]
dfn = [q.moved(d=4.5, w=3.4) if q.key == "SAM" else (q.moved(w=1.0) if q.key == "MIKE" else q) for q in dfn]
p = Play(ace_condensed(), dfn, los=40, to_go=10, title="Drill 2: outside zone right is called")
go_to(p, "RB", (-1.3, 4.9), "run", via=[(-4.3, 2.6)])
f = draw(p, width_in=5.4, lateral=(-12, 12), window=(-8, 12.5))
spot(f, p, -0.2, 5.3)
say(f, p, 2.9, 8.6, "end aligned\nwide (9-tech)", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
plt.show()








Figure 4.17: Drill 2: outside zone right (the back’s track to the aiming point is shown), against a play-side end aligned wide in a 9-technique.











NoteAnswer





Most likely bang, inside the end. Run the rules. The tight end is covered by a man lined up outside him, the edge case with no help: he has to block the 9 alone, and reaching him (getting the tight end’s head across his outside shoulder) is close to impossible, so his job becomes “ride him wider.” The right tackle now has nobody on him and nobody in his play-side gap: uncovered. His backside neighbor, the right guard, is uncovered too (the 1 sits in the center’s play-side gap, so the RG helps the center), so the right tackle has nobody to double and climbs straight to the Sam stacked behind him. The back’s first read is the end: he will not be pinned inside, so bounce is off. But a wide end riding wider stretches the gap inside him, so the crease is likely to appear between the tight end and the tackle, in the Sam’s gap. If the right tackle gets to the Sam, bang.
What would make it bend: that is the second read. If the Sam beats the right tackle into that gap, or the Mike scrapes hard over the top to fill it, the back’s third answer is the cutback. A wide 9-technique is a defense saying “we will not let you have the edge”; outside zone’s answer is to stop trying for it and take what the alignment gives.











TipPredict the play



Drill 3. Third time this drive: the offense lines up in the same two-tight-end set it has run outside zone right from twice already. Both times the backside end (on the offense’s left) beat the U’s cut-off by crashing hard inside him at the snap, then flattened down the line and chased the back from behind (the orange arrow shows what he did; the faint dashed line is the back’s track on those runs). It is second-and-6. What call punishes him?


Show the Python
p = Play(ace_condensed(), even_front(+1, cb_w=10.0), los=40, to_go=6,
         title="Drill 3: the same look, third time this drive")
go_to(p, "BE", (-3.0, 1.4), "path", via=[(0.3, -4.0), (-1.3, -3.9), (-2.5, -1.6)])
f = draw(p, width_in=5.4, lateral=(-12, 12), window=(-8, 12.5))
branch(f, p, [(-7.0, 0.0), (-4.3, 2.6), (-1.3, 4.9), (1.5, 5.6)], color=style.MUTED, lw=1.3, dash=(0, (2, 2.5)))
say(f, p, -3.4, -7.2, "what this end did on\nthe last two zone runs", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
plt.show()








Figure 4.18: Drill 3: the same two-tight-end look for the third time. The orange arrow shows what the backside (left) end did on the last two outside zone runs: crash inside the U at the snap, then flatten behind the line, chasing the back’s track (faint dashes).











NoteAnswer





A bootleg the other way (left), probably naked. An end who crashes hard on every outside-zone fake is the exact defender the bootleg is built to beat: the quarterback fakes outside zone right, the end chases the fake, and the quarterback rolls left behind him with the flat open and a crosser coming across. The end has been beating the U’s cut-off anyway, so the boot turns his speed into a liability: the harder he crashes, the farther behind the quarterback he ends up. Second-and-6 is a comfortable down for it, too: even a short completion in the flat keeps the offense on schedule.
A second good answer: split zone, with a tight end kicking out that end. If the end is going to crash, block him and let the back cut back behind him. Coaches choose between the two by asking whether they want to punish the end (the boot, for a potential big play) or neutralize him (split zone, for a safer run). Either way, his habit has become information, and that is how a zone offense talks to itself across a drive.











TipPredict the play



Drill 4. This one is after the snap. Shotgun, back offset to the quarterback’s left, an H-back off the ball on the left. Figure 4.19 shows the first second: everyone’s first steps and paths. Inside or outside zone? Which tag is this? What is the quarterback looking at, and what does he do if that man chases the back?


Show the Python
off = [q for q in named_line(offense("gun_2x2")) if q.key in (*OL_NAMES, "QB", "Y", "Z", "X")]
off = [q.moved(d=-0.7, w=4.8) if q.key == "Y" else (q.moved(d=-1.5) if q.key == "Z" else q) for q in off]
off += [Player("H", "TE", "off", -1.5, -6.6, label="H"), Player("RB", "RB", "off", -5.0, -1.6, label="R")]
dfn = [q for q in front7() if q.key != "SAM"] + [D("SS", "SS", 5.0, -9.6, "SS"), D("NB", "NB", 4.5, 8.0, "NB")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10, title="Drill 4: name the play and the tag")
p.block("C", pts=[(0.9, 0.5)]); p.block("RG", pts=[(0.8, -0.8), (4.3, -0.4)])
p.block("RT", pts=[(0.9, 0.6)]); p.block("Y", pts=[(0.6, -0.6), (3.6, 1.5)])
p.block("LT", pts=[(0.9, 0.7)]); p.block("LG", pts=[(0.8, -0.6), (4.3, -0.8)])
go_to(p, "H", (4.1, -9.3), via=[(0.4, -7.6), (2.6, -9.0)])
go_to(p, "RB", (-1.4, 2.3), "run", via=[(-4.0, -0.4)])
p.read("BE")
f = draw(p, width_in=5.6, lateral=(-12.5, 11), window=(-8, 9))
plt.show()








Figure 4.19: Drill 4: the first second after the snap. Lines ending in a bar are blocks (look at the direction of each lineman’s first step); the dashed line from the quarterback shows where his eyes are.











NoteAnswer





Inside zone right, with an arc tag. The linemen’s first steps go up, not across, and the back is crossing the quarterback’s face toward the right B gap: inside zone. The H runs past the backside end without touching him and heads for the safety outside him: that is an arc block, not split zone (he would hit the end) and not a bootleg (he would turn into the flat and look for the ball). The quarterback is reading the unblocked backside end. If the end stays home, he hands off. If the end chases the back down the line, he pulls the ball and runs around the end, behind the H’s block on the safety.

title: Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback
text:
Takeaways

Zone blocking assigns blockers by rule, not by name: step play-side; block the man head-up on you or in your play-side gap; if nobody is, help the neighbor on your backside and climb to a linebacker. Because the rules are applied after the snap, slants and blitzes get picked up, and the same call re-pairs itself against every front.
Inside zone attacks the guard-tackle area with double teams that drive defenders backward; outside (wide) zone aims at the tight end’s outside leg and moves the defense sideways with reach-and-overtake blocks; stretch is the widest track, edge first; split zone adds a crossing H to kick the backside end. Tell them apart by the line’s first step (up or across) and the back’s aiming point.
The running back makes the play’s last decision: press the aiming point, then bang, bend or bounce, with one cut. On inside zone the order is bang-bend-bounce; on outside zone it is bounce-bang-bend.
The cutback is designed, not improvised: it works because the defense over-runs the play and the backside cut-off keeps the backside defenders out of the lane (in Gibbs’s Denver, often with a cut block, a legal but controversial low block that the rules have steadily narrowed).
Tags change one or two jobs to fix one problem: insert adds a lead blocker, arc runs past the unblocked end to block the next man while the quarterback reads the end, bash sends the back away and makes the quarterback the inside runner. Defenses fight back with penetration, a cutback player and coordinated run fits.
Outside zone’s biggest payoff is the bootleg that looks identical for the first second. The data shows zone running is efficient for a run game, not magic; its value is in what it sets up.

title: Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback
text:
Connections
Builds on: The Language of the Run Game (gaps, techniques, covered and uncovered, the core blocks) and the EPA primer in Downs, Distance, and Field Position.
Sets up:

Gap Schemes: the other blocking family (including duo), and when coaches choose it over zone.
Option Football: reading the unblocked end instead of blocking him, the idea behind arc and bash.
Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens: the bootleg and the play-action game built on outside zone.
Even Fronts, Odd and Hybrid Fronts and Run Fits: the fronts drawn generically here, named and explained from the defense’s side, and how defenses fit zone runs.
Contact Rules and Penalties as Strategy: the full rules on cut and chop blocks.

See also (case study): The Shanahan Tree: Wide Zone, Boots, and the Illusion of Complexity.
If you want to go deeper: Chris B. Brown’s The Art of Smart Football and his Smart Football writing on the inside and outside zone; Alex Gibbs’s zone-running clinic tapes, still widely circulated among coaches; and the Super Bowl XXXII broadcast and the 2019 49ers’ All-22, watched with nothing but the line’s first step and the running back’s feet in mind.






NoteGo deeper



Names you will hear. Zone vocabulary is a dialect map. Alex Gibbs called inside zone tight zone, and many coaches still do. Some analysts describe a mid zone between inside and outside zone, in which the play-side tackle pushes the end outward instead of trying to reach him, so the back’s read moves to the defensive tackles; one coach-analyst used the name for Sean McVay’s Rams’ base run.27 Split zone is also called zone slice, and bash is sometimes spelled out as back away. And duo, a two-back or one-back run with double teams that a casual viewer can mistake for inside zone, is not a zone play at all: the linemen do not take zone steps and the back reads a linebacker. It belongs to the gap family in 03-03.








NoteGo deeper



From diagrams to real tracking data. Every animation in this chapter is a gridiron simulation written in NFL Big Data Bowl (BDB) coordinates, the format of the league’s public tracking-data competition, so real tracking data drops into the same drawing code. The 2025 Big Data Bowl release (2022 season, weeks 1–9) includes pre-snap and post-snap frames for every player, and its plays.csv carries a run-concept label from PFF, so you can pull real outside-zone runs and watch the line step together. The data is hosted on Kaggle (a data-science competition site) and needs your own free login, so the code for this (in the web edition of this chapter, under “Show the Python”) is not run when this book is built.


Show the Python (real Big Data Bowl tracking; not run in the build)
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb, show_animation

plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
oz = plays[plays["pff_runConceptPrimary"].astype(str).str.upper().str.contains("OUTSIDE ZONE")]
print(len(oz), "outside zone runs")
g, pl = oz.iloc[0][["gameId", "playId"]]

trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")
one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=g, play_id=pl)
show_animation(one, times=[0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.6])   # same call as the simulated plays

title: Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage
text:
Why a defense would lie
Third-and-7 from midfield. As the offense breaks the huddle, the broadcast’s high camera shows two safeties standing 13 yards deep, one on each side of the field, with a wide-open patch of grass between them. The quarterback sees it too. Two deep safeties usually mean the deep middle is empty, so he plans to throw a deep in-cut right into that patch. He takes the snap, sets his feet, and lets it go, and a safety who had been standing 13 yards deep and 7 yards to the side is suddenly sitting at 11 yards, right in the throwing lane. Interception. On the replay the analyst circles both safeties and says “the coverage rotated.” What does that mean? Why did one safety sprint to the middle while the other one came forward? And if defenses can do that, why does anyone bother to read the defense before the snap? This chapter is about the gap between what a defense shows and what it plays, and about the last half-second in which that gap closes.
You’ll be able to…
Start with what the quarterback is trying to do before the snap. In the 20 or so seconds he spends at the line, he decides a lot: which way his linemen slide in pass protection, which defender he must throw away from if that defender blitzes, which side of the field his progression starts on, and whether the called play is any good against what he sees. If it isn’t, he can change it (The Pre-Snap Phase). Almost all of that depends on one question: what coverage is this? If he knows the coverage before the snap, he knows roughly where the open grass will be before anyone has moved. Then the play is half over before it starts.
The defense, meanwhile, has to put eleven people somewhere. And where they stand leaks information, because of plain physics. A safety can only cover ground so fast. If he is going to guard the deep middle of the field, he has to stand somewhere from which he can get there before the ball does. If a cornerback is going to cover one receiver man-to-man, he tends to line up facing that receiver, close to him, on the side he wants to protect. A defense that simply lined up where its call works best would be handing the quarterback its call sheet.
Disguise is the answer: lining up in a way that hides or misrepresents the coverage the defense will actually play. It comes in three flavours, and good defenses use all of them:
There’s an asymmetry in the rules that makes this possible. The offense must be set: after a shift, all eleven players have to be still for a full second before the snap, and only one player may be in motion when the ball is snapped, and not toward the line. The defense has no such rule. Defenders may move, shift, walk up and back out as much as they like before the snap, as long as they stay out of the neutral zone (the strip, one ball long, between the two teams) and don’t use words or acts meant to disconcert the offense at the snap, such as imitating its snap count.1 The offense has to hold still and be read, while the defense can keep moving.

title: Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage
text:
Show one thing, play another. Line up in a two-high shell and play a one-high coverage, or the reverse. This is the dramatic kind, and the next three sections are about it.
Show the same thing every time. Line up in one shell for nearly everything, and play many coverages out of it. The quarterback isn’t fooled so much as left without information. This is the quieter kind, and it is how the two-high defenses that spread through the NFL after 2018 live. Case Study: Fangio’s Two-High Revolution and Macdonald’s Answer tells that story in full.
Move at the right moment. Hold a picture until the last instant and change it at the snap, so there’s no time to react. We’ll call that late rotation below.







ImportantWhy it exists



Disguise is about time. A quarterback who knows the coverage before the snap can decide where to throw before the pass rush has started. A quarterback who must work it out after the snap spends part of his roughly 2.5 to 3 seconds of protection just finding out what he is looking at. The defense isn’t trying to make the quarterback wrong so much as late. A late quarterback holds the ball, takes sacks, throws into windows that close, or settles for a short checkdown.




What disguise costs

The real job starts from the wrong spot. A safety who shows two-high but is really the robber has to travel to his real landmark; one who shows one-high in the box and is really a deep-half player has a long way to run. Every yard of travel is time out of position.
The run defense gets worse. A nickel defense usually has six or seven players near the line (four linemen, two linebackers, sometimes the nickel), the box. A safety who comes down makes it seven or eight, but a safety standing 13 yards deep who is supposed to be that extra run defender arrives late. A safety walked down to look like a run defender who is really bailing to a deep half has left the box one man short. Offenses that run the ball well punish disguise by simply handing it off (Run Fits and Box Math).
Communication and mistakes. Every rotation is a little play inside the play, with its own timing and its own way to go wrong. When one safety rotates and the other doesn’t, the defense ends up with two players in one zone and nobody in another: the “bust” you see when a receiver runs untouched through the middle of the field.
Practice time. A defense that can play five coverages from one look has to rehearse all five from that look, and every extra starting look multiplies the reps. Something has to give. Some defenses keep one look and many coverages (flavour 2 above); others keep a short list of coverages and practise reaching each one from several looks (flavours 1 and 3). Few can afford both.







NoteMadden vs. real life



In a video game the defense picks a play from a menu, and each defender walks to the spot that play’s diagram gives him. What you see is close to what was called. In the NFL, alignment is a separate decision from the call. Coordinators design their calls so that several coverages start from the same picture, and coach players to hold that picture until a set moment. Real quarterbacks are taught to treat the pre-snap shell as a hypothesis, a best guess they expect to confirm or overturn in the first second after the snap.

title: Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage
section: The physics of a disguise: what leaks before the snap
text:
The physics of a disguise: what leaks before the snap
If you can’t hide where you’re going, you can at least make it hard to see. But the distances involved put limits on what a defense can fake, and those limits are exactly what a good quarterback (and now you) can read.
Some rough numbers. A deep pass is usually released around 3 seconds after the snap (in 2025 the middle half of throws travelling 20 or more yards left between 2.6 and 3.6 seconds).2 But the safety’s real deadline is earlier: he has to be on top of the receiver before the receiver runs past him, and in this chapter’s simulated plays a slot receiver running up the seam is 15 yards downfield about two seconds after the snap. The safety also can’t sprint at the snap. His first step or two are a read (is it a pass? where are the quarterback’s eyes?), and a backpedal covers ground noticeably more slowly than turning and running. The fastest safeties top out around 22 miles an hour, roughly 10 yards a second, but a safety reading the quarterback is rarely anywhere near that.3
So give him a working speed of 5 to 6.5 yards a second once he goes (the figure the simulated plays use) and a few tenths of a second to read. That leaves about 1.6 seconds of running before the seam receiver arrives: roughly 8 to 10 yards. A safety 13 yards deep and 7.5 yards from the middle (a few yards outside the hash) is about 8 yards from the deep-middle landmark at 16 or 17 yards: inside the budget. One standing on the numbers, about 14 yards from the middle, is about 14 yards away: far outside it.
Each defender’s real job therefore draws a circle around his real landmark. He can line up anywhere inside it, and the disguise has to fit inside every defender’s circle at once. Within the circle there is still a trade. A safety who will really be a robber at 10 or 11 yards can line up at 13 and still get there, which keeps the two-high picture intact, but the trip costs him time. Lining up at 11 makes his job easy, and it is also a tell. Every disguise is that bargain, made defender by defender: the closer to the real job, the easier the job and the louder the tell. (These are model numbers for teaching the idea, not measurements; with the real tracking data in Tracking Data and the Big Data Bowl you can measure the circles.)
That is why disguises leak. Here is what to look at, and why each one tells you something. The figure shows the textbook two-high spots as faint outlines so you can see how far each defender has cheated from them.


Show the Python
off, dfn = nickel_vs_2x2()
tell_moves = {"SS": (10.0, 5.0), "FS": (13.5, -5.5), "LCB": (1.2, -15.8), "RCB": (1.2, 15.8),
              "NB": (1.5, -8.2), "WILL": (4.5, 7.0)}
textbook = {k: (pl.d, pl.w) for k, pl in ((q.key, q) for q in dfn) if k in ("SS", "FS", "LCB", "RCB")}
dfn = [p.moved(d=tell_moves[p.key][0], w=tell_moves[p.key][1]) if p.key in tell_moves else p for p in dfn]
tells = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=7)
tells.highlight("SS", "FS")
fld = tells.draw(lateral=(-22, 22), window=(-7.5, 18.5))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, tells, widths=True)
ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
for k, (d0, w0) in textbook.items():
    gx, gy = fld.xy(*tells.to_abs(d0, w0))
    ghost_marker(fld.ax, float(gx), float(gy), "", ppy, color=style.MUTED)
pointer(fld, tells, "shallower and narrower:\nhe can reach the box\nor the hole, not a deep half",
        (16.6, 13.0), (10.0, 5.0))
pointer(fld, tells, "narrower than usual:\nhe can reach the deep middle", (17.0, -12.0), (13.5, -5.5))
pointer(fld, tells, "press, eyes on the receiver,\noutside shade: man,\nexpecting help inside", (10.0, -11.0),
        (1.2, -15.8))
pointer(fld, tells, "nickel tight on the slot", (-4.6, -12.0), (1.5, -8.2))
fld.ax.legend(handles=[Patch(facecolor="none", edgecolor=style.MUTED, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (2, 1.2)),
                             label="textbook two-high spot")],
              loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0.0), fontsize=7.5, frameon=False)
plt.show()








Figure 5.1: A two-high shell that isn’t going to stay two-high. The dashed outlines are the textbook two-high spots (safeties 13 deep, a few yards outside the hashes; corners 7 off). Against them, the right safety (SS) is three yards shallower and two and a half yards narrower, and the left safety (FS) is two yards narrower. The corners (CB) are pressed on the outside receivers, square to them, shading slightly outside (outside leverage): man technique, expecting help inside. The nickel ($) is tight on the left slot receiver, H; the slot to the right, Y, is the tight end, with the Will (W) over him. Each detail on its own means little. Together they suggest a rotation to one-high man at the snap: Cover 1, with the SS as a robber in the hole and the FS in the deep middle.






Safety depth. Deep-zone safeties in a two-high shell usually stand 12–14 yards off the ball. A safety at 8–10 yards is probably either coming down (into the box, the flat or the hole as a robber) or about to sprint backward, and the second is hard to do well. Why it tells: the deeper he is, the fewer underneath jobs he can reach in time; the shallower, the fewer deep ones.
Safety width. A safety within about 8 yards of the middle (on the hash or a few yards outside it) can reach the deep middle. One splitting the hash and the numbers, 9 to 11 yards out, is probably staying on his half of the field. When one safety pinches toward the middle and the other widens or creeps down, the shell is leaning toward one-high. Why: the deep middle is a destination, and the safety who will go there likes to start close to it.
Corner technique, then leverage. Two different questions. Technique (stance, eyes, depth) says man or zone: a man corner is square to his receiver with his eyes on him; a zone corner is turned toward the quarterback, seven or eight yards off and ready to backpedal or turn and run to a deep third, or five or six yards off and flat-footed (a squat Cover 2 corner). Leverage says where his help is. A corner who gives up the inside expects a safety or robber there (Cover 1, Cover 3). One who takes away the inside expects help over the top or has none (2-Man, Cover 0). Why it tells: the corner’s technique has to match his job, and technique is hard to fake. Corners can disguise too: a corner pressed in a two-high look who bails at the snap, one who shows deep-third depth and comes up into the flat (the cloud rotation), or a corner and safety who trade jobs (an invert: the safety comes down to the flat and the corner bails to the deep half, as Palms does on one side). They have less room to lie than safeties do, but an invert means the deep player can be a corner, so on the replay watch the two deepest defenders, whoever they are.
Eyes and weight. Zone defenders look at the quarterback. Man defenders look at their man. A safety leaning forward on his toes is thinking about coming downhill; one sitting on his heels is thinking about getting depth. This is the hardest tell to see on a broadcast, but the All-22 film coaches use (a high, wide camera showing all 22 players) shows it.
Timing. When does anyone move? A safety who drifts toward his real spot during the cadence (coaches say he creeps or walks down) is giving away his rotation; one who stands still until the ball moves is not. That discipline has a name, late rotation, and its own section below.
Situation and tendency. A defense that always rotates to the field on third-and-long has a habit opponents will have found on film (Tendencies). The best disguises also break the defense’s own patterns.







CautionCommon misconception



“Two high safeties means Cover 2.” It doesn’t. Two-high is a shell, a picture, not a coverage. From the same two-high look a defense can play Cover 2, 2-Man, quarters, Cover 6 or Palms, or rotate into Cover 3 or Cover 1 at the snap. What the shell tells you is which coverages are easy from here, and so which ones are likely. To name the coverage, look again one second after the snap.

title: Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage
section: Post-snap rotation, part 1: two-high becomes one-high
text:
Post-snap rotation, part 1: two-high becomes one-high
Post-snap rotation is defenders (almost always the safeties) moving at the snap from the shell they showed into a different one. The most common version starts two-high and ends one-high: one safety races to the deep middle and the other comes down. Where the down safety lands decides the coverage. If he goes to the flat, it’s a sky rotation into Cover 3. To the curl area, a buzz rotation. To the hole in the middle of the field at 10 or 11 yards, it’s Cover 3 or Cover 1 with a robber. In Cover 3 robber the robber is one of the four underneath defenders: the two curl-flat players and the hook player keep their zones and the robber takes the hole in front of the deep safety. (You’ll also hear rat: some staffs use it for any robber, others only for a linebacker sitting in the low hole at 5 to 8 yards, as in “Cover 1 rat”.) (Cover 3 built all three from a one-high start; here they start from two.)
Coaches describe all this movement with a pile of short verbs, and some of them mean different things in different mouths. This chapter uses them like this:







Word
What the defender does




rotate, spin
The whole shell turns: one safety goes to the post, the other comes down. “He spun down” and “he spun to the post” are both used; the verb names the rotation, not the direction.


come down, drop down
A deep safety moves toward the line, into the box, the flat, the curl or the hole.


bail
A defender who looked shallow turns and runs to a deep zone at the snap.


sink
A defender gives ground a few yards straight back, keeping his eyes forward.


creep, walk down, cheat
Small moves toward the real job before the snap; they are tells.


rob
Sit in a throwing lane (usually the hole) and jump in-breaking routes.


poach
A backside safety leaves his side to help on the trips side (see below).





Show the Python
def rob_play():
    off, dfn = nickel_vs_2x2()
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=55, to_go=7)
    # pre-snap: nobody in the secondary moves. The Mike's tiny shuffle only gives the play
    # pre-snap frames to draw (gridiron starts the clock at the first pre-snap movement).
    p.motion("MIKE", to=(4.5, 1.6), speed=0.12)
    # offense: dagger to the right (the seam clears out, the dig comes in behind it)
    p.route("Y", r.path((12, -1.0), (20, -2.0))); p.route("Z", r.dig(12, 11)); p.route("X", r.go(20))
    p.route("H", r.hitch(5)); p.route("RB", r.flat(1.5, 6), side=-1)
    p.dropback(2.5)
    p.pass_to("Z", t=1.7)
    protect(p)
    # defense: four rush; the rest rotate to Cover 3 with a robber
    p.drop("FS", (16.5, 0.0), speed=6.5)
    p.drop("SS", (11.0, 4.0), speed=4.5)
    # the boundary corner keeps his cushion on X's go route; the field corner squeezes over the dig
    p.drop("LCB", (20.5, -16.0), speed=5.5); p.drop("RCB", (15.0, 15.5))
    p.drop("NB", (6.5, 12.0)); p.drop("WILL", (6.5, -11.0)); p.drop("MIKE", (7.0, -2.0))
    p.highlight("FS", "SS")
    return p


rob = rob_play()
ROB_T = [-1.4, 0.0, 1.0, 2.6]
if PDF:
    strip(rob, ROB_T, ["−1.4 s · Two-high, as shown", "Snap · nothing has moved",
                       "+1.0 s · FS to the post, SS comes down", "+2.6 s · Cover 3 robber: the dig is thrown into him"],
          ghosts=("FS", "SS"), ghost_t=-1.4, window=(-8.5, 23.0),
          notes_at={3: [("robber", (13.4, 8.6)), ("deep middle", (20.2, -4.5))]})
    plt.show()
else:
    show_animation(rob, times=ROB_T)





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 5.2: Two-high rotates to Cover 3 with a robber. Before the snap (panel 1) both safeties sit 13 yards deep, one on each side: the deep middle looks open. Panels 1 and 2 are identical, and that is the point: no defensive back moves until the ball does. At the snap the free safety (FS) runs to the deep middle while the strong safety (SS) comes down and in to the hole at about 11 yards, right where Z’s dig is heading; the ball (panel 4) is thrown into him. The dashed outlines show where the safeties stood before the snap. The corners turn and run to deep thirds (the left one stays on top of X’s go route); underneath, the Will and the nickel ($) take the curl-flat zones, the Mike the hook and the SS the hole. In print, the four panels are four moments of one play.




Follow the play from the quarterback’s side. Before the snap he sees two-high and an empty deep middle. Against two-high, the space between the safeties and behind the linebackers is often where the ball should go, and dagger (a seam route that pulls the underneath and deep defenders away, with a deep dig coming in behind it; see Dropback Concepts) is built to hit it. Here Y’s seam bends slightly inside to push the middle open. At the snap, the defense changes the answer. The free safety’s sprint to the middle puts a defender over the top of the seam. The strong safety’s short trip down and in puts him exactly where the dig is going to arrive. The quarterback who decided before the snap, and throws on time without looking, throws it to the robber.
Notice the distances. The free safety travels about 8 yards to the deep middle, inside the 8-to-10 yard circle from the previous section. That’s possible only because he lined up 7 or 8 yards from the middle, not on the numbers. The strong safety travels about 4 yards. Neither had far to go, which is the whole design. The shell was two-high, but each safety was standing where his real job was still within reach.
The same rotation can land in man coverage instead: Cover 1 robber. The safeties move exactly as they do here, so the difference is in the corners. In Cover 3 they turn and run to deep thirds with their eyes on the quarterback; in Cover 1 they stay on their receivers, pressing or trailing them wherever they go. One second after the snap, the corners tell you which.
What beats the robber, once the quarterback sees him? The throws he left behind. He has come down from one side, so the seam and the curl on that side are thinner, and his spot in the hole is in front of the deep safety, so a route that gets behind him (a post or deep crosser) is open if the post safety is late. The rest of Cover 3’s weaknesses are still there too: the seams between the deep middle and each deep third, and four underneath defenders who can’t cover every short zone, so stress the curl-flat defender on the far side with a route in front of him and one behind. Concepts Versus Coverages builds the quarterback’s side of this.






ImportantWhy it exists: two-high to one-high



What it solves. It gets an extra defender near the line against the run, or a robber against in-breaking routes, without announcing either before the snap. Offenses facing two-high tend to run the ball, because with both safeties 12 or more yards deep only six or seven defenders are near the line to face the offense’s blockers, and to throw between the safeties. The rotation punishes both: the down safety adds a run defender or sits in the throwing lane.
What it gives up. The rotating safety starts late and from deep, so he arrives in the box after the run has started. The safety spinning to the middle has a long run, so a quick deep throw outside him (a post or a deep corner route released before he gets there) can beat it. And the robber looks only at the quarterback, so a quarterback who looks him off with his eyes and shoulders, then throws elsewhere, can move him out of the play (Concepts Versus Coverages).



Which safety comes down? A rule, not a whim
A defense doesn’t decide on the field which safety rotates. The call says so, usually by tying the rotation to something the offense shows: rotate to the passing strength (the side with more receivers), to the field (the wide side), toward motion, or the other way, weak or to the boundary. Staffs build names for these out of a direction and a landing spot (“sky strong,” “buzz weak” and the like); one of Nick Saban’s trips calls, for example, drops the safety down to the passing strength.4 Before the snap, then, your best guess about direction is:

Toward the strength or the motion is the default. That is where the extra receivers are, so that is where an extra underneath defender helps most. Quarterbacks are taught to expect it.
Away from the strength is itself a disguise. A defense that knows the quarterback expects the strong safety to come down can spin the weak safety down instead, so the robber appears on the side the quarterback thought was clean.
Look for the tells on one safety, not both. The safety who is shallower, narrower or leaning forward is the likely down safety; the other one is the likely post safety. Combine that with the strength of the formation and you can usually call the direction.

title: Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage
section: Post-snap rotation, part 2: one-high becomes two-high
text:
Post-snap rotation, part 2: one-high becomes two-high
The rotation can run the other way. Show one-high: a single safety deep in the middle, the other safety walked down near the box, corners off and ready to bail, the classic Cover 3 or Cover 1 picture. Then, at the snap, the deep safety bails to one deep half and the down safety bails to the other. The corners, instead of bailing to deep thirds, hold their depth and widen into the flats, the Cover 2 corner’s job. That is Cover 2 (or, with man coverage underneath, 2-Man), reached from a one-high start.


Show the Python
def spin_play():
    off, dfn = nickel_vs_2x2("single_high")
    dfn = [p.moved(d=13.5, w=0.0) if p.key == "FS" else p for p in dfn]
    dfn = [p.moved(d=9.0, w=6.0) if p.key == "SS" else p for p in dfn]
    dfn = [p.moved(d=8.0) if p.pos == "CB" else p for p in dfn]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=55, to_go=7)
    p.motion("MIKE", to=(4.5, 1.6), speed=0.12)      # pre-snap frames only; the secondary stays still
    # offense: outs outside (good against one-high with off corners), seams inside
    p.route("X", r.out(8, 5)); p.route("Z", r.out(8, 5)); p.route("H", r.seam(20))
    p.route("Y", r.path((10, 0.0), (19, -5.0)))            # a seam that bends into the open middle
    p.route("RB", r.flat(1.5, 6), side=-1)
    p.dropback(2.5)
    protect(p)
    p.drop("FS", (17.0, -9.5), speed=6.5)
    p.drop("SS", (17.0, 9.5), speed=6.5)
    p.drop("LCB", (8.5, -19.0), speed=2.5); p.drop("RCB", (8.5, 19.0), speed=2.5)   # sink and widen
    p.drop("NB", (8.0, 9.0)); p.drop("WILL", (8.0, -8.0)); p.drop("MIKE", (8.5, 1.0))
    p.highlight("FS", "SS")
    return p


spin = spin_play()
SPIN_T = [-1.4, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0]
if PDF:
    strip(spin, SPIN_T, ["−1.4 s · One-high, as shown", "Snap · nothing has moved", "+1.0 s · Both safeties bail",
                         "+2.0 s · Cover 2: halves, corners in the flats"],
          ghosts=("FS", "SS", "LCB", "RCB"), ghost_t=-1.4,
          notes_at={3: [("½", (18.4, -13.0)), ("½", (18.4, 13.0)), ("middle open", (17.0, 0.5))]})
    plt.show()
else:
    show_animation(spin, times=SPIN_T)





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 5.3: One-high bails to Cover 2. Before the snap the free safety (FS) is alone in the deep middle and the strong safety (SS) is down at 9 yards: middle of the field closed. Panels 1 and 2 are the same picture: no defensive back moves before the snap. At the snap both safeties bail to deep halves, landing between the hash and the numbers, and the corners (CB), who looked as though they would bail to deep thirds, hold their depth and widen three yards toward the sideline (compare each corner with his dashed outline). That puts them right where the outside receivers’ 8-yard outs are breaking. They play the flat from on top, at about 8 yards rather than the flat’s usual 0 to 6, because a corner who starts deep keeps the out in front of him. What opened is the deep middle between the two safeties: H’s seam holds the left safety, and Y bends his route inside into the open middle.




Why bother? One-high with off corners invites certain throws. With a safety in the deep middle and the corners backing off, the outside is where the quarterback looks: quick outs and hitches in front of the bailing corners, curls under them, back-shoulder throws to receivers facing one-on-one coverage. The bail to Cover 2 takes all of that away at once. The corners now sit exactly where the outs are going, and there’s a safety over the top on each side to take away the deep ball outside.
What opens instead is the deep middle, between the two safeties, which is exactly what the quarterback ruled out before the snap. A quarterback who reads the safeties after the snap sees them split and throws between them, up the seam or on a post (the throw that Cover 2 and Tampa 2 shows the Tampa 2 Mike running to carry). The other Cover 2 window is the sideline hole shot, the gap behind the corner and in front of the half-field safety, 18 to 22 yards deep. A quarterback who decided before the snap throws the out into a waiting corner.






ImportantWhy it exists: one-high to two-high



What it solves. It lets a defense look like it is loading up against the run, with the down safety near the box, and still play two deep defenders against the pass. Offenses that see one-high often check to throws outside or to deep shots against single (one-on-one) coverage. The bail punishes both.
What it gives up. The down safety was a run defender in the picture, and now he’s running away from the line, so a run against this look faces one fewer defender than it seemed to. He also has the longest trip on the field, 8 or more yards of depth plus width, so a fast vertical route outside can reach his area before he does.

title: Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage
section: Late rotation: winning the last half-second
text:
Late rotation: winning the last half-second
The two plays above have something in common. In both, nothing moves until the snap. That is the difference between a rotation the quarterback can see and one he can’t.
Late rotation means timing the rotation to start at the snap or just after it, rather than during the cadence. A defense that rotates early (safeties drifting into place while the quarterback calls signals) gives him a free look: he sees the real coverage, still has time to change the play, and the disguise has bought nothing. A defense that rotates late shows him the real coverage only after the play has begun. He has to recognise it while dropping back, with the pass rush coming.
It is also why late rotation is risky. A safety who starts moving at the snap is a step behind one who was already there, so the rotation has to be fast and the distances have to be short. Every late rotation is a race between the safety and the first throw.
The clearest way to see a rotation is to track just the two safeties, how deep each one is and how far from the middle, frame by frame from three seconds before the snap to two seconds after. Player-tracking data records exactly that: every player’s position ten times a second, from chips in the shoulder pads. The figure below is built from simulated plays written out in the format of the NFL’s Big Data Bowl tracking files (that chapter builds it step by step from the real files).


Show the Python (simulated BDB-format tracking used by the next two figures)
def _seg(p, key, start, end, tau, speed):
    """Move `key` from start to end at `speed`, starting at time tau (negative = before the snap)."""
    start, end = np.array(start, float), np.array(end, float)
    L = float(np.linalg.norm(end - start))
    if tau < 0:                                  # part of the trip happens before the snap
        pre = min(L, speed * -tau)
        mid = start + (end - start) * (pre / L if L else 0)
        p.motion(key, to=tuple(mid), speed=max(pre / -tau, 0.05))
        if L - pre > 0.05:
            p.drop(key, tuple(end), speed=speed)
    else:
        p.drop(key, tuple(end), speed=speed, delay=tau)


def sim_play(kind, rng, tau=None, play_id=0):
    """One simulated dropback, returned as Big Data Bowl-style tracking rows (10 frames a second).

    kind: 'stay2' (two-high shown and played), 'rot1' (two-high shown, rotated to one-high),
          'stay1' (one-high shown and played), 'spin2' (one-high shown, bailed to two-high).
    tau : when the safeties start their post-snap move (seconds; negative = before the snap).
    """
    off, dfn = nickel_vs_2x2()
    side = rng.choice([-1, 1])
    if kind in ("stay2", "rot1"):
        d1, d2 = rng.uniform(11.5, 14.0, 2)
        w1, w2 = rng.uniform(5.5, 8.5, 2)
        fs0, ss0 = (d1, -side * w1), (d2, side * w2)
    else:
        fs0 = (rng.uniform(13.0, 15.5), rng.uniform(-1.5, 1.5))
        ss0 = (rng.uniform(7.0, 10.0), side * rng.uniform(4.0, 7.0))
    dfn = [q.moved(d=fs0[0], w=fs0[1]) if q.key == "FS" else q for q in dfn]
    dfn = [q.moved(d=ss0[0], w=ss0[1]) if q.key == "SS" else q for q in dfn]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=10)
    p.motion("MIKE", to=(4.5, 1.5), speed=0.1)   # a slow 3-second shuffle so frames start 3 s early
    p.route("X", r.go(22)); p.route("Z", r.go(22)); p.route("H", r.seam(20)); p.route("Y", r.seam(20))
    p.dropback(2.5)
    tau = rng.uniform(-0.9, 0.3) if tau is None else tau
    v = rng.uniform(5.0, 6.5)
    if kind == "stay2":
        _seg(p, "FS", fs0, (fs0[0] + rng.uniform(2, 4), fs0[1] - side * rng.uniform(0.5, 2.5)), max(tau, 0), v * .6)
        _seg(p, "SS", ss0, (ss0[0] + rng.uniform(2, 4), ss0[1] + side * rng.uniform(0.5, 2.5)), max(tau, 0), v * .6)
    elif kind == "rot1":
        _seg(p, "FS", fs0, (rng.uniform(15.5, 18.0), rng.uniform(-1.0, 1.0)), tau, v)
        _seg(p, "SS", ss0, (rng.uniform(8.0, 10.5), side * rng.uniform(3.0, 6.0)), tau, v * 0.8)
    elif kind == "stay1":
        _seg(p, "FS", fs0, (fs0[0] + rng.uniform(2, 4), fs0[1]), max(tau, 0), v * 0.6)
        _seg(p, "SS", ss0, (ss0[0] + rng.uniform(-1, 1), ss0[1] + side * rng.uniform(1, 4)), max(tau, 0), v * 0.6)
    else:
        _seg(p, "FS", fs0, (rng.uniform(15.5, 18.0), -side * rng.uniform(9.0, 12.0)), tau, v)
        _seg(p, "SS", ss0, (rng.uniform(15.5, 18.0), side * rng.uniform(9.0, 12.0)), tau, v)
    trk = p.to_tracking(fps=FPS, play_id=play_id)   # columns: gameId, playId, nflId, frameId, x, y, s, a, ...
    trk["kind"], trk["los"], trk["ball_y"] = kind, p.los, p.ball_y
    return trk


def shell_at(frame, deep=10.0, split=3.5):
    """Classify one frame of any BDB-style play: 'two-high' if two or more defenders are 10+ yards
    deep and none of them is within 3.5 yards (sideways) of the ball; otherwise 'one-high'.
    Meant for pre-snap frames only: after the snap, a corner bailing past 10 yards would count."""
    dfn = frame[frame["side"] == "def"]
    d = dfn["x"] - frame["los"].iloc[0]
    w = (frame["ball_y"].iloc[0] - dfn["y"]).abs()
    deep_w = w[d >= deep]
    return "two-high" if len(deep_w) >= 2 and deep_w.min() >= split else "one-high"




Show the Python
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
rows = []
# 30 honest plays; 30 rotations, 22 of them late (start at or just after the snap) and 8 early
taus = [0.0] * 30 + list(rng.uniform(0.0, 0.25, 22)) + list(rng.uniform(-1.0, -0.5, 8))
for i, kind in enumerate(["stay2"] * 30 + ["rot1"] * 30):
    trk = sim_play(kind, rng, tau=taus[i], play_id=i + 1)
    rows.append(trk[trk["displayName"].isin(["FS", "SS"])])
saf = pd.concat(rows, ignore_index=True)
saf["frame_rel"] = np.round(saf["time"] * FPS).astype(int)       # frames from the snap
saf = saf[saf["frame_rel"].between(-30, 20)].copy()
saf["depth"] = saf["x"] - saf["los"]
saf["from_middle"] = (saf["ball_y"] - saf["y"]).abs()        # sideways from the ball (= mid-field here)
# in rotated plays, the safety who finishes deepest is the one who spun to the middle
end = saf[saf["frame_rel"] == 20].set_index(["playId", "displayName"])["depth"]
deepest = end.groupby(level=0).idxmax().map(lambda t: t[1])
saf["role"] = np.where(saf["kind"] == "stay2", "stayed",
                       np.where(saf["displayName"] == saf["playId"].map(deepest), "spun", "dropped"))
COL = {"stayed": style.SERIES[0], "spun": style.SERIES[1], "dropped": style.SERIES[2]}
LAB = {"stayed": "stayed two-high", "spun": "ran to the middle", "dropped": "came down"}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.5, 5.6), sharex=True)
for ax, col, ylab in ((axes[0], "depth", "Depth past the line of scrimmage (yd)"),
                      (axes[1], "from_middle", "Sideways from the middle (yd)")):
    ax.axvspan(-30, 0, color=style.GRID, alpha=0.35, lw=0)
    for _, g in saf.groupby(["playId", "displayName"]):
        ax.plot(g["frame_rel"], g[col], color=COL[g["role"].iloc[0]], lw=0.6, alpha=0.35)
    for role, g in saf.groupby("role"):
        med = g.groupby("frame_rel")[col].median()
        ax.plot(med.index, med.values, color=COL[role], lw=2.4)
        v = med.iloc[-1] + ({"spun": 0.7, "stayed": -0.7}.get(role, 0.0) if col == "depth" else 0.0)
        ax.text(20.6, v, LAB[role], color=COL[role], fontsize=8, va="center", fontweight="bold")
    ax.axvline(0, color=style.INK_2, lw=1.0)
    ax.set_ylabel(ylab, fontsize=8.5)
    ax.set_xlim(-30, 30)
axes[0].text(-29, axes[0].get_ylim()[1] - 0.3, "before the snap", fontsize=8, color=style.INK_2, va="top")
axes[0].text(0.6, axes[0].get_ylim()[1] - 0.3, "after the snap", fontsize=8, color=style.INK_2, va="top")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Frames from the snap (10 frames = 1 second)", fontsize=8.5)
axes[0].set_title("The two safeties around the snap (simulated, BDB-format tracking)", fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 5.4: Simulated, BDB-format tracking (not real plays): the two safeties on 60 plays that all showed two-high, from 30 frames (3 seconds) before the snap to 20 frames after. Thin lines are single plays; thick lines are medians. Top panel: how deep each safety is. Bottom panel: how far he is sideways from the middle of the field (0 = straight down the middle). On 30 plays the shell stayed two-high (blue): both safeties drift back and a little wider. On the other 30 it rotated: one safety ran to the middle (orange: his sideways distance falls to about zero) while the other came down to robber depth (green: depth falls to about 9 or 10 yards, and he also pinches in from about 7 yards to under 5, toward the hole). We told the simulation to start 22 of the 30 rotations at the snap (late rotation), so the thick lines barely move before frame 0 and split sharply after it; the other 8 start 5 to 10 frames early, and their thin lines peel away before the snap: rotations the quarterback could have seen.





Read it as a picture of the idea, not as evidence: the simulation only plays back the timings we gave it. What it shows is the shape to look for. A rotation is a divergence: before it starts, the rotated plays and the honest plays are indistinguishable, and within about ten frames (one second) the safeties are in completely different places. When the divergence starts before the snap, even by half a second, the quarterback still has time to use it: he can change the protection, check to another play, or decide which side his progression starts on. A defense coached for late rotation pushes that starting point to zero or past it. (In these simulated plays the ball sits in the middle of the field, so “sideways from the middle” is also sideways from the ball. With the ball on a hash the two differ by about 3 yards, and coaches set the post safety’s landmark by one or the other depending on the system.)
Real safeties won’t look this tidy. They shuffle, bounce on their toes, take false steps and adjust to motion, so real tracking lines are noisier and the plays are far less alike. We haven’t checked these simulated paths against real tracking; the chapter on tracking data does that with the real files.
With the real Big Data Bowl files, the same figure takes a few more steps: load the tracking weeks, flip every play so the offense moves the same way, find the two deepest defenders, and align every play on its snap frame. On the website, the code under “Show the Python” shows the shape of it. It isn’t run here, because the files need a free Kaggle login to download; Tracking Data and the Big Data Bowl walks through it on real plays.


Show the Python (the same figure from real Big Data Bowl 2025 files; not run here)
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb

# BDB 2025: 2022 season, Weeks 1-9, with pre-snap frames. Files from Kaggle (login required).
plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")          # has pff_passCoverage, absoluteYardlineNumber
trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")

frames = []
# One bdb.prepare() call per play is slow over nine weeks (minutes, not seconds). For speed, group
# the tracking by (gameId, playId) once and prepare each group; this loop is written for clarity.
for (g, pl), _ in plays.groupby(["gameId", "playId"]):
    one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=g, play_id=pl)   # offense moving +x, time 0 = snap
    ball = one[(one["side"] == "ball") & (one["frameType"] == "SNAP")]
    los, ball_y = float(ball["x"].iloc[0]), float(ball["y"].iloc[0])
    one["frame_rel"] = (one["time"] * 10).round().astype(int)
    # "Safeties" = the two deepest defenders one second before the snap, not roster FS/SS:
    # teams play three-safety nickel, and corners rotate to the post in cloud or invert calls.
    pre = one[(one["side"] == "def") & (one["frame_rel"] == -10)]
    ids = pre.nlargest(2, "x")["nflId"]
    s = one[one["nflId"].isin(ids)].copy()
    s["depth"] = s["x"] - los
    s["from_middle"] = (s["y"] - ball_y).abs()             # sideways from the ball, as in the simulation
    frames.append(s[s["frame_rel"].between(-30, 20)].assign(gameId=g, playId=pl))
saf = pd.concat(frames).merge(plays[["gameId", "playId", "pff_passCoverage"]], on=["gameId", "playId"])
# ...then label each safety's role and plot exactly as in the simulated figure above.
