title: Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage
section: Split-field coverage: two halves, two answers
text:
Split-field coverage: two halves, two answers
So far the whole defense has rotated together. A different idea, and one of the most important in modern defense, is to not treat the field as one problem at all.
Split-field coverage means playing a different coverage on each half of the field, with each half following its own rules for the receivers on its side. The split is usually made one of two ways: by formation (the side with more receivers, the strong side, against the side with fewer) or by field position (the field side, the wider side of the field when the ball sits on a hash mark, against the boundary side, the shorter one).
You have already met the most common split-field coverage: Cover 6, quarters on one half and Cover 2 on the other. Here it is with the split made by field position: the ball is on the left hash, so the field (wide) side is to the offense’s right.


Show the Python
def cover6():
    off = offense("gun_2x2")
    # ball on the left hash: the field-side receivers split wider, Z to the field numbers
    off = [p.moved(w=18.0) if p.key == "Z" else p.moved(w=11.0) if p.key == "Y" else p for p in off]
    dfn = defense("nickel", "two_high", off)
    moves = {"WILL": (5.0, -6.0), "RCB": (7.0, 18.8), "LCB": (5.0, -16.0), "FS": (12.5, -7.5),
             "SS": (12.5, 8.5), "NB": (5.0, 11.0)}
    dfn = [p.moved(d=moves[p.key][0], w=moves[p.key][1]) if p.key in moves else p for p in dfn]
    dfn = [p.moved(label="CB") if p.pos == "CB" else p for p in dfn]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=45, ball_y="left", to_go=10)
    # field side: quarters
    p.drop("RCB", (15.0, 17.0), speed=4.0); p.zone((17.0, 15.5), (8, 11), "¼")
    p.drop("SS", (15.0, 6.0), speed=4.0); p.zone((17.0, 5.0), (8, 10), "¼")
    p.drop("NB", (5.5, 12.5)); p.zone((6.0, 14.0), (5, 7), "curl-flat")
    # boundary side: Cover 2 (the half-field safety owns everything from the sideline to the middle)
    p.drop("FS", (15.5, -9.0)); p.zone((17.5, -9.0), (8, 17), "½")
    p.drop("LCB", (5.5, -17.0)); p.zone((4.0, -18.5), (4.5, 6), "flat")
    p.drop("WILL", (7.0, -7.5)); p.zone((7.5, -9.5), (4.5, 6), "curl")
    p.drop("MIKE", (6.5, 3.0)); p.zone((7.5, 3.2), (4.5, 5.5), "hook")
    for k in ("SDE", "SDT", "WDT", "WDE"):
        p.rush(k, pts=[(-1.4, 0.0)], speed=2.0)
    p.highlight("LCB", "RCB")
    return p


c6 = cover6()
fld = c6.draw(lateral="full", window=(-7, 23))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, c6)
divider(fld, c6, "BOUNDARY · Cover 2", "FIELD · quarters")
plt.show()








Figure 5.5: Split-field Cover 6 against a 2x2 formation, ball on the left hash. The dashed line runs through the ball, so the two halves are unequal on purpose: the boundary (short) side on the left is about 24 yards to the sideline, the field (wide) side about 30. To the field side the defense plays quarters: the corner and the safety each take a deep quarter and the nickel ($) plays the curl and flat, matching the two receivers on that side. To the boundary side it plays Cover 2: the safety takes the whole deep half, from the sideline to the middle, and the corner squats in the flat. Nearly the same alignment, two coverages: look at the corners. The boundary corner (left) is two yards shallower than the field corner, and that shallower depth is the tell that he will squat in the flat.





Why split the field? Because the two halves really are different problems.

The field and the boundary are different sizes, a little. NFL hash marks sit 70 feet 9 inches from each sideline, so with the ball on a hash there are about 23.6 yards to the near (boundary) sideline and 29.7 to the far (field) one, a difference of about 6 yards. In college the hashes are 60 feet from the sidelines, so the split is about 20 yards against 33.5 A boundary corner has the sideline as an extra defender; he can squat in the flat because a throw over his head has little room to land. That difference is big in college, which is where field/boundary quarters grew up. In the NFL it is modest, which is one reason pro split-field calls are often keyed to the formation’s strength (the trips side, the tight-end side) rather than to the field.
The two halves face different receivers. A tight end and a slot to one side, a lone wideout to the other: those sides threaten different things, and one coverage rule can’t be ideal for both.
Each player’s job is simpler. Each player only has to know his own half: who is #1 and #2 on my side, and what is my rule against them? The defense gets flexibility from combining simple halves, not from teaching eleven people one complicated call. The defenders in the middle, the Mike and the hook players, belong to whichever half the call assigns them; in the figure above the Mike takes the hook in the middle, the Will the curl for the Cover 2 half and the nickel the curl-flat for the quarters half.
But the communication is harder. Both halves have to agree where the split is: by formation, by field, or, with the ball in the middle and a balanced formation, by a default the staff sets in advance. A safety or the Mike typically makes that strength call by shout and hand signal. When a receiver motions across the formation, the strength can flip, and both halves must re-declare in the last second before the snap. That is a big reason offenses motion so much against split-field defenses (see below).

Split-field coverage is also a disguise machine, and that’s why it belongs in this chapter. From one two-high alignment the defense can play quarters on both halves, Cover 2 on both, Cover 6 to either side, Palms on one side, or rotate to one-high. The quarterback now has to read two coverages, one per half. A pre-snap guess that is right about the left half can be wrong about the right.
How do you tell Cover 6 from its neighbours after the snap? Count the deep safeties first, then watch the corners. Cover 3: one safety in the deep middle, both corners bail. Cover 2: two safeties split the field, both corners sit down in the flats. Cover 6: two safeties split the field, and the corners disagree: one sits in the flat (the Cover 2 half), the other backpedals with his eyes on the quarterback and plays a deep quarter. One squatting corner and one bailing corner under two deep safeties is the Cover 6 picture.
One naming warning before the history. Coverage numbers are dialect, not law (Coverage Fundamentals and the dialect table in the coverage atlas), and “Cover 7” is the clearest example. In Nick Saban’s vocabulary, Cover 7 names a whole family: a two-high, quarters-based pattern-match coverage in which each side of the formation gets its own small call, so the full call is a split-field call assembled from parts.6 Other staffs use “Cover 7” for a man-match coverage, a bracket on one receiver, or nothing at all.

A short history: from college laboratories to the NFL
Split-field quarters grew up in college football in the 1990s and 2000s, and the problem it solved is easy to state. College offenses spread the field and ran option and play-action from the same looks, on wide college hashes. A defense that put a safety in the box to stop the run gave up the deep ball; one that kept both safeties deep got run over. Quarters let it have both: safeties at 10 to 12 yards who read the receivers in front of them and fit the run if it came, but stayed deep if it was a pass. TCU’s Gary Patterson, one of the coaches most identified with the approach, summed up the safeties’ job at a 2015 coaches’ clinic: “Don’t go till you know.” His safeties didn’t backpedal at the snap; they shuffled flat-footed and read, because, as he told the same clinic audience, “we want to take away the short game, we want to take away combination routes, and we want to stop the run.”7
Saban’s pattern-matching quarters, which goes back to his years as Bill Belichick’s defensive coordinator in Cleveland (1991 to 1994), went with him to Michigan State, LSU and Alabama. Michigan State under Mark Dantonio and Pat Narduzzi, Patterson’s TCU and Iowa’s long-running quarters defenses became reference points that other coaches studied at clinics.8
The NFL caught up later, and fast. NFL Next Gen Stats (NGS, the league’s tracking-data arm) measures how often defenses play a split-safety (two-high) coverage after the snap: 32.9% of dropbacks in 2018, 37.8% in 2021, 40.4% in 2024 and 42.0% in 2025, the highest since tracking began. In 2025, Cover 6 alone was 9.2% of coverages.9 Brandon Staley’s 2020 Rams (below) are one of the teams that made the approach fashionable in the league. Staley came from the staff of Vic Fangio, the defensive coordinator most associated with the NFL’s two-high wave, and coaches from Staley’s staff and Fangio’s wider tree, such as Ejiro Evero (the Rams’ safeties coach in 2020, then Denver’s defensive coordinator in 2022 and Carolina’s since 2023), have leaned on rotation from a two-high shell: by one count, Carolina stayed two-high and rotated to one-high in almost equal measure.10 The full story of the two-high spread, Vic Fangio and the counterpunch that followed, is told in Case Study: Fangio’s Two-High Revolution and Macdonald’s Answer and The Modern Era.

title: Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage
section: Trips: the formation that forces a decision
text:
Trips: the formation that forces a decision
Split-field rules work beautifully against 2x2: two receivers and two or three defenders per side. A 3x1 formation (trips) breaks the symmetry on purpose. Three receivers go to one side and one to the other, and now the count is ugly.
Count only the players who can run with a receiver 20 yards downfield. On the trips side the defense has the corner, the safety and the nickel against three receivers who can all go deep. On the backside it has a corner and a safety against one receiver. (The backside linebacker, the Will, is there too, but his jobs are the run and a short zone; he can’t chase a receiver up the field.) If the defense just plays quarters as usual, the trouble is the third receiver (#3, the one closest to the ball). Quarters rules are built for two receivers per side: the corner takes #1 deep and the safety reads #2. Most systems do give #3 to someone underneath, the hook or apex player who walls him off (stays in his path and keeps him from running free across the middle). But if #2 and #3 both run vertical, the safety can carry only one of them, and the underneath defender can’t carry a fast receiver 20 yards deep. Meanwhile two defenders on the backside guard one man. Offenses love this: send #2 and #3 vertical and see who covers the second one. The problem is sharpest when #3 is a detached receiver, a slot or a tight end split off the line, who can get up the field fast; an in-line tight end is slower to release, and many quarters teams just play their normal rules against him.
So every two-high defense carries a set of 3x1 checks: pre-planned adjustments that tell each player what to do when trips appears. They fall into a few families. All of them answer the same question: who takes #3 if he goes deep, and who gets left alone because of it?

Poach: the backside safety comes across
Poach is the most aggressive answer. The backside safety ignores the lone receiver, leaves him to the cornerback in pure man coverage, and works across the field to take #3 if #3 runs deep. The trips side can then play its normal quarters rules on #1 and #2.


Show the Python
off = trips(detached=True)
dfn = trips_defense(off)
dfn = [p.moved(d=5.0, w=-13.8) if p.key == "LCB" else p for p in dfn]
poach = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=10)
poach.route("Z", r.go(20)); poach.route("H", r.seam(20)); poach.route("Y", r.path((4, -1.0), (20, -2.5)))
poach.route("X", r.fade(18))
for k in ("SDE", "SDT", "WDT", "WDE"):
    poach.rush(k, pts=[(-1.4, 0.0)], speed=2.0)
poach.drop("FS", (17.0, 3.0)); poach.drop("SS", (17.0, 10.5)); poach.drop("RCB", (17.0, 18.5))
poach.drop("NB", (6.5, 14.0)); poach.drop("MIKE", (7.0, 5.0)); poach.drop("WILL", (7.0, -4.5))
poach.man("LCB", "X")
poach.note("poach: FS takes #3 deep", at=(20.0, -7.0))
poach.note("CB alone on X", at=(6.0, -19.0))
number_receivers(poach, extra={"Y": "Y detached"})
poach.highlight("FS")
fld = poach.draw(lateral="full", window=(-8, 22))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, poach)
plt.show()








Figure 5.6: Poach against detached trips: the tight end Y has flexed off the line, about four yards outside the right tackle, to be a third slot receiver (#3). The backside safety (FS, highlighted) starts on the left but is reading #3, and runs across to carry him when he goes up the middle. On the trips side the corner and strong safety play #1 and #2 with quarters rules, and the nickel ($) and Mike take the curl-flat and hook underneath. The price is on the left: the corner (CB) covers X man-to-man with no safety anywhere near him (the dotted line is his man assignment).





Poach is a read, not a man assignment. If #3 goes vertical, the poaching safety carries him. If #3 stays short or breaks outside, the safety doesn’t stand around: he robs inside, jumping #2’s in-breaking route or the backside dig, or works back to help on X. That is what separates poach from a backside safety simply locked on #3 in man coverage.
The trade is stated in the picture. Poach turns the trips side into a fair fight and gives the defense a deep player over #3, but the corner on the backside is now on an island. Offenses who expect poach build “poach beaters”: they put their best receiver alone on the backside (often called an X-iso look) and attack him knowing no safety is coming, or they attack the poaching safety himself with a route that breaks behind him as he runs to #3.11 The poaching safety’s alignment is also a tell: a backside safety who starts closer to the middle than usual, or who leans toward the trips side, is probably not staying home.


Solo and stubbie: other ways to solve the count
The 3x1 check (solo / stubbie) family covers the other common answers. The names are shared across many playbooks but the details aren’t, so treat these as the typical versions rather than the only ones.
Solo. A warning first: if you search for “solo coverage”, most of what you’ll find, from pro and big-college quarters writers, uses Solo for the backside corner alone on X while the backside safety takes #3 vertical. That is the call this chapter has just shown you as poach. The version here comes from other playbooks, and we keep it under the name solo because it is a genuinely different answer, with a different defender on #3: the backside corner plays the single receiver by himself, and a linebacker, usually the Mike, takes #3 if he runs deep. That frees the backside safety to be an extra run defender against trips runs and run-pass options.12 The trade: a linebacker running with a tight end or slot up the seam is a mismatch the offense will look for, which is why NFL defenses rarely ask a linebacker to carry a detached #3 deep. Solo shows up mostly against tight-end trips, where #3 is in-line and slower to get going.


Show the Python
off = trips()
solo = Play(off, trips_defense(off), los=35, to_go=None)
number_receivers(solo, extra={"Y": "Y in-line"})
for k in ("SDE", "SDT", "WDT", "WDE"):
    solo.rush(k, pts=[(-1.4, 0.0)], speed=2.0)
solo.man("LCB", "X"); solo.man("MIKE", "Y")
solo.drop("MIKE", (12.0, 3.5)); solo.drop("FS", (5.5, -4.0))
solo.drop("SS", (16.0, 10.0)); solo.drop("RCB", (16.0, 18.0)); solo.drop("NB", (6.0, 14.0))
solo.drop("WILL", (6.5, -1.0))
solo.highlight("FS", "MIKE")
solo.note("FS free:\nextra run fitter", at=(4.2, -12.5))
solo.note("Mike: #3 deep", at=(14.2, -0.5))
fld = solo.draw(lateral=(-20, 21), window=(-6.5, 16.5), title=False)
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, solo)
plt.show()








Figure 5.7: Solo against a tight-end trips set, #3 in-line (dotted lines are man assignments). The backside corner is alone on X, the Mike linebacker takes #3 (the tight end) if he runs deep, and the backside safety (FS) is freed to come down as an extra run defender. The trips side plays #1 and #2 with its normal quarters rules.





Stubbie. Instead of sending help across, the defense solves trips on the trips side alone, four defenders against three receivers. In the version taught in Saban’s system (as decoded in Cameron Soran’s guide to Saban’s coverages, cited above) the corner plays #1 man-to-man wherever he goes, the nickel takes #2, a linebacker walls off #3 underneath, and the safety takes #3 deep while staying over the top of #2. He can do both because he lines up deeper than either and between them: if #3 goes vertical he carries him, and if #3 stays short he sits over #2, helping the nickel on anything deep. The backside safety stays home, so the lone receiver faces two defenders. The trade: the trips-side corner is locked in man coverage, and those four players are spread thin against crossing routes.


Show the Python
off = trips()
stub = Play(off, trips_defense(off, fs_w=-9.0), los=35, to_go=None)
number_receivers(stub)
stub.route("Y", r.seam(18)); stub.route("H", r.out(5, 4)); stub.route("Z", r.go(16))
for k in ("SDE", "SDT", "WDT", "WDE"):
    stub.rush(k, pts=[(-1.4, 0.0)], speed=2.0)
stub.man("RCB", "Z"); stub.man("NB", "H"); stub.man("LCB", "X")
stub.drop("MIKE", (5.5, 5.5)); stub.drop("SS", (15.5, 5.0)); stub.drop("FS", (15.0, -14.0))
stub.drop("WILL", (6.5, -3.0))
stub.highlight("SS", "FS")
stub.note("SS: #3 deep,\nover #2", at=(17.6, -2.5))
stub.note("2 on X", at=(14.8, -9.0))
fld = stub.draw(lateral=(-20, 21), window=(-6.5, 19.5), title=False)
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, stub)
plt.show()








Figure 5.8: Stubbie against 3x1 (dotted lines are man assignments). On the trips side the corner locks on #1 and the nickel ($) on #2; the Mike walls off #3 underneath while the strong safety takes #3 deep and stays over the top of #2. Here #3 (the tight end, Y) runs up the seam and #2 runs a short out, so the safety carries #3. The backside safety stays home, so X sees two defenders: the corner on him and the safety over the top.





Rotate. The defense can also give up on two-high against trips and rotate to a one-high, three-deep Cover 3 match coverage, with the trips-side safety coming down toward the passing strength and the backside safety becoming the deep-middle player.
Why does this matter to a viewer? Because trips is how offenses force the defense to declare. The 3x1 check the defense uses usually shows up in the backside safety’s alignment before the snap: home and wide (stubbie), cheated in toward the middle (poach, or a rotation in which he becomes the post safety), or creeping down (solo). Poach and rotation can look the same before the snap; the difference shows in the first second after it. The poaching safety keeps reading #3 and goes where #3 goes; the rotating safety runs to the deep middle and stays there, while the trips-side safety comes down. And offenses use motion to create trips at the last moment, so the defense has to make that decision with a second left on the play clock. Usually a safety or the Mike shouts and signals the check. A defender who doesn’t hear it plays the old call, and that is how the busts described at the start of the chapter happen: two defenders on one receiver, nobody on #3.
The same question comes up against other three-receiver sides. An empty 3x2 set has a trips side too, and the defense answers it with the same families. A bunch, three receivers packed tightly together, adds a different problem, receivers crossing each other at the line, which Man Coverage handles with its banjo calls.

title: Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage
text:
How offenses fight back
Offenses’ counters share one idea: make the defense show its hand earlier, or make the hand not matter.
Motion. Moving a receiver before the snap forces defenders to adjust, and adjustments are information (Motion and Shifts as Weapons). A cornerback who travels across the formation with the motion man hints at man coverage. A safety who spins down hints at one-high. Motion also changes the receiver count: turning 2x2 into 3x1 forces the defense into its trips check with no time to disguise it. The league has gone all in. PFF (Pro Football Focus, a charting and grading company) counted pre-snap shifts or motion on 63.9% of plays in 2025, up from 43.0% in 2018.13
Defenses answer motion in three ways:

Match rules. In a pattern-match zone, defenders hand receivers off by rule, so a defender may follow the motion man a few steps (looking like man) and then pass him to the next zone. The motion read says “man” and the coverage is zone, or the reverse.
Fake spins. A safety spins down with the motion on purpose and goes back to his old job at the snap.
Many starting points. The defense rehearses every rotation from more than one pre-snap picture, so no single picture means one coverage.

The offense’s counter to all three is motion at the snap: the receiver is still moving when the ball is snapped, so the defense must react to him and rotate at the same instant, with no time for a second move.
Tempo. Snapping the ball quickly gives the defense less time to line up, communicate and disguise. Under tempo (the pace at which an offense gets to the line and snaps the ball; see In-Game Adjustments and Tempo), defenses often fall back on one simple call, and simple calls are easier to read.
Hard counts. A hard count isn’t only fishing for an offside flag. Safeties drilled to move “on the snap” sometimes move on what sounds like the snap, and a safety who flinches at a fake reveals where he’s going. The defense’s answer is discipline: key the ball, not the voice.
Read it after the snap. The deepest answer is for the quarterback to stop relying on the pre-snap picture. Modern quarterbacks are taught to form a pre-snap guess, then confirm it in the first steps of the drop by looking at the safeties: is the middle of the field closed or open now? Which safety moved, and where? Pass concepts are built to have an answer against either rotation. The classic example is a slot receiver on a “bender” in four verticals: if the middle opens (two safeties split), he bends his seam into a post between them (see four verticals), as Y does in the Cover 2 figure above; if the middle closes (one safety in the post), he stays on his seam and the ball goes away from the post safety. The route changes after the snap, on the same read the quarterback makes. Eye manipulation, looking off a robber to move him, is the advanced version (Concepts Versus Coverages).
Play-action and RPOs. The safety who rotates down is usually the defense’s extra run defender, and that makes him a target. A run-pass option can read him: if he comes down to fit the run, throw where he left; if he stays deep, hand off into a box that is one defender short. Play-action attacks the other safety: a run fake holds the post safety’s eyes for a beat, and his long trip to the middle is exactly the kind of run a deep shot behind him is built to beat. Rotation buys the defense a run defender it never announced; a good run fake makes it pay for him.
Throw before it matters. The quick game (throws out in about two seconds or less; The Quick Game) doesn’t care much about rotations, because the ball is gone before the safeties have finished moving. Against heavy disguise, a steady diet of quick throws is a way of declining the contest.

title: Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage
text:
Measuring the lie
Can you count how often a defense lies? Broadcasters and charting services label the coverage after the snap, and the nflverse data used throughout this course carries those labels (2018–2025). What they don’t record is the picture the defense showed before the snap. For that you need tracking data: the safeties’ positions in the frames before the snap.
That is exactly what the 2025 Big Data Bowl asked for. Its theme was pre-snap behaviour, and it was the first edition whose tracking files included full pre-snap frames, from the first nine weeks of the 2022 season. The winning entry, by NYU students Smit Bajaj and Vishakh Sandwar, was called “Exposing Coverage Tells in the Pre-Snap.”14 NFL Next Gen Stats then built a pre-snap model of its own, crediting that project as inspiration. It classifies the shell a quarterback sees before the snap and compares it with the coverage after. In its words: “If a defense shows split-safety zone and rotates to single-high man (or spins to Cover 0), we flag it as disguised.”15 The article that introduced the model gave no league-wide disguise rate, we found no other published one, and the Big Data Bowl files cover only half of one season. So “how often does an NFL defense lie?” has no public league-wide answer yet (one analyst’s count for a single team is in the Film room below).
Here is how you would get one. First fix what “the shell” means: the picture once the offense is set and the quarterback starts his cadence, say two seconds before the snap. Then classify that picture with a simple rule (two or more defenders at least 10 yards deep and none of them near the middle means two-high), do the same at the snap, and compare both with the coverage the defense actually played. A defense that rotates during the cadence has still disguised, but the quarterback had time to see the truth; one that rotates at the snap did not give him that time.
The chart below runs that measurement on eight made-up defenses. We typed in how often each one disguises and how late it moves, simulated 90 plays for each as BDB-format tracking, and let the classifier score them, so the chart can only give back what we put in. Its job is to show what the measurement looks like and how to read it, not to tell you anything about real teams. Read each row from left to right: the hollow dot is how often the picture two seconds before the snap told the truth, the filled dot how often the picture at the snap did, and the bar between them is how much of the lie the defense gave away during the cadence.


Show the Python
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
# hypothetical defenses: (share shown two-high, share disguised, share of disguises that move only at/after the snap)
DEFS = {"A": (0.50, 0.05, 0.5), "B": (0.55, 0.12, 0.4), "C": (0.45, 0.25, 0.1), "D": (0.60, 0.30, 0.2),
        "E": (0.65, 0.30, 0.5), "F": (0.70, 0.35, 0.9), "G": (0.75, 0.40, 0.6), "H": (0.75, 0.45, 0.9)}
N = 90
res, pid = [], 0
for name, (p_two, p_dis, p_late) in DEFS.items():
    n_dis = round(N * p_dis)
    for i in range(N):
        pid += 1
        shown_two = rng.random() < p_two
        disguised, late = i < n_dis, i < round(n_dis * p_late)
        kind = {(True, False): "stay2", (True, True): "rot1",
                (False, False): "stay1", (False, True): "spin2"}[(shown_two, disguised)]
        tau = rng.uniform(0.0, 0.3) if late else rng.uniform(-1.6, -0.6)
        trk = sim_play(kind, rng, tau=tau, play_id=pid)
        played = "two-high" if kind in ("stay2", "spin2") else "one-high"   # the post-snap label
        res.append((name, played,
                    shell_at(trk[np.isclose(trk["time"], -2.0)]),
                    shell_at(trk[np.isclose(trk["time"], 0.0)])))
chk = pd.DataFrame(res, columns=["defense", "played", "shell_early", "shell_snap"])
agree = (chk.assign(early=chk["shell_early"] == chk["played"], snap=chk["shell_snap"] == chk["played"])
            .groupby("defense")[["early", "snap"]].mean().mul(100))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.6))
y = np.arange(len(agree))[::-1]                   # Defense A at the top
ax.hlines(y, agree["early"], agree["snap"], color=style.BASELINE, lw=2.0, zorder=1)
ax.scatter(agree["early"], y, s=46, facecolor="white", edgecolor=style.SERIES[0], lw=1.6, zorder=2,
           label="2 seconds before the snap")
ax.scatter(agree["snap"], y, s=46, color=style.SERIES[0], zorder=3, label="at the snap")
ax.set_yticks(y, [f"Defense {d}" for d in agree.index], fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_xlabel("Plays where the pre-snap shell matched the coverage played (%)", fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_xlim(50, 101)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=8)
ax.set_title("Pre-snap shell vs coverage played (simulated defenses, BDB-format)", fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 5.9: Did the shell tell the truth? Eight made-up defenses (not real teams) whose disguise rates we chose, 90 simulated dropbacks each, listed from the least disguise (A) to the most (H). Hollow dots: how often the shell two seconds before the snap matched the coverage played. Filled dots: the same, measured at the snap. A and B are honest: they disguise on only 5% and 12% of plays, so their dots sit high (between about 88 and 98), though not at 100. C and D disguise often but rotate during the cadence: low hollow dots, long bars, and by the snap the picture is true again. F and H disguise often and move late: short bars, low scores. Those are the hardest to read. E and G sit in between. A filled dot can’t fall left of its hollow dot here, because the defenses only ever move toward the truth.





Two numbers, then, describe a defense’s disguise: how often it lies sets how low its early score can go, and when it moves decides whether the lie can be caught in time. With the real 2025 Big Data Bowl files, whose plays carry a charted post-snap coverage, the same code would give real values; the website’s “Show the Python” holds it, and Tracking Data and the Big Data Bowl runs it on real defenses.


Show the Python (the real version from Big Data Bowl 2025 files; not run here)
from gridiron import bdb

plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")        # pff_passCoverage is the post-snap label
trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")
TWO_HIGH = {"Cover-2", "2-Man", "Quarters", "Cover-6 Right", "Cover 6-Left"}   # check the year's label list
ONE_HIGH = {"Cover-1", "Cover-3", "Cover-3 Seam", "Cover-3 Cloud Left", "Cover-3 Cloud Right",
            "Cover-3 Double Cloud", "Cover-1 Double", "Cover-0"}

out = []
for row in plays.dropna(subset=["pff_passCoverage"]).itertuples():
    one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=row.gameId, play_id=row.playId)
    snap = one[one["frameType"] == "SNAP"]
    one["los"] = float(snap.loc[snap["side"] == "ball", "x"].iloc[0])
    one["ball_y"] = float(snap.loc[snap["side"] == "ball", "y"].iloc[0])
    played = ("two-high" if row.pff_passCoverage in TWO_HIGH
              else "one-high" if row.pff_passCoverage in ONE_HIGH else None)
    if played is None:
        continue
    out.append((row.defensiveTeam, played,
                shell_at(one[np.isclose(one["time"], -2.0)]), shell_at(one[np.isclose(one["time"], 0.0)])))
# ...then group by defensiveTeam and plot exactly as in the simulated chart above.

title: Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage
text:
Film room






NoteFilm room: Vikings 2023–2025 — Brian Flores and the defense that is both



Brian Flores became the Vikings’ defensive coordinator in 2023 and was still there in 2026. His defenses have been described as close to unreadable before the snap. The back seven (the linebackers and defensive backs, everyone behind the defensive line) move constantly, safeties change the shell during the cadence and again at the snap, and pressure comes from players who don’t look like rushers. In 2023 the Vikings blitzed on 50.7% of opponents’ dropbacks, the highest rate in the league. After a 23–17 Vikings win in Week 2 of 2024, 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy told Flores on the field, “The scheme, man, it’s crazy.”16
What to notice: CBS’s breakdown of that 49ers game shows the two halves of the trick. On one snap six Vikings stand on the line before the snap and the play becomes a four-man rush with seven in coverage. On another, a blitz look is real but the coverage behind it is split-field Cover 6 (both plays are in the same CBS piece). Watch the number of defenders at the line before the snap, then count the rushers after it. With Flores, the two numbers often differ.
What makes it work is the spread of possibilities behind one look. In the nflverse post-snap coverage labels for 2023–2025, the Vikings played two-high coverage more often than any other defense (51.4% of charted dropbacks, just ahead of Buffalo’s 50.5%) and Cover 0, man with no deep safety, at 5.8%, behind only Kansas City and level with Baltimore; the Chiefs under Steve Spagnuolo sit right beside them on both counts. The chart shows the menu, not the disguise: post-snap labels can’t say what the shell looked like. But the menu is what makes disguise pay. Against most defenses a quarterback who sees two-high can lean on the odds that it stays two-high; against a defense that lives at both ends, the odds are no help. (The blitz numbers are pressure disguise, the subject of Part 7; the logic is the same.)




Show the Python
from gridiron.data import nfl

part = nfl().load_participation([2023, 2024, 2025]).to_pandas()
cv = part[part["defense_coverage_type"].notna()
          & ~part["defense_coverage_type"].isin(["BLOWN", "COMBO"])].copy()
gid = cv["nflverse_game_id"].str.split("_", expand=True)        # e.g. 2024_02_SF_MIN
cv["week"] = gid[1].astype(int)
cv["defteam"] = np.where(cv["possession_team"] == gid[3], gid[2], gid[3])
cv = cv[cv["week"] <= 18]                                      # regular season only
cv["two_high"] = cv["defense_coverage_type"].isin(["COVER_2", "2_MAN", "COVER_4", "COVER_6"])
cv["zero"] = cv["defense_coverage_type"].eq("COVER_0")
team = cv.groupby("defteam")[["two_high", "zero"]].mean() * 100

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.0))
rest = team.drop(["MIN", "KC", "BUF"])
ax.scatter(*team.loc["BUF", ["zero", "two_high"]], s=30, color=style.INK_2, zorder=3)
ax.annotate("Bills", tuple(team.loc["BUF", ["zero", "two_high"]]), xytext=(7, 0), textcoords="offset points",
            ha="left", va="center", fontsize=8, color=style.INK_2)
ax.scatter(rest["zero"], rest["two_high"], s=26, color=style.MUTED, alpha=0.7, zorder=2)
ax.scatter(*team.loc["MIN", ["zero", "two_high"]], s=64, color=style.SERIES[1], zorder=3)
ax.scatter(*team.loc["KC", ["zero", "two_high"]], s=64, color=style.SERIES[0], zorder=3)
ax.annotate("Vikings (Flores)", tuple(team.loc["MIN", ["zero", "two_high"]]), xytext=(-9, -1),
            textcoords="offset points", ha="right", va="center", fontsize=8.5, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
ax.annotate("Chiefs (Spagnuolo)", tuple(team.loc["KC", ["zero", "two_high"]]), xytext=(-9, -12),
            textcoords="offset points", ha="right", fontsize=8.5, color=style.INK)
ax.axvline(team["zero"].median(), color=style.BASELINE, lw=1, ls=(0, (3, 3)))
ax.axhline(team["two_high"].median(), color=style.BASELINE, lw=1, ls=(0, (3, 3)))
ax.text(team["zero"].max(), team["two_high"].median() - 0.9, "median", fontsize=7.5, color=style.MUTED, ha="right")
ax.set_xlabel("Cover 0 (no deep safety), % of charted dropbacks", fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_ylabel("Two-high after the snap, %", fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_ylim(team["two_high"].min() - 2.5, team["two_high"].max() + 3)
ax.set_title("Two-high and Cover 0 by defense, 2023–2025", fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 5.10: Post-snap coverage mix by defense, 2023–2025 regular seasons pooled: share of charted dropbacks played as a two-high coverage (Cover 2, 2-Man, quarters or Cover 6) against share played as Cover 0. Each dot is a defense; dashed lines are league medians. The Vikings lead the league in two-high, by less than a point over Buffalo (which plays very little Cover 0), and are tied in effect with Baltimore for second in Cover 0, behind Kansas City, which sits close by: both extremes from the same team. Source: nflverse participation data, charted for 2023–2025 by FTN Data (a football charting company); plays the charters marked as a blown coverage or a mix of coverages are left out.





A caution about the chart: the coverage labels are charted by people watching film, and the 2023–2025 seasons come from a different charting source than earlier years, so compare teams within these seasons rather than across the 2022/2023 break.17 The labels describe what was played after the snap; they can’t tell you what was shown before it. That is the job of the tracking data in the previous section.






NoteFilm room: Rams 2020 — Brandon Staley’s first year



Brandon Staley arrived in Los Angeles in 2020 as a first-time NFL defensive coordinator, from Vic Fangio’s staff in Denver, and took over a defense with two great individual players: Aaron Donald inside and Jalen Ramsey at cornerback. He built it around a two-high shell. Most snaps looked alike before the snap, and the coverage was decided at and after it: quarters and Cover 6 to the field or the boundary, rotations down into Cover 3 or a robber, and Ramsey moved around the formation, from outside corner to the nickel (“star”) spot, to follow the matchup.18 Three things made the light-box, two-high approach affordable. Donald’s four-man pass rush meant the Rams didn’t need to blitz more than an average defense (they sent five or more rushers on about a quarter of dropbacks, close to the league median). The front, with Donald inside, could hold up against the run with fewer defenders in the box, while the safeties fitted the run from depth (Run Fits and Box Math). And the defense was disciplined enough to rotate late.
What to notice: on a 2020 Rams passing down, find Ramsey first (outside or in the slot), then the two safeties: level and deep while the quarterback calls signals, with the rotation, if there is one, coming only as the ball moves. The results: the 2020 Rams finished the regular season first in the NFL in points allowed (18.6 a game), total yards allowed (281.9) and passing yards allowed (190.7).19 Staley was hired as the Chargers’ head coach after one season, and the Rams’ approach spread through his coaching tree and the league. Its parent, Fangio’s system, is the subject of Case Study: Fangio’s Two-High Revolution and Macdonald’s Answer.








NoteFilm room: Panthers under Ejiro Evero — the coin-flip rotation



Ejiro Evero, a safeties coach on Staley’s 2020 Rams staff, has run Carolina’s defense since 2023. His Panthers are the cleanest public example of this chapter’s main move: show two-high, then decide at the snap whether to stay there or rotate a safety down to a single-high, “closed-post” coverage. In Cody Alexander’s charting of the Panthers’ defense, published in April 2026, they stayed two-high 397 times and rotated 375 times, what he called “an almost perfect 1:1 ratio.” Cornerback Jaycee Horn described what that felt like from inside: “Everything is really out of a shell, not many tells or pre(-snap) things. It was just on the snap; everything happened.”20
What to notice: on a Carolina passing down, call the shell as the quarterback starts his cadence; it will almost always be two-high. Then, on the replay, watch the two safeties at the snap. Roughly half the time one of them comes down and the other runs to the middle; the rest of the time both stay deep. Nothing before the snap tells you which, and that is the design. It also gives you a benchmark for your own log below: one charted NFL defense built around disguise rotated out of its two-high shell on about half the snaps that started there.








TipWatch for it on Sunday: call it twice



For one quarter (two if you’re keen), on every obvious passing down, make two calls out loud and write them down.

Call 1, as the quarterback starts his cadence: the shell. One-high or two-high? Then the details that could change it: how deep is each safety, is one narrower or shallower, are the corners pressed or off? Which side is the formation’s strength?
Call 2, one second after the snap: what it became. Is the middle of the field closed (one safety in the post) or open (two safeties splitting the field)? Closed: Cover 1 if the corners turn and run with receivers, Cover 3 if they bail into deep thirds. Open: then the corners tell you which, squatting in the flats for Cover 2 (or that side of Cover 6), backpedalling with eyes on the quarterback for quarters, trailing their man for 2-Man. No safety deep at all: Cover 0. If the two safeties went to two different jobs, notice which one came down and where he landed.
Log the lie. Mark each play S (same) or R (rotated). By the end of the quarter you’ll have a disguise rate for that defense. For scale, the Panthers in the film room above rotated out of two-high on about half their two-high snaps. Also note whether the rotation started before the snap (you could see it coming) or at the snap (you couldn’t). Both count as a lie; only the second one worked.
Bonus: trips. When the offense shows 3x1, watch the backside safety. Did he stay home (stubbie), come across to #3 (poach), run to the deep middle (rotate), or come down (solo)? Then watch where the ball went.

Live, Call 1 needs a shot that shows the safeties: the wide pre-snap view some broadcasts use while the quarterback surveys the defense, or a high camera behind the offense. The standard live angle sits at the line and often cuts the safeties out of frame at the snap, so on many plays Call 1 has to wait for the replay. The high, wide replays (the closest a broadcast gets to the All-22 film coaches use) are the best place to check yourself: use the first replay to see the shell and the second to check the rotation.

title: Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage
text:
Predict the play






TipPredict the play 1: the leaning safety





Show the Python
off, dfn = nickel_vs_2x2()
mv = {"SS": (10.0, 5.0), "FS": (13.5, -7.0), "LCB": (8.0, -16.3), "RCB": (8.0, 16.3)}
dfn = [p.moved(d=mv[p.key][0], w=mv[p.key][1]) if p.key in mv else p for p in dfn]
pr1 = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=9)
pr1.highlight("SS", "FS")
fld = pr1.draw(lateral=(-22, 22), window=(-7.5, 17))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, pr1, widths=True)
plt.show()








Figure 5.11: Second-and-9, ball in the middle of the field, play clock at 3. The defense shows two-high; the two safeties are highlighted. Use the depth numbers on the left and the hash marks to size them up.





What will the shell turn into at the snap, and which side of the field should the quarterback be wary of?

Show the Python
answer(r"""
**Most likely a rotation to one-high zone, Cover 3, with the right safety (SS) coming down.**
The safety tells: the SS has crept to 10 yards and stands 5 yards from the middle, while the FS is
at 13.5 and 7 yards out. The SS is shallower and narrower, so he can reach the curl or the hole
quickly, and he has crept down as the play clock runs out (a timing tell). The FS is the deeper
one and can reach the deep middle. The corner tells: they are 8 yards off, outside and turned to
the quarterback, which is zone technique, the way deep-third corners line up, not the square,
pressed stance of man corners. You can't tell before the snap whether the SS will land in the curl
(a **buzz** rotation) or in the hole (a robber), and you don't need to: either way he lands in the
in-breaking lanes on the right.

For the quarterback, the danger is to the **right**: curls and digs on that side run straight into
the SS. The opportunities are the classic Cover 3 ones away from the rotation, such as stressing
the left [curl-flat defender](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-curl-flat-defender) with a curl-and-flat
combination, or the seam on the left between the deep middle and the deep third (the Cover 3
weaknesses listed with the robber rotation). Of course a disciplined defense could show exactly this and
stay two-high.
""")







TipAnswer





Most likely a rotation to one-high zone, Cover 3, with the right safety (SS) coming down. The safety tells: the SS has crept to 10 yards and stands 5 yards from the middle, while the FS is at 13.5 and 7 yards out. The SS is shallower and narrower, so he can reach the curl or the hole quickly, and he has crept down as the play clock runs out (a timing tell). The FS is the deeper one and can reach the deep middle. The corner tells: they are 8 yards off, outside and turned to the quarterback, which is zone technique, the way deep-third corners line up, not the square, pressed stance of man corners. You can’t tell before the snap whether the SS will land in the curl (a buzz rotation) or in the hole (a robber), and you don’t need to: either way he lands in the in-breaking lanes on the right.
For the quarterback, the danger is to the right: curls and digs on that side run straight into the SS. The opportunities are the classic Cover 3 ones away from the rotation, such as stressing the left curl-flat defender with a curl-and-flat combination, or the seam on the left between the deep middle and the deep third (the Cover 3 weaknesses listed with the robber rotation). Of course a disciplined defense could show exactly this and stay two-high.











TipPredict the play 2: the safety who isn’t home





Show the Python
off = trips(detached=True)
dfn = trips_defense(off, fs_w=-4.0)
pr2 = Play(off, dfn, los=50, to_go=6)
number_receivers(pr2)
pr2.highlight("FS", "LCB")
fld = pr2.draw(lateral="full", window=(-7.5, 17))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, pr2, widths=True)
plt.show()








Figure 5.12: Third-and-6. The offense shows detached trips (3x1) to the right and X alone on the left. The defense is two-high. Compare the two safeties’ widths, and look at where the left corner stands on X.





Which 3x1 check does this look like, and where would you throw?

Show the Python
answer(r"""
**Poach, or a rotation; either way, X is alone.** The left (backside) safety is only about 4 yards
from the middle, much narrower than the right safety at 9. A backside safety staying home to help
on X would be wider and square to X, so he isn't home: he is getting ready to go somewhere on the
trips side. Before the snap there are two candidates. In **poach** he reads #3 and carries him if
he goes up the middle. In a **rotation** to one-high he becomes the deep-middle safety and the
trips-side safety comes down. The clue here is that the right safety is still deep and wide, not
creeping down, which leans toward poach, but you confirm it after the snap: the poacher goes where
#3 goes; the rotating safety runs to the middle and stays there. The left corner fits both. He is
pressed a yard inside X (inside leverage), taking away the inside, which is what a corner does when
he expects no help over the top.

**Throw to X**, especially if X is the offense's best receiver. Against poach, X is one-on-one with no help. The classic poach beaters are a
[back-shoulder](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-back-shoulder-throw) fade or a go route outside (the corner gave up the outside to take away the inside),
or a [double move](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-double-move). Against the rotation, X still
faces his corner with the post safety starting far away. It's also worth sending #3 vertical
anyway, so the safety has to commit.
""")







TipAnswer





Poach, or a rotation; either way, X is alone. The left (backside) safety is only about 4 yards from the middle, much narrower than the right safety at 9. A backside safety staying home to help on X would be wider and square to X, so he isn’t home: he is getting ready to go somewhere on the trips side. Before the snap there are two candidates. In poach he reads #3 and carries him if he goes up the middle. In a rotation to one-high he becomes the deep-middle safety and the trips-side safety comes down. The clue here is that the right safety is still deep and wide, not creeping down, which leans toward poach, but you confirm it after the snap: the poacher goes where #3 goes; the rotating safety runs to the middle and stays there. The left corner fits both. He is pressed a yard inside X (inside leverage), taking away the inside, which is what a corner does when he expects no help over the top.
Throw to X, especially if X is the offense’s best receiver. Against poach, X is one-on-one with no help. The classic poach beaters are a back-shoulder fade or a go route outside (the corner gave up the outside to take away the inside), or a double move. Against the rotation, X still faces his corner with the post safety starting far away. It’s also worth sending #3 vertical anyway, so the safety has to commit.











TipPredict the play 3: the safeties spin with the motion





Show the Python
off, dfn = nickel_vs_2x2()
# Z must start off the line to go in motion, so Y steps up to be the end on the line (still 7 on it)
off = [p.moved(d=-0.7) if p.key == "Y" else p.moved(d=-1.5) if p.key == "Z" else p for p in off]
pr3 = Play(off, dfn, los=30, to_go=10)
pr3.motion("Z", pts=[(-1.5, -7.0), (-1.5, -17.0), (-1.5, -18.0)], speed=7.0)   # offsets from his start
pr3.motion("FS", to=(9.0, -8.0), speed=2.0)      # motion side: walks down toward the motion
pr3.motion("SS", to=(13.5, 1.0), speed=2.5)      # side the motion left: rotates to the post
pr3.highlight("FS", "SS", "RCB")
pr3.note("CB stays: deep third,\nno man", at=(11.0, 16.0))
fld = pr3.draw(lateral=(-22, 22), window=(-7.5, 17))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, pr3)
plt.show()








Figure 5.13: First-and-10. Two-high before the motion. Z then motions across the formation from right to left. No defender follows him. The left safety (FS), on the side Z is heading to, walks down to about 9 yards; the right safety (SS) drifts toward the middle and gains depth; the right corner (CB) stays where he was, now over empty grass. Every arrow here is movement before the snap.





What did the motion tell the offense? And what could the defense still do to it at the snap, and how would the offense take that away?

Show the Python
answer(r"""
**It suggested one-high zone, Cover 3 rotating toward the motion.** Nobody went with Z across the
formation, and the right corner stayed home over empty grass: a corner with no man to cover is
playing a zone, here a deep third. The left safety coming down toward the motion while the right
safety rotates to the post is the defense moving to a single deep safety, with the FS as an
underneath (buzz or sky) defender on the side Z is going to. That is the
[spin](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-spin-safety-rotation-on-motion) from
[Motion and Shifts as Weapons](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd), and it
goes the default way: toward the motion, which is where the receivers now are.

**The catch:** a defense that knows you use motion to read it can spin on purpose and then rotate
*back* at the snap. That is late rotation used against the motion read, and it's a favourite of
heavy-disguise defenses. The offense's counter is in the timing: snapping the ball as Z passes the
quarterback (motion at the snap) leaves the safeties almost no time to re-rotate, so the picture
they show during the motion is much more likely to be the real one. It is still a strong hint, not
a certainty.
""")







TipAnswer





It suggested one-high zone, Cover 3 rotating toward the motion. Nobody went with Z across the formation, and the right corner stayed home over empty grass: a corner with no man to cover is playing a zone, here a deep third. The left safety coming down toward the motion while the right safety rotates to the post is the defense moving to a single deep safety, with the FS as an underneath (buzz or sky) defender on the side Z is going to. That is the spin from Motion and Shifts as Weapons, and it goes the default way: toward the motion, which is where the receivers now are.
The catch: a defense that knows you use motion to read it can spin on purpose and then rotate back at the snap. That is late rotation used against the motion read, and it’s a favourite of heavy-disguise defenses. The offense’s counter is in the timing: snapping the ball as Z passes the quarterback (motion at the snap) leaves the safeties almost no time to re-rotate, so the picture they show during the motion is much more likely to be the real one. It is still a strong hint, not a certainty.

title: Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage
text:
Checklist so far (Parts 1–6)
Part 6 ends here, so it’s time to update the pre-snap card. The lines this part of the book exists for are shell → rotation → leverage. Read them in that order: the shell gives you a first guess, the rotation (or its absence) confirms or overturns it, and the corners finish the read: their technique (eyes, stance, depth) tells you man or zone, and their leverage tells you where the help is.


Show the Python
items = [
    ("BEFORE THE SNAP", None, None),
    ("1", "Situation: down, distance, field zone, clock and score", "Part 1", False),
    ("2", "Personnel: who is on the field for each side", "02-01, 02-05", False),
    ("3", "Formation and strength: 2x2, 3x1, where is the tight end?", "02-02 to 02-04", False),
    ("4", "Motion: does a defender travel (man), bump (zone) or spin a safety?", "02-06", False),
    ("5", "Box count: blockers against defenders near the line", "02-05, 05-05", False),
    ("6", "Shell: one-high or two-high? Depth and width of each safety", "06-01, 06-06", True),
    ("7", "Corners: technique (eyes, stance, depth) says man or zone; leverage says where the help is", "06-01 to 06-06", True),
    ("AT THE SNAP", None, None),
    ("8", "Run or pass: the offensive linemen's first step (a rotating safety may be a run fitter)", "Parts 3–4", False),
    ("9", "Rotation: did a safety move during the cadence, at the snap, or not at all?", "06-06", True),
    ("ONE SECOND AFTER", None, None),
    ("10", "Middle of the field: closed (1 deep safety) or open (2)? Then the corners: squat, bail or trail", "06-01 to 06-06", True),
    ("11", "Trips? Backside safety: home (stubbie), across to #3 (poach), to the middle (rotate), or down as a run defender (solo, mostly vs tight-end trips)?", "06-06", True),
    ("12", "Log it: your pre-snap call against what it became (call it twice)", "06-06", True),
]
import textwrap

rows = []                                      # (kind, payload, height in lines)
for it in items:
    if it[1] is None:
        rows.append(("head", it[0], 1))
    else:
        lines = textwrap.wrap(it[1], 60)
        rows.append(("item", (it[0], lines, it[2], it[3]), len(lines)))
n_lines = sum(h for _, _, h in rows) + 4
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 0.24 * n_lines))
ax.set_xlim(0, 100); ax.set_ylim(0, n_lines); ax.axis("off")
ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((0.8, 0.3), 98.4, n_lines - 0.6, boxstyle="round,pad=0.2,rounding_size=0.8",
                            fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=1.2))
ax.text(3, n_lines - 1.3, "Watching checklist · after Part 6", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold",
        color=style.INK, va="center")
ax.text(97, n_lines - 1.3, "new in Part 6", fontsize=8, color=style.INK_2, ha="right", va="center",
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.3", fc=style.OFFENSE_TINT, ec="none"))
y = n_lines - 2.8
for kind, payload, h in rows:
    if kind == "head":
        ax.text(3, y, payload, fontsize=8, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK_2, va="center")
        y -= 1.0
        continue
    num, lines, where, new = payload
    top, bottom = y + 0.45, y - (h - 1) - 0.45
    if new:
        ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((2.2, bottom), 95.6, top - bottom, boxstyle="round,pad=0.05,rounding_size=0.4",
                                    fc=style.OFFENSE_TINT, ec="none"))
    ax.text(5.5, y, num, fontsize=8.5, fontweight="bold", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, va="center", ha="center")
    for j, line in enumerate(lines):
        ax.text(9.0, y - j, line, fontsize=8, color=style.INK, va="center")
    ax.text(97, y, where, fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2, va="center", ha="right")
    y -= h + 0.15
plt.show()

Earlier lines come from Parts 1–5; the highlighted lines are new in Part 6: the shell before the snap, the corners’ technique and leverage, the rotation at the snap (after you have seen run or pass), the middle of the field one second later, the trips check, and the log. title: Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage
text:
Takeaways

The shell is a hypothesis, not an answer. Defenses choose their alignment separately from their coverage, and the best ones show the same picture for many calls. Name the shell before the snap, and expect to check it one second after.
Disguise buys time, and it costs something. Every defender must line up where his real job is still reachable, so disguises leak: safety depth and width, corner technique and leverage, eyes, and above all the timing of movement. Late rotation hides the most and risks the most. Which safety rotates is set by the call, most often toward the strength or the motion.
Rotations run both ways. Two-high can become Cover 3 or a robber (taking away the middle throws two-high invites); one-high can bail into Cover 2 (taking away the outside throws one-high invites). Each rotation opens the area the quarterback ruled out.
Split-field coverage plays two coverages at once, one per half, keyed to strong and weak or (more in college, with its wide hashes) field and boundary. Each player’s job is simpler; the communication is harder, and motion across the split tests it. It is a big part of why two-high defenses spread through the NFL after 2018.
Trips forces a decision, and the decision is about #3: the backside safety comes across (poach), a linebacker takes him (solo), the trips side handles it four-on-three (stubbie), or the defense rotates. Whoever is left alone is where the offense will attack.
Offenses answer by forcing the defense to show earlier or by making the picture not matter: motion, tempo, hard counts, post-snap reads, play-action and RPOs that target the rotating safety, and quick throws.

title: Expected Points, EPA, and Success Rate: The Model, the Noise, and the Broadcast Metrics
text:
The data this chapter uses
Super Bowl LX, third quarter. Seattle faces third-and-12 at its own 19. Sam Darnold finds Cooper Kupp over the middle for 8 yards, and the box score adds 8 to Darnold’s passing total. Seattle punts on the next snap. Eight yards, and yet the expected-points ledger scores that completion as a small loss. In the fourth quarter New England’s Drake Maye throws an interception that gains no yards at all, and the same ledger charges it with almost ten points.1 If you have read the EPA primer in Downs, Distance, and Field Position you know what those numbers mean. This chapter opens the hood: where expected points come from, how to compute them yourself, how much one game, one season or one fumble can fool you, and how the stats the broadcast quotes (passer rating, QBR, DVOA, PFF grades) relate to the expected-points scorecard.
You’ll be able to:
Every number in this chapter comes from code you can run. Part 13 shows its code (other parts fold it), so read the cells as part of the text. The course’s gridiron.data module wraps nflreadpy and caches each season under data/cache/, so the ten seasons below download once.
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from IPython.display import Markdown
from gridiron import style
from gridiron.data import pbp, nfl

style.apply()
SEASONS = range(2016, 2026)   # ten completed seasons, 2016-2025
COLS = ["season", "season_type", "week", "game_id", "play_id", "game_half", "qtr",
        "posteam", "defteam", "home_team", "away_team", "home_score", "away_score",
        "down", "ydstogo", "yardline_100", "goal_to_go", "half_seconds_remaining",
        "play_type", "pass", "rush", "qb_scramble", "sack", "interception",
        "fumble", "fumble_recovery_1_team", "td_team", "field_goal_result", "safety",
        "yards_gained", "ep", "epa", "success", "wp", "cpoe",
        "passer", "passer_id", "pass_attempt", "complete_pass", "passing_yards",
        "pass_touchdown", "penalty_type", "first_down"]
raw = pbp(SEASONS, columns=COLS)
reg = raw[raw.season_type == "REG"]          # regular season only

# Scrimmage plays: every dropback (including sacks and scrambles) and every designed run.
# Kneels, spikes, kicks and penalties that wipe out the play are left out.
plays = reg[reg.play_type.isin(["pass", "run"])
            & ((reg["pass"] == 1) | (reg["rush"] == 1))
            & reg.epa.notna() & reg.down.notna()].copy()
plays["kind"] = np.where(plays["pass"] == 1, "Dropback", "Designed run")

# Garbage-time filter (13-01): win probability 10-90% and outside the last two minutes
# of each half. The plays that survive are what this chapter calls "neutral".
neutral = plays[plays.wp.between(0.10, 0.90) & (plays.half_seconds_remaining > 120)]


def md_table(df, digits=2):
    """Show a small DataFrame as a Markdown table (presentation plumbing, not football)."""
    out = df.copy()
    for c in out.select_dtypes("number"):
        whole = (out[c].dropna() % 1 == 0).all()                # downs, yard lines, counts
        sep = "" if c in ("season", "week") else ","             # 2025, not 2,025
        out[c] = out[c].map(lambda v: f"{v:{sep}.{0 if whole else digits}f}")
    align = ["---:" if pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(df[c]) else ":---" for c in df]
    rows = [list(out.columns), align] + out.astype(str).values.tolist()
    return Markdown("\n".join("| " + " | ".join(map(str, r)) + " |" for r in rows))
Four choices in that cell matter for everything that follows. Regular season only, because playoff games are few and played by the best teams. Dropbacks versus designed runs, not “pass plays versus run plays”: a sack or a scramble starts as a pass call, so nflverse files it under pass, while a designed quarterback run counts as a run.
Snaps wiped out by a penalty are dropped. nflverse marks them no_play, and the filter above removes them. That is the usual choice for “EPA per play,” but it is a choice, and it shades the run-pass comparison:
flagged = reg[(reg.season == 2025) & (reg.play_type == "no_play") & reg.epa.notna()
              & ((reg["pass"] == 1) | (reg["rush"] == 1))]
dpi = flagged[flagged.penalty_type == "Defensive Pass Interference"]
hold = flagged[flagged.penalty_type == "Offensive Holding"]
both = reg[(reg.season == 2025) & reg.epa.notna() & reg.down.notna()
           & reg.play_type.isin(["pass", "run", "no_play"])
           & ((reg["pass"] == 1) | (reg["rush"] == 1))]
with_pen = both.groupby(np.where(both["pass"] == 1, "Dropback", "Designed run")).epa.mean()
without = plays[plays.season == 2025].groupby("kind").epa.mean()
print(f"2025 snaps wiped out by a penalty: {len(flagged):,}; "
      f"defensive pass interference {len(dpi)} (mean EPA {dpi.epa.mean():+.2f}), "
      f"offensive holding {len(hold)} (mean EPA {hold.epa.mean():+.2f})")
print(f"Dropback EPA/play {without['Dropback']:+.3f} without penalty snaps, "
      f"{with_pen['Dropback']:+.3f} with them; designed runs "
      f"{without['Designed run']:+.3f} vs {with_pen['Designed run']:+.3f}")

2025 snaps wiped out by a penalty: 1,488; defensive pass interference 279 (mean EPA +1.73), offensive holding 374 (mean EPA -1.06)
Dropback EPA/play +0.043 without penalty snaps, +0.063 with them; designed runs -0.046 vs -0.060
A coach would say that drawing a pass interference flag on a go route, or getting a hold called, is part of what a play call produces. Pass interference is mostly a deep-ball outcome, so leaving those snaps out makes passing look a little worse than it is. It is also why EPA per play in this book will not always match other sites: nflfastR’s own beginner’s guide filters on pass == 1 | rush == 1, which keeps penalty snaps, and says to drop play_type == "no_play" only when you want to match official statistics.2
Last, the garbage-time filter for team numbers, because a defense protecting a 24-point lead in the fourth quarter is playing a different game. It keeps plays where the offense’s win probability (the model’s chance that it wins the game from here, the subject of Win Probability and Decision Analysis) is between 10% and 90%, outside the last two minutes of each half. The plays that survive are what analysts call neutral situations, and every team number in this chapter uses them. Tendencies: PROE, Personnel, Motion, and Coverage formalises the idea.3

title: Expected Points, EPA, and Success Rate: The Model, the Noise, and the Broadcast Metrics
text:
What expected points actually estimates
The primer in 01-02 described EP as “what a situation is worth.” The precise version is narrower and more useful: EP is the average value of the next score in the same half, from the point of view of the team that has the ball. The next score can be the offense’s touchdown (+7), field goal (+3) or safety (+2, when its own defense later tackles the opponent in their end zone), the opponent’s touchdown (−7), field goal (−3) or safety (−2), or nothing at all before halftime or the end of the game (0).
Why the next score, and not “points on this drive”? Because a drive that ends in a punt still matters. Punting the opponent back to their own 5 makes their next score less likely and yours more likely, and a model that only counted points on the current drive would score every punt as a zero. Counting through to the next score lets field position, punts and turnovers all carry value.
Why an average? Because the model knows nothing about who is playing. EP describes an average NFL offense against an average NFL defense in that situation. That is a feature: it gives every play the same yardstick, so you can ask how much better than average a team, a quarterback or a play call was.
The simplest expected-points model is no model at all: take every first-and-10 from the same yard line and average what happened next. The cell below finds the next score for every play in ten seasons.

d = reg.sort_values(["game_id", "play_id"]).copy()
# Mark scoring plays: who scored and how many points (touchdowns count as 7).
d["s_pts"] = np.select([d.td_team.notna(), d.field_goal_result.eq("made"), d.safety.eq(1)],
                       [7, 3, 2], np.nan)
d["s_team"] = np.where(d.td_team.notna(), d.td_team,
                       np.where(d.safety.eq(1), d.defteam, d.posteam))
d.loc[d.s_pts.isna(), "s_team"] = None
# Fill each play with the NEXT scoring play in the same game and half.
nxt = d.groupby(["game_id", "game_half"])[["s_pts", "s_team"]].bfill()
d["next_score"] = np.where(nxt.s_pts.isna(), 0,
                           np.where(nxt.s_team == d.posteam, nxt.s_pts, -nxt.s_pts))

# Situations the model learns from: snaps with a down (runs, passes, punts, field goals).
sit = d[d.play_type.isin(["pass", "run", "punt", "field_goal"]) & d.down.notna()].copy()
first10 = sit[(sit.down == 1) & ((sit.ydstogo == 10) | (sit.goal_to_go == 1))]
by_yard = first10.groupby("yardline_100").agg(n=("next_score", "size"),
                                              empirical=("next_score", "mean"),
                                              nflverse_ep=("ep", "mean"))
print(f"{len(sit):,} situations; {len(first10):,} first downs")

359,991 situations; 138,873 first downs



bins = (by_yard.reset_index()
        .assign(bin=lambda t: (t.yardline_100 - 1) // 5 * 5 + 3)
        .groupby("bin")
        .apply(lambda g: pd.Series({"emp": np.average(g.empirical, weights=g.n),
                                    "n": g.n.sum()}), include_groups=False))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.6))
ax.plot(by_yard.index, by_yard.nflverse_ep, color=style.SERIES[0], lw=2,
        label="nflverse model EP")
ax.scatter(bins.index, bins.emp, s=26, color=style.SERIES[1], zorder=3,
           edgecolor=style.SURFACE, linewidth=1, label="Actual average next score")
ax.axhline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1)
ax.set_xlim(100, 0)
ax.set_xticks([99, 90, 80, 70, 60, 50, 40, 30, 20, 10, 1],
              ["Own 1", "10", "20", "30", "40", "50", "40", "30", "20", "10", "Opp 1"])
ax.set_xlabel("Ball on (offense moving right)")
ax.set_ylabel("Points")
ax.set_title("First-and-10: what happened next, on average")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
plt.show()







Figure 6.1: The expected-points idea is an average. Dots: the actual average next score after first-and-10 (first-and-goal inside the 10) at each yard line, 2016-2025, in 5-yard bins. Line: nflverse’s model EP for the same plays. They agree almost everywhere; the model’s job is to smooth the noise and fill the gaps.





Read the chart from left to right as a drive moves downfield. Pinned at your own 1, the next score is slightly more likely to be the opponent’s: you will probably punt from your end zone and hand them good field position, and a safety is a real risk. By your own 25, for decades the spot after a kickoff touchback (it moved to the 30 in 2024 and the 35 in 2025),4 first-and-10 is worth about 1.1 points. Midfield is worth about 2.6; the opponent’s 20, the edge of the red zone, about 4.5; first-and-goal at the 1, about 6.3. These values come back at the end of the chapter as the anchors for keeping EPA in your head.






ImportantWhy it exists



Yards are not all worth the same. Ten yards from your own 5 to your own 15 mostly buys you room to punt; ten yards from the opponent’s 12 to the 2 nearly turns a field goal into a touchdown. Coaches always knew this (“field position”), but there was no common currency to compare a punt, a third-down conversion and an interception. Expected points provide one: every situation gets a point value, so every play can be scored by how much it changed that value.
