title: Expected Points, EPA, and Success Rate: The Model, the Noise, and the Broadcast Metrics
text:
Predict the play
The pictures use the course’s position letters: on offense X, Z and H are wide receivers, Y and U tight ends, F the fullback and T the tailback; on defense E is an end, T a tackle, N a nose tackle, S, M and W the strong-side, middle and weak-side linebackers, C a cornerback, $ the nickel back, D the dime back, and FS and SS the safeties.

from gridiron import Play, offense, defense, routes as r


def situation_diagram(off, dfn, los, to_go, title, lateral="auto", width_in=5.2, setup=None):
    """A pre-snap picture with the line to gain in yellow; `setup(p)` can add routes and notes."""
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=los, to_go=to_go, title=title)
    if setup:
        setup(p)
    p.draw(lateral=lateral, width_in=width_in)
    plt.show()







TipPredict the play



Third-and-9 at your own 30, second quarter, tie game. The offense comes out in an empty backfield with five receivers spread across the field; the defense answers with six defensive backs and two deep safeties. The quarterback completes a quick out to the left slot (H) for 7 yards, and the defender over him tackles him short of the line to gain. Before reading on: what is EP before the snap, roughly what is the EPA of that completion, and is it a success? Why would the defense want this throw?

def empty_setup(p):
    p.route("H", r.quick_out(8.5, 4))           # H starts 1.5 yds off the line: catch at +7
    p.dropback(1.0)
    p.pass_to("H", t=1.6)
    p.drop("DB", (7.0, -12.0))
    p.highlight("H", "DB")
    p.note("caught at +7", at=(3.5, -14.5))


off = offense("gun_empty")
dime = [q.moved(w=2.5) if q.key == "MIKE" else q for q in defense("dime", "two_high", off)]
situation_diagram(off, dime, los=40, to_go=9, title="3rd & 9, own 30",
                  lateral=(-19, 19), width_in=6.2, setup=empty_setup)







Figure 6.12: Third-and-9 at the offense’s own 30: empty backfield (five receivers) against a six-defensive-back dime look with two deep safeties. H runs a quick out and catches it 7 yards downfield; the dime back (D) rallies from his underneath zone to tackle him short of the yellow line to gain. Every receiver has a defender over him, and both safeties stay deep.











TipAnswer






before = neutral[(neutral.down == 3) & neutral.ydstogo.between(8, 10)
                 & neutral.yardline_100.between(65, 75)]
short = before[before.yards_gained.between(6, 8) & (before.yards_gained < before.ydstogo)]
print(f"Model EP, 3rd & 9 at own 30: {my_ep(3, 9, 70)[0]:+.2f}; "
      f"after, 4th & 2 at own 37: {my_ep(4, 2, 63)[0]:+.2f}")
print(f"Real plays: EP before (3rd & 8-10, own 25-35) {before.ep.mean():+.2f}; "
      f"EPA of 6-8 yard gains short of the sticks {short.epa.mean():+.2f} ({len(short):,} plays, "
      f"{(short.epa > 0).mean():.0%} positive)")

Model EP, 3rd & 9 at own 30: -0.17; after, 4th & 2 at own 37: -0.50
Real plays: EP before (3rd & 8-10, own 25-35) +0.06; EPA of 6-8 yard gains short of the sticks -0.44 (191 plays, 4% positive)


The situation is worth about zero before the snap (a little below on this chapter’s model, a little above on the real plays in that bucket): third-and-9 is converted well under half the time, and the likely result is a punt. The 7-yard out leaves fourth-and-2 at the 37, a situation where most teams still punt, so the play’s EPA is negative and it is not a success, even though it “gained 7.” (Many fourth-down models now rate going for it there as close to a toss-up; that is a win-probability question, and Win Probability and Decision Analysis takes it up. The EP model prices the punt that teams have usually chosen.) The handful of short gains with positive EPA are oddities, such as a defensive penalty tacked on after the catch.
The two-deep, six-DB shell is one sensible answer: it keeps everything in front and rallies to tackle short of the sticks, which is exactly what happened in the picture. It is the conservative choice. Against an empty backfield, defenses also like to bring a five-man pressure or play Cover 1 man, because the quarterback has no back to help protect; which one a team prefers is a tendency you can chart (Tendencies: PROE, Personnel, Motion, and Coverage). This is the most common “empty yards” play on any broadcast.











TipPredict the play



Second-and-1 at midfield, first quarter. The offense brings in two tight ends and a fullback and lines up under center in an I-formation; the defense answers with a base 4-3 front and rolls its strong safety down beside the tight end, eight men in the box. Which is the offense more likely to call? Is that the “wrong” call by EPA, and is the gap between running and passing here as large as on first-and-10?

def short_setup(p):
    p.highlight("SS")
    p.note("8th man", at=(8.5, 6.0))


off = offense("i_form_22")
base = [q.moved(d=5.0, w=-9.0) if q.key == "LCB" else q
        for q in defense("4-3_over", "single_high", off)]
situation_diagram(off, base, los=60, to_go=1, title="2nd & 1, midfield",
                  lateral=(-17, 17), setup=short_setup)







Figure 6.13: Second-and-1 at midfield: 22 personnel in an I-formation (two tight ends, fullback and tailback) against a base 4-3 Over front with the strong safety (highlighted) rolled down to the tight-end side: four linemen, three linebackers and the safety make eight in the box. The left corner sits outside the U tight end as the force player; one safety stays deep.











TipAnswer






s21 = neutral[(neutral.down == 2) & (neutral.ydstogo == 1)]
display(md_table(s21.groupby("kind").agg(plays=("epa", "size"), epa=("epa", "mean"),
                                         success=("success", "mean")).reset_index()))
t31 = neutral[(neutral.down == 3) & (neutral.ydstogo == 1) & neutral.season.between(2021, 2025)]
print(f"Third-and-1 converted {t31.first_down.mean():.0%} of the time (2021-2025, neutral)")
fpa = ftn_sn[["nflverse_game_id", "nflverse_play_id", "is_play_action"]]

      .merge(fpa, left_on=["game_id", "play_id"],
             right_on=["nflverse_game_id", "nflverse_play_id"]))

      f"(all dropbacks {pa.is_play_action.mean():.0%})")

Run is the likely call: teams run on roughly three out of four second-and-1 snaps, and heavy personnel makes it likelier still. Is it the wrong call? The table says dropbacks earn a little more, but apply this chapter’s own lesson before you believe it. Passes on second-and-1 are a selected group, often called because the defense has loaded the box, as in the picture above: in FTN’s charting (2022-2025) about 44% of them used play-action, against 27% of all dropbacks. Their edge is the edge of a counter-punch thrown at the right moment, not proof that passing should be the default, and it is a small fraction of the two-tenths of a point dropbacks earn on first-and-10.
Notice also how hard success is here: second-and-1 is already a good situation, so a run that merely moves the chains barely raises EP, and about half of all runs end with negative EPA. That is why coaches call this a “free” down: even if a shot downfield falls incomplete, third-and-1 still converts about 70% of the time. So the prediction is “run,” and the moment to watch for is the play-action shot that the run makes possible (Constraint Theory and Sequencing).











TipPredict the play



First-and-goal at the 1. The offense is in a jumbo goal-line set; the defense has everyone within a couple of yards of the line. Three possible outcomes: (a) a 1-yard touchdown run, (b) the back is stuffed for no gain, (c) the back fumbles and the defense recovers in the end zone for a touchback. Rank them by EPA, and guess how large each is.

off = [q.moved(label="H") if q.key == "W" else q for q in offense("goal_line")]
goal_d = []
for q in defense("46", "zero", off):
    if q.pos == "CB":
        q = q.moved(d=2.0, w=np.sign(q.w) * 8.5)
    elif q.key == "MIKE":                            # second level: 1-2 yards deep in the
        q = q.moved(d=2.3)                           # end zone, ready to fill downhill
    elif q.key == "SS":
        q = q.moved(d=2.3, w=-3.5)
    elif q.key == "FS":
        q = q.moved(d=3.0, w=0.0)
    goal_d.append(q)
situation_diagram(off, goal_d, los=109, to_go=1,
                  title="1st & goal at the 1", lateral=(-11, 11), width_in=6.0)







Figure 6.14: First-and-goal at the 1: a goal-line formation (three tight ends, with the wing labelled H, plus fullback and tailback) against a 46-style goal-line defense: six men on the line, both outside linebackers set to the tight-end side, and the middle linebacker, safeties and corners all within about two yards of the goal line, ready to fill downhill. The line to gain is the goal line.











TipAnswer






ep_goal = my_ep(1, 1, 1)[0]
ep_2nd = my_ep(2, 1, 1)[0]
ep_opp_tb = my_ep(1, 10, 80)[0]      # opponent's ball on their own 20 after the touchback
print(f"EP before: {ep_goal:+.2f}")
print(f"(a) TD:      EPA = 7 - {ep_goal:.2f} = {7 - ep_goal:+.2f}")
print(f"(b) stuffed: EPA = {ep_2nd:.2f} - {ep_goal:.2f} = {ep_2nd - ep_goal:+.2f}")
print(f"(c) fumble:  EPA = -{ep_opp_tb:.2f} - {ep_goal:.2f} = {-ep_opp_tb - ep_goal:+.2f}")

EP before: +6.42
(a) TD:      EPA = 7 - 6.42 = +0.58
(b) stuffed: EPA = 5.91 - 6.42 = -0.51
(c) fumble:  EPA = -0.79 - 6.42 = -7.21


The touchdown earns surprisingly little, because first-and-goal at the 1 already “owns” most of a touchdown. The stuff costs about as much as the touchdown gains: second-and-goal at the 1 is still an excellent situation. The fumble is a disaster of a different order: the offense throws away more than six expected points and hands the opponent the ball at their 20, a swing of about seven. (The ball goes to the 20 because a touchback after a turnover is still spotted there; only kickoff touchbacks moved to the 30 and then the 35.) It is the clearest example of why ball security on the goal line matters more than an extra half-yard of push, and why one goal-line fumble can erase a short-yardage back’s whole season of EPA.

title: Expected Points, EPA, and Success Rate: The Model, the Noise, and the Broadcast Metrics
text:
Takeaways

Expected points is a probability model for the next score: seven possible outcomes, each with a probability that depends on down, distance, field position and the clock. You can fit a decent one in thirty lines of NumPy; nflverse’s model adds time, timeouts, venue and era. It values situations for an average team, which is what lets EPA measure the difference.
EPA is EP after minus EP before, with scores counted as points and changes of possession flipped. In your head: about 0.06 a yard, a growing cost for each lost down, and a little for each yard of distance. It beats yards because it prices context, sacks and turnovers in one unit, though its predictive edge over simpler stats is smaller than its descriptive one, and it ignores the score.
Run-versus-pass averages are riddled with selection effects. Hold the situation fixed and dropbacks still out-earn runs on early downs and third-and-long, while in short yardage the gap closes and runs succeed more often, partly thanks to the quarterback sneak.
Respect the noise. A play’s EPA varies by about 1.4 points; a game is a small sample; several games pass before signal matches noise. Offense repeats better than defense, success rate about as well as EPA, and fumble recovery not at all. Adjust for opponents when schedules are lopsided.
For players, separate what they were given from what they added: CPOE for quarterbacks’ accuracy, RYOE for runners, and a skeptical eye on interceptions, which carry real luck.
Place every broadcast metric on the map: what it credits, whether it is open, and how much modelling or judgement sits inside it. Passer rating and ANY/A are open but blind to context; QBR, DVOA, PFF grades and ESPN win rates add context or isolate players at the cost of being proprietary.

Connections
Builds on: the EPA primer in Downs, Distance, and Field Position and the data skills in Working with nflverse Data in Python. CPOE is introduced in Quarterback Play, pass rush win rate in The Pass Rush.

Win Probability and Decision Analysis: the score-aware cousin of EP, and the fourth-down and two-point decisions built on both.
Tendencies: PROE, Personnel, Motion, and Coverage: expected pass rate, the same “over expected” idea applied to play-calling.
Tracking Data and the Big Data Bowl: the tracking frames behind RYOE and the win rates.
Building a Roster: positional value, and why stability numbers like these shape what teams pay for.
Appendix G, the Metrics and Data Atlas, gives each metric in this chapter a one-card summary.

If you want to go deeper: Ben Baldwin’s write-up of the nflfastR expected-points, win-probability and completion-probability models on Open Source Football;25 Yurko, Ventura and Horowitz’s nflWAR paper;26 The Hidden Game of Football by Carroll, Palmer and Thorn for the history; and the public method notes from FTN (DVOA), ESPN (QBR and win rates) and PFF (grading) before trusting any of their numbers.

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text: Every term is defined where the course first teaches it. This page collects those definitions. Use the search box (top left) or your browser’s find for quick lookups, and follow the chapter link for the full picture.

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
3x1 check (solo / stubbie)

A pre-planned adjustment of a two-high coverage to a 3x1 (trips) formation. In one common version of Solo the backside corner plays the lone receiver by himself and a linebacker takes #3 deep, freeing the backside safety; in Stubbie four defenders handle the three trips receivers and the backside safety stays home with the corner. Names and details vary by staff (some playbooks use ‘Solo’ for what this book calls poach). Taught in Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage.

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
A

Adjusted net yards per attempt

See ANY/A.

Aiming point

The spot a running back’s first steps point at on a designed run, such as the play-side guard’s outside hip on inside zone or the tight end’s outside leg on outside zone. Taught in Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback.

Analytics staff

Staff who turn data into decisions. On game day, a game-management specialist advises the head coach on fourth downs, two-point tries, timeouts and challenges. Taught in What a Play Really Is.

ANY/A

Adjusted net yards per attempt: passing yards plus 20 per touchdown pass, minus 45 per interception and minus yards lost on sacks, divided by pass attempts plus sacks. Taught in Expected Points, EPA, and Success Rate: The Model, the Noise, and the Broadcast Metrics.

Arc block

A tight end or H-back’s release around the outside of an unblocked end to block the next defender out (an overhang or safety), usually paired with a quarterback read. Taught in Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback.

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
B

Backside cut-off

The job of the linemen away from the play on a zone run: get in front of the defenders on their side so those defenders cannot chase the play from behind. Taught in Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback.

Bang-bend-bounce

The zone runner’s three choices after pressing the aiming point: hit the designed gap (bang), cut back against the flow behind the blocks (bend), or take it outside (bounce). Taught in Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback.

Bash

Short for ‘back away’: a zone tag in which the running back runs away from the line’s zone flow while the quarterback reads the end man and can keep the ball on the inside-zone track. Taught in Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback.

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
C

Call sheet

The play-caller’s game-day menu: that week’s plays sorted by situation (down and distance, field zone, clock) on one or two laminated pages. Taught in What a Play Really Is.

Cover 7 (match family)

A label whose meaning depends on the staff. In Nick Saban’s vocabulary it names a split-field, quarters-based pattern-match family built from a separate call for each side; other teams use ‘Cover 7’ for different coverages. Taught in Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage.

Cut block

A legal block aimed at a defender’s thighs or below, from the front, to put him on the ground; restricted by rule to protect knees and banned when combined with a high block (a chop block). Taught in Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback.

Cutback

A ball carrier’s cut against the flow of the play, back toward the side the line stepped away from, into a lane created by defenders over-running the play. Taught in Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback.

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
D

DC

See Defensive coordinator.

Defensive coordinator

The assistant in charge of the defense’s game plan. Usually, but not always, the defense’s play-caller. Taught in What a Play Really Is.

Delay of game

A five-yard penalty, almost always on the offense, for not snapping the ball before the play clock reaches zero. Taught in What a Play Really Is.

Disguise

Lining up in a way that hides or misrepresents the coverage (or pressure) the defense will actually play, so the quarterback’s pre-snap read is wrong or useless. Taught in Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage.

DVOA

Defense-adjusted Value Over Average: a proprietary efficiency rating created by Aaron Schatz at Football Outsiders (now published by FTN) that scores every play against a league baseline for its situation and adjusts for the opponent; 0% is average. Taught in Expected Points, EPA, and Success Rate: The Model, the Noise, and the Broadcast Metrics.

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
E

Explosive play rate

The share of a team’s plays that gain a big chunk. Coaching staffs often count runs of 12+ yards and passes of 16+; analysts often use 10+ and 20+ (definitions vary by source). Taught in Expected Points, EPA, and Success Rate: The Model, the Noise, and the Broadcast Metrics.

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
G

Game-management staff

See Analytics staff.

Green dot

The green sticker on the back of a helmet that has the radio speaker, and by extension the player wearing it. Only one such player per team may be on the field at a time. Taught in What a Play Really Is.

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
H

Head coach

The person in charge of the whole team and staff. On game day he makes the big decisions (fourth downs, challenges, timeouts) and sometimes calls the offense’s or defense’s plays as well. Taught in What a Play Really Is.

Helmet radio

The one-way speaker in one offensive player’s and one defensive player’s helmet that lets a coach talk to him between plays. It cuts off with 15 seconds left on the play clock or at the snap. Taught in What a Play Really Is.

Huddle

The brief circle, usually seven to ten yards behind the ball, in which the quarterback (or the green-dot defender) repeats the play call to his teammates before they line up. Taught in What a Play Really Is.

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
I

Insert (zone insert)

A zone tag in which a fullback, H-back or tight end leads up through a gap to block a linebacker, adding a blocker at the point of attack. Taught in Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback.

Inside zone

A zone run aimed at the play-side guard or B gap, in which double teams drive the defensive linemen back and the running back reads for a crease, often cutting back. Taught in Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback.

Install

Teaching a set of plays to the players through meetings, walk-throughs and practice. Also the set of plays taught in one session (‘the third-down install’). Taught in What a Play Really Is.

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
L

Late rotation

A rotation timed to start at the snap or just after it, not during the cadence, so the quarterback gets no clean look at the real coverage before the play begins. Taught in Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage.

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
N

No-huddle

Lining up without a huddle and getting the call to players at the line by words, hand signals, boards or wristbands. Used to play fast, to see the defense before the call is final, or to stop the defense from changing players. Taught in What a Play Really Is.

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
O

OC

See Offensive coordinator.

Offensive coordinator

The assistant in charge of the offense’s game plan. Often, but not always, the offense’s play-caller. Taught in What a Play Really Is.

One-cut runner

A running back who presses the aiming point, makes a single decisive cut and goes straight upfield, rather than dancing or bouncing around in the backfield. Taught in Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback.

Opponent adjustment

Correcting a team’s or player’s numbers for the strength of the opponents faced, so that a good day against a strong defense counts for more than the same day against a weak one. Taught in Expected Points, EPA, and Success Rate: The Model, the Noise, and the Broadcast Metrics.

Outside zone

A zone run aimed at or just outside the tight end, in which the line steps laterally to get the defense running sideways and the back makes one cut into the first crease. Taught in Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback.

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
P

Passer rating

The NFL’s official passing formula since 1973: completion rate, yards per attempt, touchdown rate and interception rate, each capped and combined onto a scale from 0 to 158.3. Taught in Expected Points, EPA, and Success Rate: The Model, the Noise, and the Broadcast Metrics.

PFF grade

Pro Football Focus’s proprietary player grade: analysts watch every snap, score each player’s performance on it, and scale the season’s scores to 0-100. Taught in Expected Points, EPA, and Success Rate: The Model, the Noise, and the Broadcast Metrics.

Play call

The instruction a team uses for one snap: usually a string of code words naming the formation, any motion, the protection and the play itself. Taught in What a Play Really Is.

Play-caller

The one coach who actually chooses each play during the game and sends it in. Can be the head coach or a coordinator. Taught in What a Play Really Is.

Playbook

The full catalog of a team’s plays and the rules for running them. Each week’s game plan is chosen from it. Taught in What a Play Really Is.

Poach

A check against a 3x1 formation in which the backside safety leaves the lone receiver to his cornerback and works across the field to take the trips side’s inside receiver (#3) if he goes deep. Taught in Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage.

Position coach

An assistant who teaches one position group (quarterbacks, offensive line, linebackers and so on) its technique and assignments. Taught in What a Play Really Is.

Post-snap rotation

Defenders, usually the safeties, moving at or just after the snap from the shell they showed into a different one: two-high into one-high, or one-high into two-high. Taught in Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage.

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
Q

QBR

ESPN’s proprietary quarterback rating (0 to 100, with 50 about average), built on expected points and win probability and crediting the quarterback’s share of every play, including runs, sacks and penalties. Taught in Expected Points, EPA, and Success Rate: The Model, the Noise, and the Broadcast Metrics.

QC coach

See Quality control coach.

Quality control coach

An entry-level assistant who breaks down film and data into scouting reports and tendency lists for the coordinators. Taught in What a Play Really Is.

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
R

Reach-and-overtake

A two-man outside-zone block: the play-side lineman of the pair gets his hands on a defender to stop him running wide, his neighbor races flat to take the defender over, and the first lineman climbs to a linebacker. Taught in Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback.

Read (post-snap)

A decision a player makes after the snap by watching one particular defender or area: ‘if he does this, I do that.’ Taught in What a Play Really Is.

RSWR

See Run stop win rate.

Run stop win rate

ESPN’s tracking-based rate of how often a defender beats his block quickly on run plays; the run-defense companion to pass rush win rate. Taught in Expected Points, EPA, and Success Rate: The Model, the Noise, and the Broadcast Metrics.

Rush yards over expected

See RYOE.

RYOE

Rush yards over expected: a runner’s actual rushing yards minus the yards a tracking-data model expected from where the blockers and defenders were when he took the handoff. Taught in Expected Points, EPA, and Success Rate: The Model, the Noise, and the Broadcast Metrics.

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
S

Snap

The center’s handing or tossing of the ball back between his legs to the quarterback (or another back). It starts every play from scrimmage. Taught in What a Play Really Is.

Solo

See 3x1 check (solo / stubbie).

Special teams coordinator

The assistant in charge of the kicking game: kickoffs, punts, field goals, and the units that return and cover them. Taught in What a Play Really Is.

Split zone

Inside zone with a tight end or H-back crossing behind the line to kick out the backside end, who would otherwise be left unblocked. Taught in Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback.

Split-field coverage

Playing a different coverage on each half of the field (for example quarters to the wide side and Cover 2 to the short side), with each half following its own rules for the receivers on its side. Taught in Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage.

Stretch

The widest zone track, aimed outside the tight end toward the sideline, whose first intent is to get the edge; in some playbooks simply another name for outside zone. Taught in Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback.

Stubbie

See 3x1 check (solo / stubbie).

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
T

Tag

A word added to a play call that changes one player’s job (for example, one receiver’s route) and leaves the rest of the play alone. Taught in What a Play Really Is.

Terminology

See Verbiage.

Total QBR

See QBR.

Turnover luck (fumble-recovery rate)

The part of a team’s turnover record that is chance rather than skill, clearest in fumble recoveries: who falls on a loose ball is close to a coin flip, so a team’s recovery rate swings at random from year to year. Taught in Expected Points, EPA, and Success Rate: The Model, the Noise, and the Broadcast Metrics.

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
V

Verbiage

A team’s play-calling language: the words it uses for formations, motions, protections and plays. Taught in What a Play Really Is.

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
W

Wide zone

See Outside zone.

Wristband

A small play card worn on the wrist, with plays listed by number, so a short code can stand in for a long call. Taught in What a Play Really Is.

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
Y

Year-over-year stability

How well a statistic in one season predicts the same statistic for the same team or player the next season, usually measured as a correlation; high stability points to skill, low stability to noise or changed circumstances. Taught in Expected Points, EPA, and Success Rate: The Model, the Noise, and the Broadcast Metrics.

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
Z

Zone blocking

A blocking scheme in which every lineman steps the same direction and blocks whoever enters his area, rather than a defender named before the snap. Taught in Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback.
